en: Now begins the third chapter.
In the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, titled "The Means" (Sādhana), there is the reflection on the consideration of going and returning and the determination of dispassion (vairāgya).
Immediately following that is the section concerning the attainment [of the self] after death (tadanantara-pratipatti-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 1–7.
In the interval between [death and rebirth], he departs enveloped [by subtle elements], as established by the questions and the explanations.
In the second chapter, the contradiction with Smṛti and reasoning regarding the realization of Brahman ordained in the Vedānta has been refuted,
and the lack of authority of rival doctrines has been elaborated.
The contradiction with the scriptures has also been resolved.
In that context, it was stated that the principles distinct from the individual soul (jīva), which serve as its instruments, are born from Brahman.

Now, therefore, [the following will be explained]: the manner of the individual soul’s journey through transmigratory existence when conditioned by those instruments, its various states, and the true nature of Brahman.

The distinctions and non-distinctions of knowledge, the inclusion and non-inclusion of qualities, the attainment of the human goal through perfect realization, the various methods for attaining perfect realization,

and the lack of restriction regarding the fruit of liberation— this collection of topics will be examined in the third chapter, along with whatever else arises incidentally. Therein, in the first section (pāda), the various paths of transmigratory existence will be demonstrated by means of the Pañcāgni-vidyā (the knowledge of the five fires) for the purpose of generating dispassion.
And because of the hearing [of this] at the end: "Therefore, one should feel aversion.

It is understood that the individual soul (jīva), accompanied by the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), the senses, and the mind, and taking hold of ignorance (avidyā), karma, and past impressions (pūrvaprajñā), leaves its former body and attains another body—according to such passages as, "Then these vital breaths gather around him," and "He fashions for himself another, newer, more beautiful form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1.4).
From this word occurring at the end of the section concerning transmigratory existence,
and because the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit is possible,
it is now considered whether that soul goes forth unenveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as seeds for a new body, or rather, enveloped by them.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
That [the self] is not enveloped. Why? Because, unlike the case of the appropriation of the instruments of action, the appropriation of the primary elements (bhūta) is not mentioned in scripture.
For here, in the passage "Taking up these particles of light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1), the term "particles of light" (tejomātrā) is used to denote the appropriation of the sense organs,
because the eyes and other organs are mentioned in the subsequent portion of the text.
There is no such mention of the appropriation of the mere elements (*bhūtamātra*). Furthermore, the mere elements are easily available everywhere;
since they exist right where the body is to be formed, their being led [to that place] would be purposeless.
Therefore, [the opponent argues] that it departs unenveloped.

To this position, the Teacher reads: "In the transition to another state, it moves enveloped. This means that in the transition to another state—that is, in the attainment of another body—it must be understood that it moves, or goes, enveloped by the subtle elements which constitute the seed of the body.
Why? Because of the question and the exposition. To explain: the question is, "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).

And the exposition is the answer, which describes [the process] through five fires—namely, those of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman—in which faith, soma, rain, food, and semen take the form of the oblations.

Having shown the five oblations with the words, "But at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.1), it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) departs, moving along, enveloped by water. Now, does not another scriptural text show that [the soul] does not leave the previous body until it has taken hold of another body, like a leech? It says: "Just as a caterpillar on a blade of grass... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3).

In that case as well, there is no contradiction, for the simile of the leech refers merely to the lengthening of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) regarding the body to be attained— which is presented by karma— belonging to the soul (*jīva*) while it is still unenveloped.

Such being the manner of attaining another body as declared by scripture, those conceptualizations arising from human intellect which hold that the all-pervading organs and the self acquire their functional activity in another body through the influence of karma are [rendered untenable].
There, the manifestation of activity belongs to the self alone in its absolute state.
The sense organs, however, arise as entirely new entities in each respective place of experience, just like the body;
or rather, it is the mind alone that establishes itself in the place of experience.

"The individual soul (jīva) itself, having leaped out from one body, attains another body, just as a parrot [flies] from one tree to another"—all such [views] are to be disregarded because they contradict the Śruti. // 1 // [FN: The means for realization are renunciation and so forth.]
The refutation of the body as the self follows as a consequence.
The meditation on the five—namely, the sky, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman—as fires is the "Knowledge of the Five Fires" (pañcāgnividyā).
Karma is that which is termed merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).
"Prior wisdom" (*pūrvaprajñā*) refers to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births.
"The prolongation of cultivation" (*bhāvanāyā dīrghībhāvaḥ*) means having as its object a future body.
"Alone" (*kevala*) refers to the conceptualization of the Sugata.
"Mind" (manas) is the conception of the Vaiśeṣikas; "living soul" (jīva) is the conception of the Digambaras;
and the conception of the Lokāyatas is included by the mention of "and so forth."
Surely, from the question and answer cited above, it follows that [the soul] proceeds enveloped by water alone,
because of the force of hearing the word "water" (apaḥ).
In that case, how can it be asserted in general that [the soul] proceeds enveloped by the subtle elements of all [the gross elements]?
To this, he recites the following: "But because it consists of three natures and because of its predominance. (BBs 3.1.2) By the word "but" (tu), he cuts off the doubt that has been raised.
For water consists of three components, according to the scriptural teaching on the tripartite transformation (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).
When those [waters] are accepted as the constituent cause, the other two elements must necessarily also be accepted.
Furthermore, the body consists of three components, because the effects of all three—fire, water, and food—are perceived therein.

Furthermore, it consists of three components because of the threefold nature of the elements, namely wind, bile, and phlegm. It is not possible for it to be produced by water alone, setting aside the other primary elements.
Therefore, this statement "water, having assumed human form" is made with regard to the predominance [of the water element].
In both the question and the answer, the word "water" (ap) does not refer to water alone.
For in all bodies, an abundance of liquid substances such as plasma and blood is observed.
[Objection: But is it not the case that the earth-element (pārthiva-dhātu) is perceived as predominant in bodies?
This is not a fault;
for even in comparison with the other [elements], there will be an abundance of water.
Furthermore, it is observed that even in the seed of the body, characterized by semen and blood, there is an abundance of fluid.
And karma is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) for the commencement of another body.
Furthermore, rites such as the Agnihotra depend upon liquid substances like Soma, clarified butter, and milk.
And it will be stated that the waters, which are inherent in the action and denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā), are offered together with those actions into the fire called the heavenly world.

Therefore, the abundance of water is well-established; and because of this abundance, it is faultless to conclude that by the word "water" (āpaḥ), all the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) which are the seeds of the body are intended. // 2 //
And because of the departure of the vital breaths.

Furthermore, the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon the attainment of another body is heard in such scriptural passages as: "When he departs, the vital breath departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

And since that movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is not possible without a substratum, it is understood that their movement—driven by the movement of the prāṇas—is also the movement of the other elements that serve as their substratum when they are joined with those [elements], even though those elements are otherwise devoid of motion.
For the prāṇas, being without a substratum, never move or remain anywhere, as is observed in the case of a living being. // 3 //
"If it be argued that [the vital breaths do not depart] because of the scriptural statement regarding their going to fire and so forth, we say no, because that is figurative.
It might be thus:
the vital breaths do not indeed depart along with the living self at the time of attaining another body, because of the scriptural statement regarding their going to fire and so forth.

For indeed, scripture shows that at the time of death the vital breaths, such as speech and the rest, go to the gods, such as Agni and the rest, in passages beginning with: "When the speech of this dead person goes into fire, the breath into wind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).
If this is argued, we say no, because [the passage] is figurative.
The scriptural statement regarding the transition of speech and the other organs into fire and the other elements is figurative, because it is not observed in the case of the hair;
for it is recorded there: "The plants [become] the body-hair, and the trees the hair of the head" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

For it is not possible that the body hairs and head hairs leap up and go toward the herbs and trees; nor is movement conceivable for the soul if the limiting adjunct of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is discarded;
nor is experience in another body tenable without the vital breaths.
Moreover, the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) along with the individual soul (jīva) to another place has been clearly proclaimed in the Śruti.

Therefore, with regard to the deities such as Agni who preside over speech and the other organs and assist them, it is merely on account of the cessation of their assistance at the time of death that it is figuratively stated that "speech and the others go to Agni and the others."
FN: [This refers to passages] such as "when he departs from there" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
If it is argued that [the soul does not depart] because it is not heard of in the first [case], we say no; for those very [channels] are indeed appropriate. BBs 3.1.5.
This might be so.
But how, again, can this be determined— that "in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3)—
when there is no mention of water at all in the first fire?
For here, the five fires beginning with the heavenly world are taught as the recipients of the five oblations;
and concerning them, after beginning with "That world indeed, O Gautama, is the fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1), it continues: "In that very fire, the gods offer faith" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2).
Thus, faith has been declared as the substance for the oblation (*haumya-dravya*);
water is not heard of there as being the substance for the oblation.
Even if one were to postulate that water is the substance for the oblation in the four subsequent fires beginning with Parjanya, let it indeed be so postulated.
For it is logical that Soma and the other substances intended for oblation in those [subsequent fires] consist largely of water;
however, to abandon *śraddhā* (faith), which is explicitly heard in the context of the first fire, and instead postulate unmentioned waters is sheer audacity.
Furthermore, by the force of common usage, *śraddhā* is well known to be a specific kind of mental conviction (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*).
If it is argued that, for this reason, it is illogical for water to attain the state of a person during the fifth oblation,
this is not a fault; because even there, in the first fire, those very waters are intended by the word "faith" (śraddhā).
Why? Because of its logical consistency (*upapatti*).
For in this way, by connecting the beginning, middle, and end, this constitutes a single coherent statement that is free from confusion.
Otherwise, however, when the manner in which water comes to be called "man" at the fifth oblation has been asked, and the occasion for the reply arrives—

If water were not the sacrificial substance (haumya-dravya) at the location of the first oblation, then the introduction of "faith" (śraddhā) by name would be inconsistent; for in that case, the question and the answer would not form a coherent unity.
Furthermore, by concluding with the statement, "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man,'" the text demonstrates this very point.
Furthermore, the effects of faith, such as the moon and rain, are observed to consist largely of gross water;
this is the reasoning for faith being of the nature of water,
for an effect conforms to its cause.

Furthermore, the quality called faith (śraddhā), which is a property of the mind or the individual soul (jīva), cannot be extracted from its substrate for the purpose of being offered, in the manner that the heart and other organs are extracted from the sacrificial animal; therefore, the waters themselves must be what is denoted by the word "faith.
Moreover, the term "faith" is appropriately applied to water.
This is because we observe such usage in the Veda, namely: "The waters, indeed, are faith" (*śraddhā vā āpaḥ*).
Since the waters, which constitute the seed of the body, attain a state of subtlety that resembles the nature of faith, they may be designated by the word "faith.
This is just as a man who possesses the prowess of a lion is called a "lion."
Furthermore, the term "faith" (śraddhā) is appropriately applied to water because of its association with actions preceded by faith, just as the word "bed" (mañca) is applied to the people on it.

Moreover, the application of the term "faith" is justified because water is the cause of faith, according to the Vedic scripture: "For him, the waters bow down toward faith for the sake of meritorious action. // 5 //
FN: In such passages as "saṃgānaṃ tam utkrāmantaṃ," etc., *anapaḥ* means "not [losing] water" or "from another source";
*asmai* refers to this sacrificer.
"They bend down and bring them forth.

If it is argued that this is not so because [the performers of sacrifices] are not mentioned, we say no, because those who perform the *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrifices and works of public utility) are understood [from the context].
Furthermore, it may be that by means of the two replies, it is understood that water, through the sequence beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), attains the form of a person in the fifth oblation.
But the souls do not depart enveloped by those [waters],
because that is not heard in scripture;
for here there is no word that makes known the souls in the same way as it does the waters.
If it is argued that, therefore, the statement "he goes enveloped" is incorrect, this is not a fault. Why?
Because those who perform sacrifices and other rites are recognized [as the subject].

Having begun with, "Now, those who here in the village meditate upon sacrifice and works of public utility as 'gifts,' they pass into smoke" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6), the text describes the attainment of the moon by those performers of sacrifices via the path of the fathers beginning with smoke: "From space [they go] to the moon; that is King Soma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.4).
These very same persons are recognized here as well: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation, King Soma arises" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2).
This is because of the commonality of the scriptural texts.

Furthermore, for those [sacrificers], the substances such as curd and milk used as means for the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites, being composed mostly of liquid, are directly perceived as water.
When these are offered into the Āhavanīya fire, they become subtle oblations in the form of *apūrva* (unseen potential), and it is these that the performers of sacrifices like the *iṣṭi* resort to.
And at their funeral pyre, the officiating priests offer their bodies into the final fire according to the prescribed rite, saying: "This one [is offered] to the heavenly world, svāhā!

Thereupon, those waters—which are associated with the ritual acts preceded by faith, which consist of the oblations, and which exist in the form of the *apūrva*—envelop the souls of those who perform sacrifices and the like, and lead them to that world for the bestowal of results; this is what is expressed here by the term "offering" (*juhoti*). "Faith... [and so forth].
Thus it is said: "They offer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.9).

Likewise, in the Agnihotra, by means of the supplementary passage consisting of the explanation of the six questions—beginning with "These two oblations, once offered, depart"—the attainment of another world for the commencement of the fruit of the Agnihotra oblations is demonstrated.

Therefore, it follows that the individual souls (jīvas), enveloped by the waters consisting of the oblations, hasten toward the enjoyment of the fruits of their own karma. [This is the meaning of the mantra: "By means of the funeral rite known as *naidhana*, may this one go to heaven."
But how is this departure of those who perform sacrifices and works of merit for the sake of enjoying the fruits of their own actions asserted?

For [the scripture] shows that when they have ascended to the moon by way of the path characterized by smoke, they become food: "This is King Soma; that is the food of the gods; the gods eat it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad); and "Having reached the moon, they become food; there the gods eat them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, 'Increase! Decrease!'—in this same manner they eat them there" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16).
And there is another scriptural passage with the same subject matter.
Furthermore, enjoyment is not possible for those being devoured by the gods, just as it is not for those being devoured by tigers and the like. Therefore, he recites the following reply:
"Or [it is] figurative because they do not know the Self; for thus the scripture shows.
The word "or" (vā) is intended to set aside the previously raised objection.
Their status as food is figurative, not primary.

For if food were the primary meaning, then injunctions regarding qualification such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" would be rendered consistent. Moreover, if there were no enjoyment for those who perform sacrifices and other rites upon the lunar orb, why would qualified persons undertake actions involving great effort, such as sacrifices?
Furthermore, the word "food" (anna) is seen to be used metaphorically even for things that are not literal food, based on the commonality of being a cause of enjoyment.
Just as the subjects are the food of kings and cattle are the food of the subjects,

so too, the "eating" intended for the gods is their dwelling in happiness with those who have performed sacrifices and other rites— who have entered into a subordinate status like beloved wives, sons, friends, and servants— and not the chewing or swallowing [of them] like sweetmeats and the like.

Furthermore, the passage, "The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.1), precludes any activity such as chewing on the part of the gods.
And for those performers of rites who have attained a subordinate status toward the gods, enjoyment is still possible, just as it is for the attendants who live off a king.
Furthermore, because they do not know the Self, it is logical that those who perform rites for the sake of rewards attain a state of being enjoyed by the gods.

For scripture shows that those who do not know the Self are objects of enjoyment for the gods: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like an animal to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).

And even in this world, while being gratified by rituals such as sacrifices, he serves the gods like a beast; thus it is understood that, subsisting upon them and enjoying the fruits prescribed by them, he serves the gods like a beast.

There is another explanation for the phrase "because they do not know the Self, for [the text] shows so": for these performers of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta* are merely performers of ritual acts (*kevalakarmī*), not practitioners of the combined performance of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*).

Here, the "knowledge of the five fires" (*pañcāgnividyā*) is figuratively termed "knowledge of the Self" (*ātmavidyā*) due to the context. And because these performers of sacrifices lack the knowledge of the five fires, their status as food is presented here by way of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) in order to extol the knowledge of the five fires.
For it is the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) that is intended to be taught here, as determined by the purport of the passage.
Thus, another scriptural text shows the existence of enjoyment in the lunar orb: "Having experienced greatness in the world of Soma, he returns again" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.4).

Likewise, another scriptural passage also shows the attainment of enjoyment by those who perform sacrifices and the like while dwelling with the gods: "Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the fathers who have conquered their worlds is equal to one bliss of the gods by action—those who attain godhood through their ritual acts" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.33).

Thus, because the statement regarding their becoming food is figurative, it is understood that the individual souls of those who perform sacrifices and the like enter here [into the body of the eater].
Therefore, it is rightly said that [the soul] ascends enveloped. [Note:
*Adhikāra* means that by which a person is qualified or connected with an injunction; it refers to the desire for results.
Just as an animal is an object of enjoyment, so too the ignorant one—not one possessing the cognition of difference—is an object of enjoyment for the gods.]
2. The Section Concerning the Expiation of What Has Been Done (Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 8–11. Sūtra 8:
"Upon the exhaustion of what has been done, [the soul] returns with a remainder, according to what was seen and what is remembered; as it went, and not so.
For those who perform sacrifices and other rites, having ascended to the lunar orb by the path of smoke and so forth, and having experienced their enjoyment there, from that point...

The descent is recorded in the scripture, beginning with: "Having dwelt there as long as their [meritorious] residue lasts, they then return again by this very same path to this world" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5), up until: "Those of pleasant conduct attain the womb of a Brāhmaṇa or other [high castes], while those of foul conduct attain the womb of a dog or other [low castes]."

In this regard, the following is investigated: Do those who have experienced their entire karma descend without residual proclivities (*niranuśaya*), or rather with residual proclivities (*sānuśaya*)?
What, then, is the initial position?
That they descend without residual proclivities.
Why? Because of the qualification "until the falling away" (*yāvat-sampātam*).

Here, by the word *sampāta*, the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is meant—so called because "by means of this [deposit], one falls from this world to that world for the sake of experiencing the fruits.
Furthermore, the phrase "having dwelt until the falling away" shows that the entirety of that performed [karma] is exhausted right there.
And by another scriptural passage, "When that [knowledge] of theirs reaches its consummation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16), this very same meaning is demonstrated.
This might be so.
"I shall imagine that one enjoys only so much karma as is to be experienced in that world"—
it is not possible to imagine it thus, except by way of a comprehensive reflection on whatever one does here;
for that karma reaches its end through whatever this person performs here.

For another scriptural passage states: "From that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). By referring to "whatever [he has done]" without distinction, it shows the exhaustion of all karma performed here in that world.
Moreover, death is the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet begun.
Because manifestation is impossible for that which is obstructed by karma whose fruit has already begun prior to death;
and since there is no distinction, that [death] manifests all that is yet to have its fruit begun.
For when the cause is common, the effect cannot be uncommon.
For it is not tenable that when the proximity of a lamp is equal for all, a jar alone is manifested and not a cloth.
Therefore, when it has been argued that those who descend do so without residual karma (*niranuśaya*), we reply: "Upon the exhaustion of what was performed, one possesses residual karma.
By whatever mass of karma they ascended to the moon for the enjoyment of its fruits, when that [karma] is exhausted through such enjoyment, their [descent occurs].

When this body, composed of earth, was begun for the sake of experience in the moon, it is—as if through contact with the fire of grief at seeing the exhaustion of that experience—like the solidification of clarified butter.

Therefore, when the "end of what has been done" occurs—that is, when the performed karma such as sacrifices and the like is exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit—they descend to this world still accompanied by their residual karma (*sānuśaya*).
For what reason?
He says, "By perception and scripture.

For thus, direct scriptural revelation (*śruti*) shows the descent of those accompanied by residual karma (*sānuśaya*): "Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant, it is likely that they will attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya."
Or else, "those who perform foul deeds here, they quickly fall into a foul womb— either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig,
or the womb of a Caṇḍāla" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7). He will explain that by the word *caraṇa* (conduct), *anuśaya* (residual karma) is indicated.
Moreover, this experience of enjoyment, consisting of various high and low forms, is observed from birth itself as being distributed [among individuals].
Since it is impossible for this to be accidental, it indicates the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
because the scriptures generally establish that prosperity and misfortune have good and evil deeds as their causes.

Smṛti also shows that the descent occurs only for those with residual karma (sānuśaya), stating: "The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after dying and experiencing the fruit of their actions, then—by means of the remainder—obtain birth distinguished by place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, happiness, and intelligence. But what, then, is this so-called "residual karma" (anuśaya)?

Some, first of all, say: "There is a certain remainder of karma performed for the sake of heaven, once its fruit has been experienced, called *anuśaya* (latent tendency), like the oil adhering to a vessel.
For just as a vessel of oil, even when being emptied, is not emptied in its entirety, but some residue of oil remains adhering to the vessel, so too is the *anuśaya*.
[Objection: But surely, because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is by nature opposed to its effect, it is not logical for a remainder to persist once the fruit has been experienced.
This is not a fault;
for we do not maintain that the fruit of karma has been fully experienced in its entirety.
[Objection: But did he not ascend to the lunar orb for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma without remainder?
"Certainly. Nevertheless, because of the mere residue of a small amount of karma, it is not possible to remain there.

It is just as, for example, a certain servant who approaches the royal court with all the requisites for service, but having exhausted most of his equipment due to a long absence, remains unable to stay at the royal court if he has only an umbrella, sandals, and so forth remaining."
It is able [to do so].
Thus, being grasped merely by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the lunar disk would not be able to remain;
yet this is not as it should be.

It has been stated that it is not possible for a residue of karma to persist once its fruit has been experienced by one residing in heaven, because that residue would be incompatible with the very effect [of the karma].
But this is incorrect;
for it cannot be that every single bit of karma whose fruit is heaven has already had its fruit experienced.
This is not tenable.

For it is claimed that ritual action performed for the sake of heaven produces its entire heavenly fruit only for one who remains in heaven, yet produces some small portion of that fruit even for one who has fallen from heaven.
Such a conceptualization is not admissible for those for whom the Vedic word is the sole authority.
In the case of an oil vessel, however, the persistence of a trace of oil is logical because it is observed;
likewise, the persistence of a trace of implements is seen in the case of a servant.

But here, such persistence of a trace of karma that has heaven as its fruit is neither observed nor can it be postulated, because that would contradict the scriptural teaching that its fruit is heaven.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way:
it is not the case that the *anuśaya* (latent tendency) is a portion of a meritorious act such as a sacrifice—which has heaven as its fruit—that persists like the oil remaining in a vessel.

For if one were to imagine that some portion of that very same well-performed act, such as a sacrifice, through which one experienced heaven, constitutes the *anuśaya*, then the *anuśaya* would be exclusively pleasant and never the opposite.

In this regard, the scriptural passage concerning the analysis of residual karma (*anuśaya*) would be contradicted: "Now, those here whose conduct was pleasant, and those whose conduct was foul" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).

Therefore, when the collection of karmas that bear fruit in the next world has been exhausted through experience, the remaining collection of other karmas that bear fruit in this world constitutes the *anuśaya*; it is those possessing such *anuśaya* who descend.

As for what was stated— that because of the non-specific reference "whatever [it may be]," they reach the end of every action performed here by experiencing its fruit and descend without residual karma (*niranuśaya*)—
this is not so;
for the existence of residual karma has been established.
It is understood that whatever action performed here has its fruit in the next world and has begun to be experienced, all of that is exhausted through the enjoyment of its results.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that death manifests all karma without distinction, even that which has not yet begun to bear fruit—this is refuted by the fact that some karma begins to produce its fruit in the next world, while other karma does so in this one. Thus, the claim of uniformity is rejected.
Furthermore, it must be stated for what reason death is asserted to be the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet begun.
For just as prior to death, the emergence of the activity of other [karmas] is impossible because they are obstructed by karma whose fruit has already begun,
so too at the time of death, due to the impossibility of multiple karmas with contradictory fruits beginning their results simultaneously, [only one] prevails by its strength.
It is impossible for there to be the emergence of the operation of a weak [karma] that is obstructed [by others].

For it cannot be said that, merely by virtue of the commonality of having uncommenced fruit, multiple karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in different births, becoming manifested simultaneously at a single death, initiate a single birth; this is because it would contradict the principle that each karma has its own specific, determined fruit.
Nor can it be said that at the time of death there is the manifestation of some karma and the destruction of others,
because this would contradict the principle that [karmic fruits] are invariably certain.
Indeed, the destruction of karmas is not possible without causes such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
Smṛti also shows that another action remains for a long time when it is obstructed by an action with a contrary result: "Sometimes a well-performed action remains here, buried deep within."

"Being churned in saṃsāra, one is released from as much suffering as [is possible]"— this is of such a nature. Furthermore, if all karma whose fruit has not yet begun were manifested in a single death and thus initiated only one birth,
then, because there would be no further engagement in heaven, hell, or animal wombs, and because dharma and adharma would not arise due to the absence of a cause, a subsequent birth could not occur.
Furthermore, the scriptural tradition that each individual act, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has the cause for its fruition across many births would be contradicted.
Moreover, it is impossible to conceive of any cause other than the scripture for the comprehension of the nature, results, and means of dharma and adharma.

Nor is death a possible manifestor of an action whose fruit is visible, such as the Kārīrī sacrifice; thus, this hypothesis that death is a manifestor is also non-pervasive (i.e., not universally applicable).
The analogy of the lamp has also been refuted by demonstrating precisely the relative strength and weakness of karma;
this should be understood as being like the manifestation or non-manifestation of gross and subtle forms.
For just as a lamp, despite being equally present [to both], manifests a gross form and not a subtle one.
Thus, although the collection of karmas whose fruits have not yet begun is equally present at the time of death, it brings about the operation of the stronger karma and not that of the weaker one.
Therefore, this admission of the manifestation of all karmas without exception is untenable, as it contradicts scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and logic (*nyāya*).
Furthermore, the fear that "if a residue of karma exists, there would be the consequence of no liberation" is misplaced.
Because it is heard in scripture that there is the destruction of all karma through right vision (*samyagdarśana*),
it is therefore established that those who descend do so while still possessing residual impressions (*anuśaya*).
And as they descend, they do so both in the same manner and in a different manner as they ascended.
"Yathetam" means "as they came";
"anevam" means "in the opposite manner.
Since smoke and space are mentioned among the stages of the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) during the descent, and because of the word "yathetam," it is understood that [the soul returns] as it came.
Because the night and so forth are not mentioned [in the rule], and because "clouds" (*abhra*) and so forth are added as exceptions (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the opposite meaning is also understood.
[Note: *anuśaya* is action (*karman*);
that is the action.]
"Returns" means it becomes exhausted.
"Manifestation" (abhivyakti) means being oriented toward the fruit.

Among those living beings descending there, those who possess "pleasant conduct"—that is, those of meritorious deeds—in this land of action (karmabhūmi), are necessarily near [to that state]; for "avaśyam hi" has the sense of "indeed necessarily."
"Kapūya" means evil. "Ricyamāna" means being separated or dissociated.
If it is argued that this refers to conduct (*caraṇa*), Kārṣṇājini says it is for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇārtha*).
It might be argued that there is a scriptural passage cited to establish the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*), namely: "Those here whose conduct was pleasant... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).
However, that passage indeed demonstrates the attainment of a new birth based on one's conduct (*caraṇa*) and so forth, not based on residual karma.
Conduct (*caraṇa*) is one thing, while latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is another. Conduct, behavior (*cāritra*), practice (*ācāra*), and virtue (*śīla*) are synonymous.
Latent disposition, however, refers to karma that remains beyond the karma whose fruit has already been experienced.

And the Śruti designates the performance of action by way of distinction: "As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5), and "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, not others;
those good deeds which are ours should be observed by you" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.2).

If it is argued that the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is not established because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of another womb based on one's conduct (*caraṇa*), this is not a valid objection;
for the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains that this scriptural mention of "conduct" is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the latent dispositions. // 9 //
If it is argued that [the term "conduct"] would be meaningless, we say no, because it depends upon that.
It might be asked:

why, moreover, is the latent disposition (*anuśaya*), which is etymological (*lākṣaṇika*), made known by the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*), while setting aside the scriptural sense of "ethical discipline" (*śīla*)?

[Objection: But surely, the result of conduct (*śīla*) itself—whether scripturally enjoined or prohibited, and whether virtuous or non-virtuous in form—will be the attainment of a favorable or unfavorable rebirth.
Furthermore, one must necessarily admit some kind of fruit for conduct as well;
otherwise, the charge of pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) would indeed follow. If this is argued:
This is not a fault. Why? Because it depends upon that;
for the collection of rites such as the *iṣṭi* depends upon conduct (*cāraṇa*).

For no one devoid of right conduct (*sadācāra*) can be qualified [for ritual action], according to such Smṛti texts as, "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of conduct. Thus, even though conduct serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it is not useless;
for when a collection of rites such as sacrifices begins to produce its fruit, conduct—being dependent upon that very [rite]—will initiate some excellence (*atiśaya*) therein.
And it is well known from Śruti and Smṛti that ritual action (*karman*) accomplishes all purposes.

Therefore, it is the opinion of Kārṣṇājini that karma alone—characterized by conduct (*śīla*) and existing as a latent tendency (*anuśaya*)—is the cause for entering a womb. For when karma is present, it is not logical that one should enter a womb based on conduct;
indeed, one who is able to flee on his feet ought not to run away on his knees. // 10 //
"But it is good and evil deeds alone," says Bādari.
The teacher Bādari, however, maintains that good and evil deeds alone are signified by the word *caraṇa*;
for *caraṇa*, performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), and action (*karman*) are not different in meaning.
For instance, the term *carati* is seen to be employed without distinction for any action whatsoever;
for when someone performs a meritorious act characterized by what is desirable and so forth, worldly people say of him, "This great soul practices dharma.
Furthermore, conduct (*ācāra*) is indeed a specific kind of dharma.

The designation of a distinction between "actions" (*karman*) and "conduct" (*cāraṇa*), however, is also possible according to the maxim of the "Brāhmaṇas and wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya*).

Therefore, the conclusion is that those of "pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacāraṇāḥ*) are those whose actions are praiseworthy, while those of "wretched conduct" (*kapūyacāraṇāḥ*) are those whose actions are censurable. (11) [FN:
This is the same as the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvarda-nyāya*).]
3. The Section on Those Who Perform Unpleasant Deeds, etc. (Sūtras 12–21).
Sūtra 12: "And it is heard [in scripture] regarding those who perform unpleasant deeds, etc.
It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious acts go to the moon.
But as for the others who perform undesirable deeds, it is now considered whether they also go to the moon or do not go there.
Regarding this, they first say: it is not the case that only those who perform sacrifices and such go to the moon.
Why?
For it is heard in scripture that even those who perform undesirable acts must go to the lunar orb;
indeed, the Kauṣītakins record this without distinction: "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2).
This is because of the fixed number of oblations prescribed in the passage beginning with "in the fifth oblation."
If it is argued that all must indeed ascend to the moon, because it is not logical for those who perform sacrifices and other rites and others to have the same destination, we say:
no, because there is no enjoyment on the lunar orb for others. // 12 //

"But for others, after experiencing [the results] in Saṃyamana, there is ascent and descent, because their course is seen. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that all go to the moon.
Why is this so?
Because the ascent to the moon is solely for the sake of enjoyment, neither for no purpose nor solely for the sake of descending again.
Just as someone climbs a tree solely for the purpose of gathering flowers and fruit, neither without purpose nor merely to fall from it;

and since it has been stated that there is no enjoyment of the moon for those who perform undesirable deeds and the like, therefore only those who perform desirable deeds and the like ascend to the moon, and not others.
Having entered Saṃyamana, the abode of Yama, and having experienced the tortures of Yama corresponding to their own evil deeds, they return once again to this world;
such are their ascent and descent.
Why? Because their course of travel is observed.

For instance, a Vedic text similar in character to Yama’s own words shows that those who perform undesirable acts and so forth fall under Yama's control: "The way to the hereafter does not reveal itself to the fool, who is deluded by the infatuation for wealth and negligent;
thinking 'this world exists, there is no other,' he falls again and again under my power" (Kaṭha Up. 2.6).
Furthermore, there are many such indicative marks of falling under Yama's control, such as "Vaivasvata, the gathering place of people. // 13 //

Moreover, cultured authorities such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others remember— in the *Nāciketa-ākhyāna* and other texts— that in the city of Saṃyamana, there is the ripening of evil karma under the jurisdiction of Yama.
Moreover, there are seven.
Furthermore, the seven hells, headed by Raurava, are recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas as the ground for experiencing the fruits of evil deeds;
those who perform undesirable acts and so forth reach them.
The intention is: how could they possibly reach the moon? // 15 //
Is it not contradictory that those who have committed evil deeds experience torments dependent upon Yama?
For it is recorded in tradition that in those places such as Raurava, there are other presiding authorities, such as Citragupta and others.
To this he says: "No."
And even in that case, there is no contradiction because of his activity.

(BBs 3.1.16) Since it is accepted that Yama himself acts as the presiding authority over those seven hells, there is no contradiction; for Citragupta and the others are recorded in tradition as presiding authorities only when appointed by Yama. 16.
"But because of the context of knowledge and action" (BBs 3.1.17).

In the Pañcāgni-vidyā, at the point of answering the question, "Do you know why that world is not filled? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3), it is heard: "Now, by neither of these two paths do those small creatures become who return again and again."
"Be born and die—this is the third station; by that, this world is not filled" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).
In this context, "of these two paths" refers to knowledge and action.
Why? Because... [the text continues].
Because they are the subject under discussion;
for knowledge and action are indeed presented as the means for attaining the two paths, the path of the gods and the path of the fathers.
By the words "those who know thus," knowledge is mentioned, and by that [knowledge], the path of the gods to be attained is proclaimed.

The path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) is proclaimed as that by which one is to proceed through ritual action (*karman*), such as "sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1, 3).
In the description of that process, it is heard in scripture: "Now, by neither of these two paths... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).

This is what is meant: those who are not qualified for the path of the gods (devayāna) by means of the practice of knowledge (vidyā), nor for the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) by means of ritual action (karman), for them there is this third path characterized by small creatures, which involves repeated return. Therefore, the moon is not reached even by those who perform undesirable acts and the like.
It might be argued:
"They too will ascend the lunar disc, descend from it, and then attain the state of small creatures.
That also is not the case.
Because the ascent would be purposeless;

furthermore, since all those who strive would reach the world of the moon, that world would become completely filled with those striving for it, and thus a reply contrary to the question would result.
For the reply ought to be given in such a way that this world is not filled.
If it is argued that the attainment [of the full result] is incomplete because of the admission of descending, we say no; for this is not heard in scripture.
It is true that even through descending, the non-completion [of the result] is logically possible.
Scripture, moreover, shows the non-filling [of the world] by mentioning it as the third station: "This is the third station; therefore that world is not filled" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).
Thus, it is logical that the non-filling results precisely from the failure to ascend.
For if descent were common even to those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds, the mention of a "third station" would result in being purposeless.
The word "tu" (but), however, cuts off the suspicion that there might be a lack of universality arising from the statement found in another recension (*śākhā*).
This being so, the word "all" (*sarva*) in the statement of the other recension remains dependent upon those who are qualified [for the ritual]:
"Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon alone. (17)
As for what was further stated— that all must go to the moon in order to obtain a body,
because of the restriction on the number of oblations in the passage beginning with "at the fifth oblation"—
that is now answered:
"Not in the third, because it is perceived thus.
(BBs 3.1.18) One need not observe a restriction to five oblations for the sake of obtaining a body in the third place.
Why? Because it is perceived thus.

For indeed, even without a fixed rule regarding the number of oblations, the attainment of the third station is observed through the manner already described: "Be born and die—this is the third station" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).
Moreover, it is said: "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).
Thus, the number of oblations is proclaimed as the cause for a human body, and not as the cause for the bodies of insects, moths, and so forth, because the word "puruṣa" denotes the human species.

Furthermore, it is taught that water attains the state of being called "puruṣa" at the fifth oblation; it is not prohibited that water attains the state of being called "puruṣa" before the fifth oblation.
Because it would entail the fault of a single sentence having two meanings.

Among those [beings] for whom ascent and descent are possible, the body will arise at the fifth oblation; however, for others, the body is commenced by means of waters joined with other elements, even without the counting of oblations. // 18 //
Moreover, it is also recorded in the world;
furthermore, it is remembered in the world that Droṇa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others, as well as Sītā, Draupadī, and others, were not born from a womb.
In that regard, for Droṇa and others, there was no single oblation pertaining to women;
for Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others, however, there were not even two oblations pertaining to both women and men.
And just as there was no concern for the number of oblations in that case, so it will be elsewhere as well.
It is a common worldly belief that even the crane conceives a fetus without the emission of semen. // 19 //
And because it is observed:

Furthermore, since among the fourfold collection of living beings—namely those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, and from a sprout—it is observed that moisture-born and sprout-born beings arise even without sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*), there is no regard for the number of oblations;
this will likewise be the case elsewhere. (20)
FN: "Born from a living being" (*jīvaja*) means born from a womb (*jarāyuja*);
"born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*) refers to trees and the like.
Now, it may be objected: "Of these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), the living-born (*jīvaja*), and the sprout-born (*udbhijja*)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.1).
In this context, only a threefold collection of beings is heard; how then is a fourfold nature of the collection of beings asserted? To this it is replied:
the third term includes those born from heat and moisture.

In the passage, "born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.1), it should be understood that the third term, "born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*), includes those "born from sweat" (*svedaja*) as well;
for both sweat-born and sprout-born beings are equally characterized by their origin through the breaking forth [of life] from earth or water.

However, since the emergence of mobile beings (*jaṅgama*) is distinct from the emergence of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), there is no contradiction in the doctrine of a distinction between those born from moisture (*svedaja*) and those born from sprouts (*udbhijja*) elsewhere. [Topic 4: The Section on Attaining Similarity (Sābhāvyāpatti)] Sūtra 22.
"Attainment of its own nature [occurs] because of the logical possibility.

It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* ascend to the moon, dwell there for as long as their karma lasts, and then descend from there with a remainder of their residual karma (*sānuśaya*).
Now, the manner of this descent is examined.
In this regard, there is this scriptural text concerning the descent: "Then they return again by this very same path as they came—to the ether;

from the ether to the air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, he rains down" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). Regarding this, a doubt arises: do those descending actually attain the very nature of ether and the rest, or do they merely attain similarity to ether and the rest?
In that regard, they first understand the very nature of space and so forth as it is directly attained.
Why? Because such is the scriptural statement;
otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Furthermore, when there is a choice between direct denotation (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), direct denotation is the more reasonable;
thus, the words "having become air, he becomes smoke," and so forth, are appropriately understood as referring to the actual acquisition of those respective forms.
Therefore, there is the attainment of the very nature of ether and the other elements.
This being the case, we reply: they attain equality with ether and the other elements.

When that body composed of water, which was begun for the purpose of experience in the lunar orb, dissolves upon the exhaustion of that experience, it becomes subtle and equal to ether; from there it comes under the power of the wind, and then it unites with smoke and the subsequent stages.
This is stated as follows: "In this very way [they go] to space, from space to air" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5), and so forth.
Why is this so?
Because it is logically consistent;
for it is only in this way that this is consistent,
since the actual existence of one thing as another is not logically possible.
Furthermore, once the true nature of space has been attained, a descent through the sequence of air and so forth is not possible.
Moreover, because space is all-pervading and thus eternally connected [to the self], no other connection with it is tenable than the attainment of similarity to it.
And when a direct literal sense (*śruti*) is impossible, it is indeed proper to resort to an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, in this context, the very attainment of equality with space and so forth is metaphorically designated as "the state of being space and so forth. // 22 //
5. The Section on Not Too Long (nāticirādhikaraṇa).
Sūtra 23: "Not too long, because of the specification.
(BBs 3.1.23) Regarding the attainment of ether and the subsequent stages prior to the attainment of rice and other grains, there arises a point of doubt.
Is it that they remain for a long time, attaining similarity with each subsequent moment through similarity with each preceding one, or is it for a short time?
In this regard, there is no fixed rule, because there is no authoritative scripture (śāstra) that establishes such a rule.
This being the position reached, he says: "Not after a very long time."
Having remained in the state of space and so forth for a very short time, they descend upon this earth with showers of rain. Why is this so?
Because a specific distinction is observed.

For instance, immediately after describing the attainment of the state of rice and so forth, the text qualifies it by saying: "From there, indeed, it is most difficult to emerge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).
One should understand that the letter *t* has been elided here according to the rules of Vedic grammar (*chandasa*).
The meaning is that it is more difficult to fall away from, more difficult to emerge from, and more painful to escape from this state of being rice and so forth.

By demonstrating here the difficulty of escaping from suffering, he shows the ease of escaping from the previous states. Furthermore, this distinction between the ease and difficulty of escaping is caused by the shortness or length of time.
Because enjoyment is impossible during that period due to the body not yet being produced, the descent must occur after only a short time prior to attaining the state of rice and so forth. // 23 //
6. The Section Concerning Being Presided Over by Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 24–27:
"In those [beings] presided over by another, it is as before, because of the scriptural statement.

(BBs 3.1.24) Regarding that very ascent, immediately after the pouring down of rain, it is recited: "Then they are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).

Thus, in this regard, there arises a doubt: do those possessing latent dispositions (anuśayin) become partakers of the pleasure and pain of stationary beings, having entered the genus of stationary things during this interval; or rather, do they merely undergo contact with the bodies of stationary beings presided over by other conscious subjects (kṣetrajña)?
What, then, is the established position? That those who have entered a stationary birth possess latent dispositions (anuśaya) and experience pleasure and pain. Why is this so?
Because birth in its primary sense is logically possible; because the state of being a stationary object (sthāvara) is well-known in both Śruti and Smṛti as a place of experience;
and because it is logical that a class of actions such as sacrifices involving the slaughter of animals would result in undesirable fruits;
therefore, this birth of those with residual karma (anuśayin) as rice and so forth is indeed primary.

It is like birth as a dog or the like. Just as for those with residual karma (*anuśayin*), birth as a dog, a pig, or a *caṇḍāla* is primary and involves that actual pleasure and pain, so too, those with residual karma attain mere contact with rice and other plants; it does not involve the pleasure and pain associated with them.
"The same applies to birth as rice and so forth.

This being the position, we reply: when rice and other plants are presided over by other living beings, those possessing residual karma (anuśayin) undergo mere contact with them; they do not become partakers of their pleasure or pain, just as before.
Just as the state of being wind, smoke, and so forth, for those possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśayin*), is merely a state of contact with them,
so too the state of being rice and so forth, for those born as stationary beings, is merely a state of contact with them. Why is this so?
In this case as well, it is due to verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). What is this "state of being like that" (*tadvadbhāva*) of the verbal expression?
It is the mention [of an object] without the operation of an action (*karmavyāpāra*).
Just as one does not perceive any activity of karma in the case of [the elements] beginning with space and ending with rain, so it is also in the case of the birth of rice and other crops.
Therefore, there is no experience of pleasure or pain for those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) in this context.
However, where one intends and perceives the experience of pleasure or pain, there one refers to the activity of karma, as in the passages: "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct."

Moreover, if the primary sense were intended—that those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) are born as rice and so forth—then when that rice and such are being reaped, threshed, cooked, and eaten, those latent dispositions identifying with it would have to depart.
For it is a well-known principle that whatever living soul identifies with a particular body departs when that body is afflicted.
In that case, the transition of the latent dispositions from the state of rice and so forth to the state of one who emits semen (*retaḥsig-bhāva*) could not be described.

Therefore, there is merely a conjunction of those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) with rice and other plants presided over by others. By this, one may refute the claim that "birth" (*janman*) is used in its primary sense [of being born from a womb], as well as the claim that the state of being a stationary object (*sthāvara-bhāva*) is a place for experiencing [karmic results].
Nor do we deny that the state of being a stationary object is a place for experiencing [results].

Let this be the place of enjoyment for other beings who, through the power of their demerit, have attained the state of stationary things; however, we maintain that those possessed of latent dispositions (*anuśayin*), while descending from the moon, do not experience the state of stationary things.

"If [it be argued that the sacrifice] is impure, we say no, because of the sacred word (śabda). As for what was stated—that because of its connection with the injury to animals and so forth, the sacrificial rite is impure, and thus even an undesirable fruit is possible for it—therefore, let the birth of the *anuśayins* as rice and so forth be taken in its primary sense; in that case, a figurative interpretation would be purposeless. This is refuted as follows: If it be argued that the sacrificial rite is impure due to its connection with the injury to animals and so forth, and that consequently an undesirable fruit is logically possible for it, and therefore the birth of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayins*) as rice and so forth should be understood in its primary sense, making a figurative interpretation therein useless—this is refuted. [The refutation continues: No, because of the sacred word. For it is established by the Vedic word that the fruit of the Agnihotra and other such rites is heaven. And since the Vedic word is authoritative, it cannot be set aside by mere reasoning. Furthermore, the injury to animals in this context is not prohibited, because it is enjoined by the scripture. And an act that is enjoined by scripture cannot be considered impure on the grounds of mere reasoning. Moreover, the scriptural statement "the sacrifice is the healing herb" (*yajña vai vācaḥ bheṣajam*) shows that the sacrifice is a means of purification. Therefore, the sacrificial rite is not impure. Consequently, the birth of those possessing residual karma as rice and so forth must indeed be understood in its primary sense. Thus, the figurative interpretation is rejected.
No, because the knowledge of dharma and adharma has the treatise as its cause.
That "this is dharma" and "this is adharma"— the treatise alone is the cause for such knowledge,
because those two are beyond the reach of the senses and because their causes are not restricted by place or time.
Whatever dharma is practiced in a particular place, at a particular time, and under particular circumstances becomes adharma when performed under different places, times, and circumstances.
Therefore, no one possesses knowledge regarding the domain of dharma and adharma except through the scripture (*śāstra*).
Furthermore, since the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—consisting of elements such as violence and favor—is determined by the scripture to be dharma, how can it be said to be impure?
But surely the scripture itself, in the injunction "One should not harm any living beings," makes it known that violence toward living beings is unrighteousness.
Certainly;
however, that is a general rule (utsarga).
The exception (*apavāda*) is: "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
And between the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception, there is a fixed scope of application.
Therefore, Vedic action is pure.
Because it is practiced by the learned and is not censured,
its corresponding fruit is not birth as a stationary being;
nor can birth as rice and so forth be like birth as a dog or similar creatures.
For that [statement] is spoken with reference to those who cross over by means of foul-smelling substances; here, however, there is no such specific qualification.
Therefore, for those who fall from the lunar orb and exist as latent impressions (anuśayin), the mere contact with rice and so forth is figuratively designated as "becoming that" (tadbhāva). // 25 //
"Furthermore, there is the connection with the shedder of semen.

For this reason as well, their becoming those [rice plants] is merely a state of contact with rice and so forth; because immediately after the state of being rice and so forth, the state of being the shedder of semen is taught for those possessing a residue (*anuśayin*): "For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very same thing again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).
Moreover, the primary state of being a progenitor of semen is not possible here;
for one becomes a progenitor of semen only after being born for a long time and reaching youth.
How, then, could the latent disposition (*anuśaya*), which follows the food being consumed, attain that state in its non-figurative sense?
In that regard, one must necessarily admit that the state of being a "seeder" consists precisely in the connection with a seeder;
likewise, the state of being rice and so forth also consists precisely in the connection with rice and so forth—thus there is no contradiction. // 26 //
From the womb comes the body.

Now, immediately after the state of being in the seed-discharger, when the semen has been poured into the womb, a body superior to the womb is born for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) to experience the fruit of that residual karma; thus says the scripture: "Those here whose conduct was pleasant...
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7), and so forth.
Therefore, it is understood from this as well that at the time of descending into the state of rice and so forth, the body of the soul is not itself endowed with pleasure and pain.
Thus, it is established that the "birth" of those possessing residual karma (anuśayin) in the form of rice and so forth consists merely in their contact with them. // 27 //
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The Second Quarter of the Third Chapter.
[In this quarter, there is an investigation into the purification of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*.]
1. The Section on the Intermediate State (Sandhyādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–6.
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says.
(BBs 3.2.1) Having in the preceding section illustrated the knowledge of the five fires, the various modes of the individual soul's journey through transmigratory existence were elaborated upon.
Now, however, the different states of that very [Self] are being elaborated upon.

They recite this, beginning with "When he falls asleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9), and continuing: "There are no chariots there, no chariot-horses, no roads; yet he creates chariots, chariot-horses, and roads," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the creation in dream also ultimately real, as it is in the waking state, or is it composed of illusion (*māyā*)? On this point, it is first established that the creation in the intermediate state (*saṃdhya*) is of a real nature. By "intermediate state," one refers to the dream state.

This is because we see its usage in the Veda: "The third state, the intermediate one, is the place of sleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9). It is called *saṃdhya* because it occurs at the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the two states of the world—namely, the state of waking and the state of deep sleep.
In that intermediate state, the creation must necessarily be of a real nature.
Why? Because the authoritative scripture (*śruti*) declares thus: "Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and paths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10), and so forth.
Furthermore, it is understood precisely from the concluding summary that "He is indeed the agent. // 1 //
And some [maintain] the creator, as well as sons and so forth.

Furthermore, some followers of a particular Vedic school, in this very intermediate state, recognize the Self as the creator of desires, according to the text: "This person who, while others sleep, remains awake, creating each and every desire" (KaU 5.8).
And in this context, "desires" (*kāma*) refers to sons and so forth, because they are desired.

[Objection: But surely, by the word "desire," only specific types of longing should be expressed. [Reply: No; for it says, "Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.23).

For this reason, because the word "desire" (*kāma*) is employed in reference to sons and other such things mentioned in various contexts— such as in the passage at the end of the *Prakṛti* section, "But I make you, who are free from desires, a partaker of desires" (KaU 1.24)—
and because we understand from both the context and the remainder of the sentence that this creator is the Wise One (*prājña*).

For this [teaching] beginning with "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (KaU 2.14) is indeed the instrument for the wise; and the remainder of the passage also has that very thing as its object: "That alone is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal;
upon it all worlds rest, and no one transcends it" (KaU 5.8).

Since creation brought about by an intelligent creator has been established as being real in nature when based on the waking state, so too must creation based on the dream state be capable of being real.

And thus the Śruti says: "Now they indeed say, 'This [dream] is for him in the very place of waking,' for whatever he sees while awake, those same things he sees while asleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14).
This scripture declares the equality of principle between the dream and the waking states.
Therefore, the creation in the intermediate state is indeed real in nature. // 2 //
This being the case, he replies:
"But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not fully manifested.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
That which was stated—that the creation in the intermediate state (saṃdhye) is ultimately real—is not so.
The creation in the intermediate state is mere illusion (māyā); it does not possess even a scent of ultimate reality.
Why? Because its essential nature is unmanifest in its entirety.

For a dream does not have its nature manifested by the characteristics of an ultimately real entity in their entirety. But what is intended here by "entirety"? It is [the presence of] place, time, causes, and non-sublation.
Indeed, place, time, causes, and non-sublation pertaining to objects that are ultimately real entities are not possible in a dream.
To begin with, a suitable location for chariots and the like is not possible within a dream;
for chariots and such could not find space within the confined area of the body.
This might be argued:
One will see dreams outside the body because of the perception of objects located in other places.
And scripture demonstrates that dreams occur outside the body: "The immortal one, having wandered outside the nest, goes wherever he desires as an immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12).
Thus, the distinction between the states of staying and moving would not be consistent if the living being did not depart [from the body].
To this it is replied: "No," for it is not possible to conceive that a sleeping being has the capacity to travel to and return from a place separated by a hundred yojanas in a mere moment.

And in some cases, he reports a dream that lacks any return, saying: "While lying here today, overcome by sleep, I went in a dream to the Pañcālas, and having awakened, I am here. If he had departed from the body, he would have awakened among the Pañcālas; yet he does not go there, but awakens right here in the Kurus. Furthermore, while he believes himself to be traveling to another region with this very body, those standing nearby see that body in the very place where it lay.

Furthermore, one sees these other places in a dream exactly as they are, yet they do not actually exist in that way. If one were to see them while running about, one would perceive them as real objects, just as when waking;

however, scripture shows that the dream occurs within the body itself, beginning with "When he moves about in this state of dreaming" and concluding with "He moves about at will within his own body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18).
Therefore, because it contradicts both scripture and reasoning, the scriptural passage concerning "outside the nest" must be interpreted figuratively as meaning "having moved as if outside the nest.
For one who, though dwelling in the body, does not employ it for any purpose, is as if outside the body.
Furthermore, since this is the case, the distinction between the notions of staying and moving must be admitted to be merely an illusion.
Furthermore, there is a discrepancy regarding time in dreams: one who has fallen asleep at night perceives it as being day in the land of Bhārata;
likewise, within a dream lasting only a single moment, one sometimes passes through many series of years.
Moreover, no signs found in a dream are suitable for either cognition or action.
For, due to the withdrawal of his instruments, he does not possess eyes or other senses for the perception of chariots and such;
furthermore, how could he have the capacity to produce chariots and so forth in a mere twinkling of an eye, or from pieces of wood?
Moreover, these chariots and other things seen in dreams are sublated upon waking.
Moreover, these [objects] in dreams are easily sublated, because deviation is observed at their beginning and end.
For instance, what is determined in a dream as "this is a chariot" may in an instant become a human being; and what is determined as "this is a human being" may in an instant become a tree.

Moreover, the scripture clearly declares the non-existence of chariots and so forth in a dream: "There are no chariots there, no yoked horses, and no roads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10), and so on.
Therefore, the vision of dreams is mere illusion (māyāmātra). [Note: *saṃvṛte* means "in a confined space"; *saṃkīrṇaḥ* means "intermingled."]
For they declare that the Śruti indicates both going (paryetuṃ) and returning (viparyetuṃ), and those who know it say so.
If it is argued that because it is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), there is not even a trace of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) in a dream, we say:
no;
for a dream is indeed indicative of future good and evil fortune.

For it is heard in scripture: "When, in dreams during rites performed for specific desires, one sees a woman, one should know that there will be success in that dream-vision" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.9).
Likewise, by such dreams as "he sees a black man with black teeth; he [the black man] kills him," scripture makes known that a short life remains.
And those who know the treatises on dreams declare: "Mounting an elephant and the like in a dream are auspicious; riding a donkey and the like are inauspicious.
Furthermore, they hold that certain dreams, caused by specific mantras, deities, or substances, possess a scent of truth.
Even in that case, let it be granted that the object indicated may indeed be real.
The intention is that for a dream-communicator, however, there is indeed falsity arising from the sight of women and so forth, because it is sublated.
Therefore, it is logical that a dream is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*).
As for what was stated, "For it says," that must be explained as being figurative (*bhākta*) given this state of affairs.
Just as it is said that "the plough draws the oxen and so forth" merely because it is the instrumental cause,
and yet the plough itself does not actually draw the oxen and so forth;
in the same way, because he is merely the instrumental cause, it is said that "the one who is asleep creates chariots and so forth," and that "he is the agent."
It is not, however, that the sleeping person creates chariots and so forth through direct perception alone.

Rather, it must be stated that his causality consists in being the agent of the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) which serve as the causes for the experiences of joy, terror, and the like that arise from the appearance of chariots and such things.

Furthermore, because the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) of the Self is difficult to discern in the waking state due to the contact with objects and senses and the interference of external lights such as the sun, the dream state is introduced in order to discern that luminosity.

In this regard, if the statement regarding the creation of chariots and so forth were taken literally according to the direct scriptural text (*śruti*), then the self-luminosity [of the Self] would not be established.

Therefore, the statement concerning the absence of chariots and so forth must be understood according to the direct scriptural text, while the statement concerning the creation of chariots and so forth must be explained as being figurative (*bhakti*).
By this, the scriptural references to "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*) are also explained.

As for what was also stated—that "they declare this [Self] to be a wise creator"—that too is incorrect; for another Śruti passage says: "Having himself struck down [the body], having himself created [the dream world], he dreams by his own light, by his own radiance" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9).
Thus, because the activity of the individual soul (jīva) is heard [in scripture];
here too, in the passage "He who wakes among those who sleep" (KaU 5.8), this very soul, as is well known, is celebrated as the creator of desires.

However, by means of the remainder of that passage, that very semen is identified as Brahman; thus, having set aside its state as a living soul (*jīva*), its state as Brahman is taught—just as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and other such texts—and therefore there is no contradiction with the context of Brahman.
Nor do we deny the activity of the conscious one (*prājña*) even in dreams.
Because he is the Lord of all, it is logical that he is the presiding controller over all states;
however, what is being established here is merely this: that this creation based on the twilight [of the two meditations] is not ultimately real, unlike the creation of space and so forth.
Furthermore, even the creation of space and so forth does not possess absolute reality.

For it has been established in the sūtra, "The non-difference from That [Brahman] follows from such terms as 'originating' and so forth" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14), that the entire phenomenal world is merely māyā;
however, prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self, the phenomenal world consisting of ether and the rest exists in a fixed form.

However, the phenomenal expansion based on the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is sublated every day; therefore, this specific illusory nature (māyāmātratva) of the intermediate state has been declared. // 4 //
"But it is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that arise its bondage and its opposite.
(BBs 3.2.5) Now, it might be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a portion of the Supreme Self, like a spark of fire.
This being so, just as fire and a spark possess the same powers of burning and illuminating, so too must the individual soul and the Lord possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty.
