And from that, it follows that by virtue of the individual soul's (jīva) knowledge and sovereignty, the creation of chariots and so forth in a dream will be produced through mere volition (sāṃkalpikī).

To this it is replied: even though there exists a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord (īśvara), the individual soul’s possession of qualities contrary to those of the Lord is directly perceived.
How much more so, then, is it the case that the individual soul does not possess qualities identical to those of the Lord?
It is not that it does not exist at all;
rather, although it exists, it is concealed by the intervention of ignorance and other factors.
That [Self], however, becomes manifest for a person who, striving and meditating upon the Supreme Lord, has shaken off the darkness [of ignorance].

Just as the power of sight, when obscured by cataracts, becomes manifest through the efficacy of medicine, so too does it appear for a certain perfected person through the grace of the Lord (Īśvara), but not by the very nature of all living beings.
Why? Because from that Lord, as the cause, the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) arise.
Bondage arises from the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the Lord, while liberation results from the thorough knowledge of His nature.

Thus says the Śruti: "By knowing God, there is the casting off of all fetters; with the afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death. Through meditation upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state: universal sovereignty as the absolute one whose desires are fulfilled" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11).
Such are the [verses] beginning with this. // 5 //
Or perhaps that [individual soul] is also [the Supreme Self] due to its connection with a body.
But why is it that the individual soul (*jīva*), though being a very part of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), has its knowledge and sovereignty obscured?
It would indeed be logical for knowledge and sovereignty to remain unobscured, just as the power to burn and to illuminate remain unobscured in a spark.
It is said:
This is indeed true;

nevertheless, that concealment of the individual soul’s knowledge and sovereignty arises from its connection with a body—that is, from its association with the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, objects, sensations, and so forth.

And there is an illustration for this: just as the power of burning and illuminating, though inherent in fire, becomes obscured when it is not yet kindled from the fire-sticks, or as it is obscured when covered by ashes;

so too, due to the connection with limiting adjuncts such as the body produced by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) presented by ignorance (avidyā), the individual soul's (jīva) concealment of its knowledge and sovereignty occurs through the delusion of non-discrimination [from them].
The word "or" (vā) is intended to exclude the suspicion that the individual soul and the Lord are different.
[Objection: Let this very living being (jīva) be [identical] to the Lord (īśvara), since its knowledge and sovereignty are merely obscured; what is the use of postulating its connection with a body?
[Reply: No, it is said in response.
For the distinctness of the living being from the Lord is not tenable, as [the scripture states]: "That divinity thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Having begun thus, [the text] refers to the individual soul by the word "Self" in the passage, "Entering with this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), as in:
"That is the Truth; He is the Self; That art thou, O Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.4).
Thus, it teaches that the individual soul (jīva) has the Lord as its self.
Therefore, the individual soul is non-different from the Lord; however, due to its connection with the body, its knowledge and sovereignty become concealed.
Consequently, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream by the will of the individual soul is not possible.
Furthermore, if the creation of chariots and so forth in a dream were merely a product of volition (*saṃkalpa*), no one would ever experience an undesirable dream;
for no one ever wills what is undesirable.

As for the argument that the scriptural mention of the "waking place" establishes the reality of the dream, that statement of equality does not intend to establish actual reality, because it would contradict the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) of the Self.

Moreover, since the absence of chariots and other such things in a dream has been shown by scripture itself, that [scriptural statement] intends to convey that the dream appears as if it were real because it is constructed from latent impressions (vāsanā) originating in the waking state.
Therefore, it is logically established that a dream is mere illusion (māyāmātra). // 6 //
2. The Section on the Absence of that [Dreaming]. Sūtras 7–8:
"The absence of that [dreaming] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements to that effect.
(BBs 3.2.7) The state of dreaming has been examined; now the state of deep sleep is being examined.
In this regard, there are scriptural passages concerning the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

In one place it is heard: "When, being thus asleep, composed, he knows no dream, then he has entered into these channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3). But elsewhere, having enumerated the channels themselves, it is heard: "Having descended by means of them, he rests in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19).
Likewise, elsewhere, after enumerating the channels themselves, it is said: "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 4.19).
Similarly, elsewhere: "He lies in that space which is within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17).
And likewise, elsewhere: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
And also: "Embraced by the intelligent Self (prājña-ātman), he knows nothing that is external, nor anything that is internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Are these channels (nāḍīs) and so forth distinct places for deep sleep, independent of one another, or is there a single place for deep sleep existing through mutual dependence? What, then, is the initial position? That they are distinct.
Why? Because they have a single purpose.
Indeed, things that serve a single purpose are never observed to be mutually dependent, such as rice and barley.
However, the fact that the channels and so forth share a single purpose is observed in the state of deep sleep: "He has entered into the channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3).
Moreover, because the use of the locative case is identical in various instances, such as "He lies in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19), one might object:
"But if that were so, the locative usage would not be seen in the passage: 'Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1)."

This is not a fault, because even there the sense of the locative case is implied. For the supplementary portion of that passage states that the living self, seeking a dwelling place, approaches Being: "Not finding any other abode, it takes refuge in the vital breath alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).
Thus, because the existent (*sat*) under discussion there is referred to by the word "breath" (*prāṇa*), and because the locative case signifies a locus (*āyatana*);
furthermore, the use of the locative case is indeed seen in the remainder of that passage: "Having reached the Existent, they do not know: 'We have reached the Existent'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2).
In all cases, deep sleep—characterized by the cessation of specific cognition—is not differentiated;
therefore, because they serve a single purpose, the soul approaches one or another location, such as the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth, for sleep by way of option.
This being the position reached, it is established in reply: "The absence [of that cognition] occurs in the channels and in the Self."
"The absence of that" means the absence of that aforementioned dream-vision; the meaning is "deep sleep.

And by the conjunction "in the channels and in the Self," the meaning is that one resorts to these—the channels and so forth—for the sake of sleep not as alternatives, but collectively. Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
For instance, it is heard in various places that all of these—the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth—are the locus of deep sleep; and this [fact] is subsumed by their conjunction (samuccaya).
For if there were an option (vikalpa) among them, there would be a contradiction in one of the alternatives.
Now, it might be argued that because they serve a single purpose, there is an option among the channels and so forth, just as in the case of rice and barley.
This is not so;
for the unity of meaning and the occurrence of an option do not follow merely from the mention of a single case-ending.

This is because we observe the mention of a single case-ending even in cases of diverse meanings and conjunctions, such as in "he sleeps in the palace" (*prāsāde śete*) and "he sleeps on the couch" (*paryaṅke śete*), and so forth.

Likewise here also, the combination [of locations]—that one sleeps in the channels, in the pericardium, and in Brahman—is appropriate. And thus the Śruti declares this combination of the channels and the vital breath (prāṇa) during deep sleep through their inclusion in a single sentence: "When he is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very breath" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 4.19).
This teaches the combination of the channels and the breath in deep sleep because they are presented within a single syntactical unit.
Furthermore, the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as Brahman has been established in the Sūtra, "The vital breath [is Brahman], because of the concordance" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.28).
Even where the text speaks of the channels (*nāḍīs*) as the place of sleep as if they were independent— saying, "At that time, he has entered into these channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3)—
there too, since there is no denial of Brahman, which is well-known from other passages, it is understood that he abides in Brahman itself by means of the channels as a gateway.
Nor does the locative case in "in the channels" (nāḍīṣu) become contradictory even in this view;
for one who approaches Brahman by way of the channels has indeed already entered the channels.
For he who goes to the ocean by means of the Gaṅgā has already arrived at the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, since the path to the world of Brahman, consisting of rays and channels, is intended here, the mention of "creeping" is for the purpose of praising the channels;
for after stating, "He has crept into the channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3), it says, "No evil touches him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3).
By saying this, he praises the channels (nāḍīs).

And he states the reason for the absence of contact with evil: the meaning is that one whose organs are pervaded by the "heat" (tejas)—namely, the bile (pitta) located within the channels—does not perceive external objects.
Alternatively, "by heat" (tejasā) is a reference to Brahman itself.
In another scriptural passage, "Brahman indeed, light indeed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7), the word "light" is applied to Brahman;
for by means of the channels (nāḍīs), one then becomes united with Brahman, and thus no evil touches him— this is the meaning.

Furthermore, the attainment of Brahman has been established as the cause for the absence of contact with evil, based on such scriptural passages as: "All evils turn back from there; for this world of Brahman is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.2).
This being the case, the conjunction of the channels with Brahman—well-known from other locations as the locus of deep sleep—is thereby established.

Likewise, because the *purītat* is also mentioned in the context of Brahman (*brahmaprakriyā*), its status as the place of sleep is understood to be consistent with that very context. In the passage, "He lies in that space which is within the heart" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.17), the space within the heart is established as the place of sleep; it is then stated, "He lies in the *purītat*" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.19). The term *purītat* refers to the membrane surrounding the heart.

Even though one is lying within that [space], namely in the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*), it can be said that "he lies in the pericardium" (*purītat*); for even one who resides in a city surrounded by a wall is said to reside in the wall. Furthermore, the nature of the space of the heart as Brahman has been established in the sūtra, *Dahara uttarebhyaḥ* (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.14).

Likewise, the combination of the channels and the pericardium is understood from their being mentioned together in a single sentence: "Having descended by means of them, he lies in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19).
Furthermore, the fact that the Sat and the Prājña are Brahman is well-established.
Thus, in these scriptural passages, only three places for deep sleep are mentioned: the channels (nāḍyaḥ), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman.
Even there, the channels and the pericardium are merely gateways; Brahman alone is the single place of deep sleep.
Moreover, the channels and the pericardium serve merely as the support for the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), and it is therein that its organs function. Indeed,
apart from the connection with limiting adjuncts, no support whatsoever is possible for the soul in its own right,
because it is non-different from Brahman and is established in its own majesty.

Even its being the support of Brahman during deep sleep is not stated with the intention of implying a distinction between the support and the supported; how then? It is stated with the intention of identity, since it says: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). By the word "own" (sva), the Self is denoted.
The meaning is that one who has attained his own true nature (*svarūpa*) becomes asleep.
Furthermore, there is never a time when the individual soul (*jīva*) is not in union with Brahman, because its own nature is imperishable.

However, with reference to the states of dreaming and waking—where, due to contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it appears as if it has assumed another form—it will be explained that upon the cessation of those adjuncts in deep sleep, it attains its own true nature.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that in the state of deep sleep one sometimes becomes united with the Existent (sat) and sometimes does not.
Furthermore, even if one accepts the alternative view regarding the locus [of the soul], deep sleep is never distinguished by the perception of specific cognitions;
in that regard, it is logical that one who has become united with the Existent does not perceive because of that oneness.
For the Śruti says: "By what means would one perceive [anything]? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that [the self] moves within the channels (nāḍīs), no cause can be discerned for the total lack of cognition in one who is lying down.
This is because it has difference as its object, according to the scriptural text: "But where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31).
Now, one might object that even for that which has difference as its object, causes such as extreme distance could be the reason for non-cognition. Certainly so.
This would be so if the individual soul (*jīva*) were admitted to be intrinsically limited,
like Viṣṇumitra, a traveler who does not see his own home; however,
no limitation exists for the soul apart from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

If it were argued that the cause for non-cognition is simply the extreme distance and so forth resulting from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), even then, since the adjunct has ceased, it would be logical to say that he has become one with Being and thus does not cognize.
Furthermore, we do not here intend to establish a collective combination (*samuccaya*) of the channels (*nāḍī*) and other factors as being equally [the locus of sleep];
for there is no purpose served by the cognition that "the channels or the pericardium (*purītat*) are the place of sleep."
For no fruit connected to this consciousness is heard of in scripture,
nor is this consciousness taught as a subordinate member of anything that possesses a fruit;
rather, we shall establish that Brahman is the imperishable locus of sleep.

However, there is a purpose for that consciousness: namely, the ascertainment that the individual soul (jīva) has Brahman as its self, and the ascertainment that it is free from the transactions of the dreaming and waking states.
Therefore, the Self alone is the place of deep sleep; hence, awakening occurs from this [Self].

And because the Self alone is the locus of sleep, for this very reason, awakening from this Self occurs as if eternally; this is taught in the section concerning sleep by way of the answer to the question, "Whence did he come? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16), namely: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so all the vital breaths [proceed] from this Self," and so on, as well as:
"Having come from Being, they do not know that they are coming from Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.10.2).

If, however, these states were being conceptualized as the locus of deep sleep, [the scripture] would have taught that one awakens from deep sleep sometimes from the channels (nāḍīs), sometimes from the pericardium (purītat), and sometimes from the Self (ātman).
Therefore, for this reason as well, the Self alone is the locus of deep sleep. // 8 //
3. The Section Concerning the Remembrance of Action, Words, and Injunctions. Sūtra 9:

"But he [returns] as that very same person, on account of the remembrance of action, words, and injunctions. (BBs 3.2.9) Now, regarding that attainment of Being (*sat-sampatti*), it is considered whether the one who awakens is the very same person who had attained Being, or whether it might be someone else.
In this regard, it is first argued that there is no fixed rule.

Why? For when a single drop of water is thrown into a mass of water, it then becomes the mass of water itself; and upon its extraction again, it is difficult to maintain that it is that very same drop of water.
Similarly, one who has fallen asleep and attained identity with the Supreme attains supreme serenity (*saṃprasīdati*); thus, he ought not to be able to rise again as that very same individual.

Therefore, when the question arises whether it is that very Lord or another individual soul (*jīva*) who awakens, the following is stated: it is that very same *jīva* who, having been dissolved and having attained his natural state, rises again, and not another.
Why?
Because of action, recollection, scripture, and injunction.
I shall demonstrate the reason by way of analysis.
First of all, because one is observed performing the remainder of a ritual action, it must be that very same person who rises [from meditative absorption], and not another.
For instance, one is seen performing on the following day the remainder of a ritual action that was performed on the previous day.
Furthermore, one person cannot be authorized by another to perform the remaining portion of an action already commenced by that other;
for this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, it is understood that a single individual alone is the performer of a particular action on both the previous day and the following day.

For this reason as well, it is that very same person who arises; for the subsequent recollection of what was previously experienced—expressed as "I saw this on the past day"—is not possible if someone else has arisen.
Indeed, one person cannot remember what was seen by another.
Furthermore, the recollection of the self expressed as "I am he" would not be tenable if a different self had arisen.
And from these words, it is understood that its emergence is indeed from that [Self].
For instance: "Again, according to the same method and according to the same path, it rushes forth toward the state of waking" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.16);
and "All creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2).
"Whether they become a tiger here, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—whatever they are, that they become" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3).
Passages such as these, recited in the context of sleep and waking, would not attain consistency if there were the arising of a different self.
This is likewise understood from the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge.
Otherwise, the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge would be purposeless.
For on the view that [the self] arises as something other [than the body], it would follow that one is liberated merely upon falling asleep.
If this were so, tell me, what would be accomplished by ritual action or knowledge, which yield results at a later time?

Furthermore, regarding the alternative position that [the self] arises from elsewhere: if the living being (*jīva*) were to arise while engaged in activity in another body, it would follow that the activity occurring there would be interrupted.
On the other hand, if it were to arise while sleeping there, the hypothesis would be purposeless;
for what benefit is gained by this hypothesis that one who was sleeping in a certain body arises in that same body, whereas one who was sleeping in one body arises in another?
If, on the other hand, the liberated one were to rise again, liberation would become finite;
moreover, it is illogical for one whose ignorance has ceased to rise again. By this, the rising of the Lord (Īśvara) is also refuted.
Because ignorance has been eternally ceased [in that state], and because,

under the view that [the self] arises from elsewhere, it would be impossible to avoid the fallacies of experiencing the results of actions not committed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of the results of actions committed (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*),
therefore it is that very same person who arises, and not another.

As for what was further stated— that just as a drop of water thrown into a mass of water cannot be extracted, so too a soul that has become merged [in Brahman] ought not to emerge— this is now refuted.
It is logical that in that case the drop of water cannot be extracted due to the absence of a cause for its separation.
In this case, however, there exists a cause for discrimination—namely, karma and ignorance—and thus there is a difference.
Furthermore, it is observed that even milk and water, which are difficult for those of our kind to distinguish when mixed together, can be separated by a swan.
Moreover, there is no such thing as a "living self" (jīva) distinct from the Supreme, which could be discriminated from the Existent as a drop of water is from the ocean.
It has been explained more than once that the very same [Self] is called the "jīva" due to contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

This being so, as long as the persistence of bondage remains associated with one adjunct, there is the conventional usage of "one jīva"; but when the persistence of bondage is associated with another adjunct, there is the conventional usage of "another jīva."

This very same adjunct (upādhi) [persists] through the states of sleep and waking according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout; therefore, it is logical that this very same individual soul (jīva) awakens. // 9 //
4. The Section on the Half-Attainment of the Fainting State. Sūtra 10:
The fainting state is a half-attainment, because of the remainder.
There exists that which is called "the fainted," which common people refer to as "one who has fainted."
In the investigation as to what state the *satu* is in, it is said:
first of all, three states of the living soul (*jīva*) while abiding in the body are well known—namely, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
the fourth is the departure from the body.
However, no fifth state of the individual soul (jīva) is well-known in either Śruti or Smṛti.

Therefore, since fainting must be one of these four states, such being the position reached, we reply: first of all, the person in a swoon cannot be in the waking state, for he does not perceive objects through his senses.
It might be argued as follows:

the person in a swoon will be like the archer. Just as an archer, though awake, does not perceive other objects because his mind is absorbed in the arrow, so too the person in a swoon, though awake, does not perceive other objects because his mind is preoccupied with the experience of pain produced by the blow of the club and the like.
This is not so, because there is no volition.
For the arrow-maker, with his mind occupied, says: "I was perceiving only the arrow for all this time."

But the one who has fainted, having regained consciousness, says, "I was cast into blind darkness for this long time; nothing at all was perceived by me. Furthermore, while the body of one who is awake—even if his mind is attached to a single object—is maintained [upright], the body of one who has fainted falls to the ground.

Therefore, it does not wake, nor does it see dreams, because it is devoid of consciousness; yet it is not dead, because warmth and breath still exist. For when a person has fainted, those who are in doubt as to whether he is dead or not touch the region of the heart to ascertain whether warmth is present or absent, and they touch the region of the nose to ascertain whether breath is present or not.
If they do not perceive the existence of breath and warmth, then, concluding "this one is dead," they carry him to the forest for cremation;
but if, however, they find breath or warmth, then, concluding "this one is not dead," they administer medical treatment to restore consciousness.
And because he rises again, it is clear that he has not gone to his destiny.
For one does not return from the realm of Yama.
Well then, let it be that the one in deep sleep [is the Self], because of being unconscious and because of immortality. No;
because of the difference in characteristics.

When in a state of fainting, he does not breathe for a long time, his body becomes trembling, and his face is terrifying with wide-open eyes. But when in deep sleep, his face is serene; he breathes repeatedly at regular intervals, his eyes are closed, and his body does not tremble.
They awaken one who is fast asleep merely by a touch of the hand, but not one who is in a swoon even with the blow of a mallet; furthermore,
there is a difference in the causes of swooning and sleep,
since swooning has its cause in the impact of a pestle and the like.
Furthermore, because sleep is caused by fatigue and other such factors,

and because it is not commonly established in the world that "one who is unconscious (mugdha) is asleep," we understand from the method of elimination that unconsciousness is a state of half-attainment [of deep sleep].
Because of the absence of perception, he is "merged" (*saṃpanna*); because of the difference from the other [states], he is "not merged.
But how can it be said that "half-mergence" constitutes the state of being stupefied?
For regarding one who is asleep, the Śruti has stated: "Then, my dear, he becomes merged with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
Thus, [it is said]: "In this state, the thief becomes non-thief" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22);
"Neither day nor night cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1), and so forth.
For the attainment of good and evil deeds by the individual soul occurs through the production of the cognitions of happiness and suffering.
Furthermore, neither the cognition of happiness nor the cognition of suffering exists in deep sleep,
and those two cognitions do not exist in one who is swooning either.
Therefore, due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts, just as in deep sleep, there must be a complete attainment [of dissolution] in the state of swoon as well, and not a partial attainment.
To this it is replied: We do not say that for one who has fainted there is a half-attainment of the soul's union with Brahman.
What then? We say that fainting belongs half to the side of deep sleep and half to the side of another state.
And the similarity and difference between fainting and sleep have already been demonstrated.
And this is the gateway to death:
when his karma still has a remainder, then speech and mind return [to the body];
but when the karma is without remainder, then the vital breath and warmth depart.
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman desire the attainment of half [of the fruit].
As for what was said— that no fifth state is well-known—
this is not a fault.
Otherwise, this state might not be well-known;
yet it is well-established in worldly usage, in Ayurveda, and so forth.
Furthermore, because it is accepted as a partial fulfillment [of the conditions], it is not counted as a fifth [cause]; thus, there is no fault. // 10 //
5. The Section Concerning Both Characteristics (Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 11–21. Sūtra 11:
"The Supreme [Self] does not possess both characteristics even from the standpoint of its locations, for [it is described as such] everywhere.

Now, the true nature of that Brahman with which the individual soul (jīva) becomes united during deep sleep and other states due to the cessation of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is determined on the basis of scriptural authority.

There are scriptural passages concerning Brahman that possess both types of characteristics; for instance, those with specific attributes such as "He whose work is all, whose desire is all, whose fragrance is all, whose taste is all" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2),
and those with negative attributes such as "Neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
These and other such passages exhibit the characteristic of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa-liṅga*).
Regarding these scriptural texts, it must be investigated whether Brahman is to be understood as possessing both characteristics (*ubhaya-liṅga*), or as possessing only one of the two;
and if it possesses only one, whether it is with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). Thus the inquiry proceeds.

In this regard, since both sets of scriptural indications regarding the two-fold characteristics are equally authoritative, it might be concluded that Brahman itself possesses both characteristics. To this we reply: first of all, it is not possible for the supreme Brahman to possess both characteristics by its own nature;

for it is impossible to maintain that a single entity, by its very nature, is both endowed with specific qualities such as form and the like, and yet the opposite of that, because of the contradiction involved.
Well then, let it be that [Brahman has both characteristics] "by way of location," due to its connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the earth and so forth.
That too is not tenable;
for even through association with an adjunct (*upādhi*), it is impossible for a thing that is of one nature to possess a different nature.
A crystal, being naturally transparent, does not become non-transparent through association with an adjunct such as lac-dye, because the adherence to its non-transparency is merely an illusion.

Furthermore, since limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), even when one adopts either of the two genders [masculine or neuter], Brahman must be understood as being devoid of all particularities and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), and not the opposite. For in all passages intended to establish the true nature of Brahman, it is said: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15).
In passages such as *muktiko* 2.72, Brahman alone, with all distinctions entirely cast aside, is taught.

[Objection: It is not so, because [the Self] is designated by its locus (*sthāna*), which is its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); [therefore, the Self appears different] due to that distinction. [Reply: No, because each [individual] is stated to be non-different from That (Brahman). (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.12)

Now, it might be argued that what was stated— that Brahman is indeed without conceptual differentiation (nirvikalpa) and possesses only a single characteristic (ekaliṅga), and does not possess both characteristics either by its own nature or from the standpoint of its states— is untenable. Why?
Because of difference;
for distinct forms of Brahman are taught according to each specific Vidyā.

Such as: "Brahman has four quarters," "Brahman has sixteen parts," "Brahman characterized by being the dwarf (Vāmanī), etc.," and "Brahman designated by the term Vaiśvānara, whose body is the three worlds"—these and others of this kind.
Therefore, it must also be admitted that Brahman possesses specific attributes.
As for the objection that it is not possible for Brahman to possess both sets of characteristics,
this too is not contradictory.
If it is argued that because the distinction in form is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
otherwise the scripture concerning distinctions would result in being entirely without a referent,
we say: no.
Why?
Because it does not speak of them as different.
For the scripture teaches that Brahman is indeed non-different with respect to each distinct limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), stating: "And he who is here in this earth... [and so forth].
"The person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is this embodied person within the self (*adhyātma*)— this very one is that which is this Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.1),
and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be asserted that Brahman possesses a connection with diverse forms according to the scriptures.
Because differentiation is for the purpose of meditation, the intended meaning lies in non-difference.
Moreover, some [scriptural branches] state it thus:

"Furthermore, in this way, certain followers of particular recensions (śākhins) record the teaching of non-difference alone, preceded by a censure of the perception of difference: 'By the mind alone is this to be attained; there is not the slightest multiplicity here. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).
"He goes from death to death who perceives here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.11).

Likewise, others also study that the entire phenomenal world, characterized by the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller, has Brahman as its sole nature: "Having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller—this threefold universe is for me Brahman alone" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12). // 13 //

But how is it that, when there exist Vedic texts concerning Brahman that teach it as having form and others that teach it as being without form, Brahman is determined to be only formless and not the opposite? To this, the author reads the following reply: "For that [Brahman] is indeed without form, because that is its primary nature. (BS 3.2.14)
Brahman alone is to be understood as being devoid of forms such as color and so forth, and not as possessing form and so forth.
Why?
Because that [absence of form] is its primary characteristic.
"It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8);

"Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15; Muktika Upaniṣad 2.72); "That which is called space is the revealer of name and form; that within which they are is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).

Statements such as, "For the divine, formless Person is both within and without, and is unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2), and "This is that Brahman— without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this self is Brahman, which has pervaded all things" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19)— have been established in the Sūtra *Tattu samanvayāt* (1.1.4) as being primarily concerned with the reality of Brahman as the Self devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), and not as having any other subject matter as their primary focus.
Therefore, regarding sentences of this kind, Brahman must be understood exactly as heard, as being indeed formless (*nirākāra*).
Other sentences concerning Brahman that describe forms, however, do not have that [form] as their primary subject;
for they primarily concern injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*). Since there is no contradiction in those cases, one should rely on them exactly as they are heard.

But when there is a conflict, those [scriptural passages] whose primary focus is that [Brahman] are stronger than those whose primary focus is something else. This is the reason for the definitive conclusion, by which, even though both types of scriptural texts exist, Brahman is determined to be formless alone, and not the opposite. // 14 //
What, then, is the status of those scriptural passages concerning objects that possess form? To this he says:
"And like light, because they are not purposeless" (BBs 3.2.15).

Just as light—whether solar or lunar—pervading space remains, yet when it comes into contact with limiting adjuncts such as a finger, it appears to assume their states, such as straightness or curvature, even though it does not truly do so.

In the same way, Brahman also, through its connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as earth and so forth, appears as if it were assuming their forms; thus, the teaching of specific forms of Brahman based on those adjuncts for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
In this manner, there will be no futility even for those scriptural passages concerning Brahman that attribute form to It.

Indeed, it is not reasonable to maintain that some Vedic statements possess meaningfulness while others are meaningless, since there is no difference in their status as authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

But even so, does this not contradict what was previously asserted—that Brahman possesses neither dual characteristics nor even the appearance of such due to association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
We say: no.
For it is impossible for that which is caused by a limiting adjunct to be an actual property of the reality itself.

Furthermore, since limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), we have stated in various places that the engagement in worldly and Vedic conventions occurs only when innate ignorance is present. (15)
And it says that it is merely that:

the Śruti also declares that Brahman is mere consciousness, devoid of any other distinct form and free from all distinctions— “Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a single mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior.”
"Entirely a mass of consciousness alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

This is what is meant: there is no form of this Self other than consciousness, either internally or externally; it is just like salt, which is a continuous mass of salty taste and has no other taste within it. // 16 // [FN:
*Saindhavaghana* refers to a lump of rock salt.]
Moreover, it is shown and also recorded in tradition.

Scripture shows that Brahman is devoid of distinctions precisely by negating any other form: "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), and "That is indeed different from the known, and moreover, above the unknown" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3).
"From whence words return, together with the mind, failing to reach it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1), and so forth;
and it is heard in scripture that Bāṣkala, having been questioned by Bādhva, spoke of Brahman through silence alone: "He said, 'Teach me!'"
"O sir! he said, and remained silent. Then, at the second or third request, he spoke to him: "We are indeed speaking, but you do not understand;
this Self is utterly tranquil.
Thus, even in the Smṛtis, it is taught solely by means of the negation of what is other: "I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality."
In such passages as, "The beginningless supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being" (13.12),
and likewise in the Smṛti, it is recorded that Nārāyaṇa, assuming his universal form, said to Nārada: "This is indeed a māyā created by me, O Nārada, that you see me thus."
"You should not know me thus as being endowed with all elemental qualities;
rather,
I am tranquil and have cast off duality."
And for this very reason, there is the simile "like the sun in water" and so forth.
(BBs 3.2.18) Since this Self is of the nature of consciousness, devoid of distinctions, transcending speech and mind, and is to be taught only by the negation of other attributes,

it is for this very reason that the simile of the sun in water and so forth is employed with the intention of referring to its appearance as possessing distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), though these are not ultimately real.

In the treatises on liberation (mokṣaśāstra): "Just as the sun, the unborn light, though one, enters into various waters and appears divided in many ways, so too this unborn Self, the Lord, assumes a form of diversity through limiting adjuncts (upādhi) within the fields (kṣetra).
"For there is only one Self of all beings, residing in every single being."
"In one way and indeed in many ways, it is seen like the moon in water" (Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 12), and so forth. // 18 //
To this, it is objected:
"But because there is no apprehension as in the case of water, there is not such a state [of identity].
(BBs 3.2.19) It is not tenable here that [the Self] is like the sun reflected in water and so forth, because it is not apprehended in that manner.

For indeed, in the case of material objects such as the sun, it is observed that their reflections arise when there is a material object distinct from them, located at a distant place; this is logical.
However, the Self is not material, nor are its limiting adjuncts (upādhis) distinct from it or located at a distance from it, because [the Self] is all-pervading and non-different from everything.
Therefore, this illustration is inappropriate. // 19 //
To this, it is replied:

"The participation in increase and decrease [is established] because of their inclusion [within the whole], due to the consistency of both; thus, this example is indeed appropriate because the intended aspect is present.
(BBs 3.2.20) However, this example is entirely fitting because the specific point intended to be illustrated exists within it.
For it is not possible for anyone to demonstrate complete similarity between an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) while excluding some intended aspect;
indeed, if there were total similarity, the very distinction between the illustration and the subject would be destroyed.
Moreover, this formulation of the analogy of the sun's reflection in water and so forth was not devised through mere personal fancy.
However, the mere purpose of this [treatise] as set forth by the author of the Śāstra is now introduced.
What, then, is intended here by "similarity"?
It is said: it is the state of participating in increase and decrease (*vṛddhihrāsabhāktva*).

For the reflection of the sun in water increases when the water increases, decreases when the water decreases, moves when the water moves, and is divided when the water is divided; thus, it conforms to the properties of the water, yet in ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), the sun does not possess such qualities.

In the same way, although Brahman is in ultimate reality unchanging and of a single nature, by being contained within limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body, it appears, as it were, to partake of the attributes of those adjuncts, such as increase and decrease.
Thus, because there is consistency between both the example and the subject of the illustration, there is no contradiction. // 20 //
And because it is seen [in scripture].
Scripture indeed shows the entry of the supreme Brahman alone into the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth: "He made bodies with two feet; He made bodies with four feet.
Having first become a bird, the Person entered the bodies" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.18).
And [it is said]: "Having entered by means of this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Therefore, it is correct that [the Sūtra states]: "And for this very reason, there is this comparison with the reflection of the sun and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.18).
Consequently, it is established that Brahman possesses only one characteristic—that of being free from conceptual differentiation—and not both characteristics, nor a contrary characteristic.
In this regard, some propose two points of inquiry.
First: Is Brahman of a single form, with all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) entirely subsided, or is it endowed with manifold forms like the phenomenal world?

Second: Assuming that the state of having all phenomenal proliferation subsided is established, is Brahman characterized by existence (*sat*), or by consciousness (*bodha*), or by both characteristics?
To this we reply: in every respect, the commencement of another section (adhikaraṇa) is purposeless.

If this effort is intended to refute the possession of multiple characteristics (anekaliṅgatva) by the supreme Brahman, then that should have been refuted by the preceding section itself, namely "Not even from the standpoint of location" (na sthānato ’pi); thus, this subsequent section is redundant, like the [section on] light (prakāśavat).
This would be entirely futile;
nor can it be said that Brahman has only the characteristic of existence and not the characteristic of consciousness,
for that would entail the absurdity of scriptural passages such as "Brahman is a mass of pure consciousness" being meaningless.
Or how could Brahman, from which consciousness has been excluded, be taught as the Self of the conscious individual soul (*jīva*)?

Nor can it be said that Brahman is characterized solely by consciousness and not by existence (*sat*), for that would result in the absurdity of rendering such scriptural passages as "He is to be perceived simply as 'He exists'" (Phaṭṭhaśruti 6.13) meaningless.
Or how could consciousness be accepted as having its existence negated?
Nor can it be said that Brahman possesses both characteristics,
for that would entail the consequence of contradicting your previous admission.

For one who asserts that Brahman is endowed with both consciousness excluded from existence and existence excluded from consciousness, that very same state of being possessed of manifoldness (prapañca) which was refuted in the preceding section would necessarily follow for Brahman.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because it is so stated in scripture, we say no.
Because it is logically impossible for a single entity to possess multiple natures. Now,
if it were argued that existence itself is consciousness and consciousness itself is existence, such that there is no mutual exclusion between the two,
even so, the alternative inquiry— whether Brahman is characterized by existence, or characterized by consciousness, or characterized by both— would remain entirely without a basis.
We have, however, interpreted the sūtras as having a single underlying subject.

Furthermore, since there are conflicting views regarding Brahman in the scriptural texts (śruti)—some presenting it as possessing form and others as being formless—once the formless Brahman is accepted, the status of the other scriptures must necessarily be explained.
In that sense, the sūtras such as "prakāśavat" (like light) and so forth become more meaningful as they serve that purpose.

Even if it is argued that those scriptural passages which speak of forms are intended solely for the realization of the formless by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and do not have a separate meaning of their own—that too does not appear to be correct.
Why?

Because certain phenomena are indeed mentioned in the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), such as: "His horses are yoked, hundreds and ten" (ŚU 3.1), and "These are indeed his horses; he is indeed thousands and many and infinite."

These and other such passages have the purpose of dissolution [of all distinctions], because of the concluding statement: "This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

Furthermore, as for the elaborations stated in the context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), such as "consisting of mind, having breath as its head, and having light as its form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2), it is not logical that they should have the purpose of dissolution (*prabilaya*). [This is because of the injunction:
"He should form a resolve" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).

Because they are connected with this very injunction for meditation (*upāsana*) which is under discussion—namely, that it is of such a kind—and because it is appropriate to understand that qualities of this sort serve the purpose of meditation according to the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is not appropriate to assume through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that they are intended for the purpose of dissolution (*pravilaya*). Furthermore, if all [qualities] were equally intended for dissolution, then [the Sūtra] would have stated: "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the principal subject" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.14).
Thus, the statement regarding the grounds for a definitive decision would have no scope.

Furthermore, it is understood that their fruits—according to the respective instructions—are, in some cases, the destruction of evil, in some cases the attainment of sovereignty, and in some cases gradual liberation;
therefore, it is logical that the meditative passages (*upāsanāvākya*) and the passages concerning Brahman (*brahmavākya*) are distinct, and not a single unified discourse.
And it must be explained how these [texts] are understood to form a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatā*).
If you argue that this is because a single *niyoga* (injunction) is perceived, as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, we say no;
for there is an absence of *niyoga* in the sentences concerning Brahman.

For it has been established in detail in the section beginning with "But that [Brahman, because of the harmony]" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.4) that the statements concerning Brahman terminate in the mere thing itself (*vastumātra*) and do not enjoin an action (*niyoga*).
Furthermore, it must be stated what object the injunction (*niyoga*) intended here would have;
for a person being enjoined is directed toward some specific activity of his own, as in the command, "Do this! (*kuru*).
But surely, the dissolution of the manifold of duality will be the object of yoga?

For as long as the manifold of duality has not been dissolved, there can be no realization of the reality of Brahman; therefore, the manifold of duality, which stands as an obstacle to the realization of the reality of Brahman, must be dissolved.
Just as a sacrifice is taught to be performed by one desiring heaven, so too is the dissolution of the manifold taught for one desiring liberation.

Just as one who desires to perceive the true nature of a jar or similar object situated in darkness must dissolve that darkness which stands in opposition to it, so too one who desires to perceive the reality of Brahman must dissolve the phenomenal world (prapañca) which stands in opposition to it;
for the phenomenal world has the nature of Brahman, but Brahman does not have the nature of the phenomenal world.
"By that dissolution of the proliferation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), there arises the realization of the reality of Brahman.
Regarding this, we ask: what is this so-called "dissolution of proliferation"?
Is the dissolution of proliferation to be effected like the melting of the hardness of ghee through contact with the heat of fire, or [is it like seeing] only one moon?

Just as the manifold appearance of many moons caused by ophthalmia must be dissolved by knowledge, so too the manifold appearance of name and form within Brahman, produced by ignorance, is to be dissolved by knowledge.

In this regard, if it were said that this manifold—consisting of the internal characteristics such as the body and the external characteristics such as the earth—is to be dissolved by the mind through knowledge, that dissolution would be impossible for a mere human being; therefore, the instruction regarding its dissolution [is given].
[Otherwise,] it would have to be an object that is possible [to dissolve].
Furthermore, since the dissolution of the earth and so forth was accomplished by one who was liberated at the beginning, the world would now be empty of earth and the other elements.
Alternatively, one might say that this phenomenal world, superimposed upon the one Brahman through ignorance, is dissolved by knowledge.
Then, by means of the rejection of the phenomenal world superimposed by ignorance, Brahman alone—unique and without a second—is to be made known through the teaching:
"That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
When that has been made known, knowledge arises spontaneously, and by that knowledge, ignorance is sublated.

Consequently, this entire manifold of names and forms, superimposed by ignorance, dissolves like the manifold of a dream. However, if Brahman has not been made known, then even if one were told a hundred times, "Realize Brahman and dissolve the manifold," neither the realization of Brahman nor the dissolution of the manifold would occur.

[Objection: But surely, once Brahman has been made known, there must be an injunction (niyoga) either regarding the cognition of that [Brahman] or regarding the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca). [Reply: No;
for both are accomplished by the very communication of the identity of the Self with Brahman, which is devoid of the phenomenal world.

For indeed, by the mere manifestation of the true nature of the rope, there occurs both the cognition of its true nature and the dissolution of the phenomenal world consisting of the snake and so forth superimposed through ignorance.
Furthermore, that which has already been accomplished is not performed again.

Moreover, as for the one called the "individual soul" (*jīva*) who is understood during the state of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), he must belong either to the phenomenal realm itself or to the category of Brahman. In the first alternative, since even the individual soul is dissolved—just like the earth and other elements—by the teaching of the reality of non-phenomenal Brahman, to whom could an injunction regarding the dissolution of the phenomenal world be addressed? Or to whom could it be said that [the soul] abides in that injunction?
It might be argued that liberation (mokṣa) is something to be attained.

Even in the second case, it is established that Brahman alone is the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is by nature incapable of being enjoined, whereas the state of being a soul is produced solely by ignorance; thus, since there is no one to be enjoined within Brahman, there is an absolute absence of injunction.

Furthermore, even words such as "should be seen" (draṣṭavya), though found in the context of higher knowledge (paravidyā), primarily aim at directing the mind toward reality, rather than primarily enjoining the cognition of reality itself.
In the world as well, in such instructions as "see this" or "hear this," one says only "perform the mental application" (*praṇidhāna*), not "produce knowledge directly.

Even for one who is oriented toward the object of knowledge, knowledge sometimes arises and sometimes does not arise; therefore, one who wishes to make something known must show the very object of that knowledge to that person.
Once that has been shown, knowledge arises spontaneously, according to the object and according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even for one who has been enjoined, a cognition contrary to reality regarding an object established otherwise by another means of valid cognition is not possible.
If, however, one who has been enjoined were to produce a contrary cognition thinking "I am being enjoined," that would not be a cognition; rather, it would be a mental action.
And if it were to arise otherwise of its own accord, it would simply be an error.
Knowledge, however, which is produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and has as its object things as they truly are, cannot be made to arise even by a hundred injunctions;
nor can it be prevented even by a prohibition.
For that [knowledge] is not dependent on a person.
For that [scripture] is indeed a vastutantra (a treatise concerning the nature of reality);
therefore, for this reason as well, there is an absence of *niyoga* (an injunction).

Furthermore, if the scripture were to terminate solely in *niyoga*, then the accepted doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self—which is not subject to injunction—would be rendered entirely without authority.

Now, if the scripture itself were to teach that Brahman is the Self of one who is not subject to injunction (*aniyojya*), and yet also enjoin a person toward the realization of that [Self], then it would follow that the single treatise on Brahman has two purposes and possesses contradictory purposes.

Furthermore, if it were intent upon injunction, there would be the abandonment of what is heard in the texts and the assumption of what is not heard; and like the fruits of ritual action, liberation would become a result of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and non-eternal—such defects could not be avoided by anyone.
Therefore, the statements concerning Brahman have as their ultimate purport the comprehension [of Brahman] itself, not the performance of an injunction (*niyoga*).
Consequently, it is incorrect to claim that they constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) based on the cognition of a single injunction.

Furthermore, even if one were to concede the existence of an injunction within the statements concerning Brahman, that unity would remain unestablished between those teachings that describe Brahman as devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*) and those that teach it as possessing phenomenal expansion (*saprapañca*).

For when a difference in injunctions (*niyoga*) is understood through means of knowledge such as distinct words and so forth, it is impossible to maintain that there is a single injunction everywhere.

In the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, unity is appropriate because they are non-different in their aspect of qualification (*adhikāra*). However, here, in the injunctions regarding the qualified and the unqualified [Brahman], there is no common element of qualification that would establish unity.
For qualities such as consisting of light do not assist in the dissolution of phenomenal diversity, nor does the dissolution of phenomenal diversity assist qualities such as consisting of light,
because they are mutually contradictory.
For it is not logical to combine within a single substratum both the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and the dependence upon a portion of that same phenomenal world.
Therefore, the distinction we have stated regarding the teachings on the "possessing form" (*sākāra*) and the "formless" (*anākāra*) is indeed more reasonable. // 21 // [Note:
For this Lord who has attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), the ten *harayaḥ* are either the objects or the sense organs.]
To that seeker of knowledge:
a word whose object is a distinct sentence-meaning is a "different word" (*śabdāntaram*).
Section on the Limitation of the Manifested (*prakṛtaitāvattva-adhikaraṇa*), Sūtras 22–30.

"For [the text] denies that the nature of Brahman is limited to what has been previously mentioned, and then declares further beyond that. Having begun with, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1),
and having divided the five great elements into two groups, [the text speaks of] the essence of food and the one denoted by the word "Person" (puruṣa).
After showing forms such as those dyed with saffron and others, it is further recited: "Now, therefore, follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this.
For there is nothing else higher than this 'not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
In this regard, we wish to know what the object of this negation is.
For here, no specific thing to be negated is perceived such that one could say "this is that.
However, by means of the word *iti*, something to be negated is indeed implied here, because the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) is directed toward the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

It is observed that when the word *iti* is employed, it relies on what is proximate and functions similarly to the word *evam* (thus), as in examples such as: "The teacher used to say thus," and so forth.
And here, by the force of the context, two forms of Brahman along with their manifold extensions are present, for these two are the forms of that Brahman.
Regarding this, a doubt arises in us: does this negation negate both the forms and that which possesses the forms, or only one of the two?
And even if it negates only one, does it negate Brahman while leaving the two forms remaining, or does it negate the two forms while leaving Brahman remaining?
In this regard, we suspect that because there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion, both [aspects] are negated;
for these two negations exist due to the twice-occurrence of the word "not.
Of these two, by one the form of Brahman along with its manifold world (saprapañca) is negated, and by the other, it is understood that Brahman possesses form (rūpavat).
Alternatively, it is Brahman itself that is denied as possessing form; for since Brahman transcends speech and mind, its existence is not easily conceived and thus it is fit to be denied.
However, the manifold of forms (rūpa-prapañca) is not fit to be denied, as it falls within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge.
The repetition [of the negation], however, is for the sake of showing reverence.
This being the case, we reply:
first of all, the negation of both [existence and non-existence] is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of nihilism (śūnyavāda).
For something is negated only by taking recourse to some ultimate reality, just as a snake and the like are negated in relation to a rope and so forth.
And that [negation] is possible only when some entity remains as a residue.
But if both are negated, what other entity could remain as a residue?

Furthermore, if another entity is not left over while one attempts to negate the other, then because that [remaining entity] cannot be negated, it follows that it alone possesses ultimate reality (paramārtha), and thus the negation becomes untenable.
Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable, because it would contradict the introductory statement, "I shall tell you of Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and so forth; [for it would imply]:
"He becomes non-existent indeed."
Because this would contradict such censures as "If one knows Brahman as non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1),
[the truth is that] "He is to be apprehended as indeed existing" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.13).
This is because it would contradict the aforementioned restriction and lead to the undesirable consequence of subverting all the Vedānta scriptures. Furthermore,
the fact that Brahman transcends speech and mind is not stated with the intention of implying its non-existence.

For it is not the case that, after Brahman has been established in the Vedāntas with such great effort through passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), its non-existence would then be asserted once again.
For there is a well-known maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
However, this is merely the method of exposition [employed here], as expressed in the passage: "From whence words return, together with the mind, not having attained it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).

This is what is meant: Brahman is that which transcends speech and mind, does not fall within the sphere of objects, is the innermost Self (pratyagātman), and is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free. Therefore, it must be accepted that [the scripture] negates the manifold expansion of forms (rūpa-prapañca) belonging to Brahman and leaves Brahman alone as the remainder. This very point is stated in the sūtra: "For it negates the extent of the manifested world as previously described."
This word negates that very form of Brahman which has been under discussion—namely, this much, limited in extent, and characterized as both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).

For that [form] was introduced and elaborated in the preceding text with reference to the divine (*adhidaivata*) and the corporeal (*adhyātma*); and from that very [form] arises another form, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), termed "the person" (*puruṣa*), which is of the nature of the essence of the formless and rests upon the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*).
This has been demonstrated through similes such as those of the great multitude;
for it is impossible for the Person (*puruṣa*), whose essence is formless, to possess a form that can be grasped by the eye.

Thus, it is understood that this form of Brahman, along with its manifold elaborations (*saprapañca*), is presented to the negative particle (*nañ*)—the negator—by means of the word "iti," which refers to what is immediately present.

In the preceding text, Brahman was indicated by the genitive case as a qualifier of "form" (*rūpa*), and not as the primary subject itself. Once its two forms have been elaborated upon, this inquiry into the true nature of that which possesses those forms is commenced with the words: "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
It is thus determined that this [instruction] is the revelation of the true nature of Brahman through the negation of its superimposed forms.
For this entire world of effects, which has that [Brahman] as its substratum, is negated by the words "not this, not this" (neti neti).

And it is logical that the non-existence of the effect is established through such negation— based on scriptural passages such as "a mere modification of speech" (vācārambhaṇam)— but this does not apply to Brahman, because Brahman is the very root of all conceptual constructions regarding agency and causality.

Nor should this doubt be raised: "How is it that the scripture itself, having shown two forms, then again prohibits them, as in the saying, 'It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off'?
For this scripture does not point out the two forms of Brahman as objects to be established [as ultimate reality].

It is faultless to hold that these two forms, well-known in the world, are referred to as being imagined upon Brahman for the purpose of negation and for the purpose of establishing the nature of pure Brahman.
Furthermore, these two negations negate both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) respectively, according to the principle of corresponding order.
Alternatively, the former negation negates the aggregate of elements (*bhūtarāśi*), while the latter negates the aggregate of latent impressions (*vāsanārāśi*).

Alternatively, this repetition "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) means that whatever may be imagined, all that is not Brahman. For if a negation were made of only a limited number of things, there would arise the inquiry: "If this is not Brahman, what else could be Brahman?"

But when there is the repetition [of the particle "not"], because the entire range of objects is negated, the inquiry ceases with the realization that Brahman is the inner self (pratyagātman), which is not an object [of cognition].

Therefore, the conclusion is that [the scripture] negates only the phenomenal world (prapañca) imagined upon Brahman, while leaving Brahman itself intact. For this reason as well, this alone is the conclusion.
Because of that very negation, he speaks further: "There is something else beyond" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
For if the negation were intended as a mere non-existence, why would he say, "There is something else beyond"?
In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: having indicated Brahman by saying "not this, not this," he then explains that very indication.
What is the meaning of "not this, not this" (neti neti)?
It means that there is nothing other than this Brahman; therefore it is said "not this, not this," but it does not mean that Brahman itself does not exist.
And it shows that there exists another, supreme, unprohibited Brahman.
When, however, the syllables are construed in this way— "Not indeed, not indeed" (*neti neti*)—
meaning that there is no further instruction regarding Brahman other than this teaching in the form of the negation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*),
then the phrase "and he speaks again from that" should be construed as referring to the matter of the name.
Now, regarding the name: "The truth of truth—life-breath (prāṇa) is indeed truth, and of these, this [ātman] is the truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20).
For it says this;
and that [name] becomes appropriate when the negation culminates in Brahman.
But if the negation were to terminate in non-existence (abhāva), how could it be said that "the Truth of truths" exists?
Therefore, we conclude that this negation terminates in Brahman, and does not terminate in non-existence. [Note:
The three elements—earth, water, and fire—are "mūrtam" (possessing form).]
Because wind and space are formless, they constitute two groups;
mahārājana is turmeric, for it is said that this is unmanifest. (BBs 3.2.23)
If that Supreme Brahman, which is other than the prohibited realm of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), exists, why is it not perceived?
It is said in reply: It is unmanifest (*avyakta*) and cannot be grasped by the senses, because it is the witness of all that is visible.
For the Śruti declares thus: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other deities, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8).
"This very Self is 'not this, not this'; it is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26);
"That which is invisible and ungraspable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6);
"For when he [the wise man] has entered into that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1), and so forth.
Smṛti also states: "This is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.25), and so forth. // 23 //
Moreover, [the existence of the Self] is established through perception and inference during its propitiation (saṃrādhana).
Furthermore, at the time of propitiation, yogins perceive this Self as unmanifest and devoid of all phenomenal proliferation (prapañca).
Propitiation consists in the practice of devotion, meditation, focused concentration, and so forth.
How, then, is it understood that they see [the Self] at the time of propitiation?
The meaning is: through perception and inference, that is, through Śruti and Smṛti.
For thus says the Śruti: "He pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self."
"A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned inward" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1);
and likewise, "With the clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified then sees Him, the partless, through meditation" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8),
and other such passages.

Smṛti also says: "Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, have conquered their breath, are contented, and have restrained their senses, perceive as light while practicing yoga."

"And yogis behold that eternal Blessed One," and so forth. [FN: The Self-existent Lord, having made the senses—which are directed outward and do not grasp the Self—withdrawn, has shone forth; he whose eye is turned inward has restrained his senses.]
Free from sleep and free from darkness;
those who practice yoga are meditators;
the Self attainable through yoga is the yogic Self.

[Objection: But surely, because of the acceptance of the relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator, there would be a difference between the self of the other and one's own self.
[Reply: No, it is said— "And as in the case of light and so forth, there is non-differentiation; and light [is manifested] through practice in action. (BS 3.2.25)

Just as light, space, the sun, and so forth appear as if possessing distinctions when limited by conditions such as a finger, a hand, or water, yet do not abandon their own inherent nature of non-distinction, even so this differentiation of the Self is caused solely by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), while its true essence remains one with the Absolute.
For instance—in the Vedāntas, the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme conscious self (prājña) is established through repeated practice. // 25 //
Therefore, [the Self] is infinite; for such is the indicative mark.

And because non-difference is innate and difference is produced by ignorance, the individual soul, having shaken off ignorance through knowledge, attains oneness with the supreme, infinite, conscious Self.
For there is an indicative mark to this effect: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
"Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), and so forth. // 26 //
"But because of the designation of both [aspects], it is like a snake and its coils" (3.2.27).
With regard to that very relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator, he presents another view for the sake of clarifying his own position:

"In some places, a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the wise Self (prājña) is designated, as in: 'But from Him, seeing Him as partless through meditation... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8).
Thus, by way of the meditator and the object of meditation, and the seer and the object seen;
and by way of the goer and the goal to be reached, [one attains] the divine Person who is higher than the high (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).
In some places, however, the non-difference of those two is designated: "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10),
and "This is your Self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).
"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3).
Since both [kinds of] designations occur there, if non-difference alone were taken as the absolute truth, the designation of difference would be without any basis.
Therefore, because we observe both designations, the reality here must be like that of a serpent and its coils.
Just as "snake" refers to non-difference [of the essence], while "coiledness," "expansion," and "length" refer to difference, so it is here as well. // 27 //
Or, it is like light and its locus, because of its being luminous (tejastva).
Alternatively, this should be understood as being like light and its locus:
just as light and its locus, the sun, are not absolutely distinct, since there is no difference between the two in their nature as luminosity.
And yet, just as in those cases they are indeed subject to distinct designations, so it is here as well. // 28 //
Or as before; or rather, it must be exactly as previously proposed— that there is no distinction [between the two], like light and so forth— for in this way,
since bondage is produced by ignorance, liberation through knowledge becomes logically possible.

If, however, it were admitted that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) there exists some bound self that constitutes a particular configuration of another self— according to the analogy of a snake and its coils— or that it occupies a specific part of it— according to the analogy of light and its substrate— then, because an ultimately real bondage could not be dispelled, the futility of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would follow as a logical consequence.
Nor does the Scripture here designate both difference and non-difference as being of equal status;
for it points out non-difference alone as that which is to be established, whereas it merely restates difference—which is already well-known—as a means to intend a different meaning.
Therefore, the final conclusion is precisely this: "And like light and so forth, there is no distinction. // 29 //
And because of the prohibition [of another].
For this very reason, this alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The reason is that the scripture prohibits any conscious being other than the Supreme Self, stating: "There is no seer other than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
And so forth.
"Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) is the instruction from the Father;
"This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

And thus, because of the refutation of the phenomenal world as distinct from Brahman and because of the remaining of Brahman alone, it is understood that this indeed is the established conclusion. // 30 //
7. The Section on the Other (Topic): Sūtras 31–37.
"On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference, [Brahman] is different from the highest.

(BBs 3.2.31) A doubt arises due to conflicting scriptural statements regarding whether there exists some other reality higher than this Brahman, which has been determined as being devoid of all manifoldness (prapañca). Some texts suggest that there is something else beyond it, while others suggest there is not. Thus, there is uncertainty.
For indeed, certain passages, appearing at first glance, seem to establish a reality even higher than Brahman;
it is for the purpose of providing a refutation of these that this undertaking is begun.
Therefore, there ought to exist a reality other than the supreme Brahman.
Why? Because of the designation as a bridge, the designation of measurement, the designation of relation, and the designation of difference.
First, regarding the designation as a bridge: "Now, that which is the Self is a bridge, a support" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).
This proclaims the state of being a bridge for Brahman, who is denoted by the word "Self."
For in common worldly usage, the word *setu* (bridge/dam) is well known to refer to a collection of earth, wood, and so forth that interrupts the flow of water;
