yet here, the word *setu* is applied to the Self (*ātman*). Thus, it implies the existence of something other than the worldly bridge—namely, the "bridge of the Self"—as in the passage: "Having crossed the bridge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.2).
And because of the use of the word "crosses" (*tarati*) in this way:

just as one crosses a worldly bridge and reaches a non-bridge, a desert region (*jāṅgala*), so too it is understood that having crossed the Self which is the bridge, one reaches the non-Self which is not a bridge.
Furthermore, there is a designation of measurement: "This Brahman has four quarters, eight hooves, and sixteen parts."
Furthermore, it is well known in the world that there exists an object other than a kārṣāpaṇa coin or the like, which is measured and delimited as "this much.
Similarly, from the measurement of Brahman, it is understood that there must exist an entity other than it.
Likewise, there is also an expression of relationship: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).

Thus [it is said]: "the embodied self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.3.1), and "completely embraced by the conscious self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21). Furthermore, the connection of limited things with that which is limited is observed, as for example, that of men with a city.
Furthermore, it designates the relationship between individual souls and Brahman during deep sleep;
therefore, it is understood that there exists something else beyond that which is immeasurable.
Moreover, the designation of difference leads to this very same conclusion.
For instance: "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6)—thus the Lord residing in the sun is designated;
then, by way of distinction, He designates the Lord residing in the eye: "Now, this person who is seen within the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).

Furthermore, He extends [the attributes] of the former to the latter regarding form and so forth: "The form of this one is the very same as the form of that one; whatever the two songs of that one are, these are his two songs; whatever the name of that one is, this is his name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
Thus, it designates the lordship of both as being limited: "And he rules over those worlds which are beyond that [sun], and over the desires of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8), referring to one;
and "And he rules over those worlds which are below this [moon], and over the desires of men" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.6), referring to the other.
"Just as this [is called] the kingdom of the Magadha king, or this the kingdom of the Vaideha king.
[FN: A region abounding in wind is *jāṅgala*.
Thus, when it has been established on the basis of these designations such as "bridge" (*setu*) and so forth that there exists something superior to Brahman, the following is set forth:
"But on account of generality" (sāmānyāt). The word "but" (tu) precludes the [logical] consequence that has been indicated.
Nothing other than Brahman can exist, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) [to establish it].
For we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of anything else; indeed,
it has been established that for every class of produced entities, their birth and so forth proceed from Brahman,
and that the effect is non-different from its cause.

Furthermore, nothing unborn other than Brahman is possible, because of the restrictive determination [in the scripture]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Moreover, since there is the promise of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, the existence of any entity distinct from Brahman cannot be conceived.
Now, it was argued that designations such as "bridge" and so forth indicate a reality distinct from Brahman;
to this we reply: no.
First of all, the designation "bridge" is not capable of establishing the existence of something external to Brahman.
For it is said, "The Self is the bridge," and "There is nothing beyond that.
Since there is no "beyond" in that context, the nature of being a bridge would not be possible; thus, something further must be postulated.
But this is not logical.

Because it would contradict scriptural passages such as "unborn" (*ajātva*), the term "bridge" (*setu*) is applied to the Self only by way of a commonality; thus, it is appropriately used. The commonality of being a "bridge" in the case of the Self consists in its being the supporter of the world and its boundaries.

Therefore, the Self under discussion is praised as being "like a bridge" (seturiva setuḥ). Even in the expression "having crossed the bridge" (setuṃ tīrtvā), since it is impossible for one to cross over a bridge [in the literal sense], the verb *tṛ* functions in the sense of "reaching" or "attaining.
Just as in the case of the expression "he has crossed grammar" (*vyākaraṇaṃ tīrṇaḥ*), which means he has mastered it, not that he has passed beyond it, so it is here. // 32 //

"It is for the purpose of cognition, like the feet" (BBs 3.2.33). As for what was stated—that there exists something beyond [the Self] because of the designation of measurement—that is now addressed: even the designation of measurement is not intended to establish the existence of an entity distinct from Brahman.
What, then, is the purpose of this conceptualization?

It is for the sake of meditation—that is to say, so that a cognition in the form "Brahman has four feet, eight hooves, and sixteen parts" might indeed become firmly established in Brahman; thus, by means of its manifestations, the measurement of Brahman is merely being imagined.

For it is not possible for all persons to establish their understanding in Brahman, which is changeless and infinite, because of the differences in the intellects of men—whether they be of dull, middling, or superior capacity.
It is like the case of the "feet.

Just as in the case of the mind and space, which are taught as symbols (*pratīka*) of Brahman with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine realm (*adhidaivata*), four "feet" consisting of speech and so forth are attributed to the mind, and four consisting of fire and so forth [are attributed to space].
[The quarters] belonging to space are likewise [divided] for the purpose of meditation.

Alternatively, "like the quarters" means that just as a division into quarters is conceptually constructed for a kārṣāpaṇa coin for the sake of facilitating common transactions—since not all people are always able to transact using the entire kārṣāpaṇa due to the lack of fixed rules regarding quantities in buying and selling—the same applies here. This is the meaning. // 33 //
FN: The attribution of measurement to Brahman is for the sake of the meditative practice of those of dull intellect, just as a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin is spoken of in terms of its quarters;
it is due to its particular location, like light and so forth.
In this Sūtra, the refutation of both [the objections regarding] the difference in connection and the difference in designation is provided.
As for what was also stated—that on account of the designation of relationship and the designation of difference, there must be something higher than that—this too is incorrect;
because even for a single entity, these two designations are possible with respect to particular locations.
Regarding the designation of relationship, this is the meaning:

When the specific cognition that has arisen through association with particular limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) ceases upon the cessation of those adjuncts, that cessation is designated as "union with the Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). This is a figurative expression (*upacāra*) dependent solely upon the adjuncts, not dependent upon any limitation [of the Self].

Likewise, even the designation of difference regarding Brahman is figuratively applied in dependence on the difference of adjuncts, and not in dependence on a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*), as is indicated by the employment of the analogy "like light and so forth."

Just as in the case of a single light—whether solar or lunar—which acquires particularity through association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there occurs a designation of relation upon the cessation of those adjuncts, and a designation of difference due to the diversity of the adjuncts;
or just as in the cases of the space within a needle's eye or a water-jar, these two designations of relation and difference occur solely in dependence on limiting adjuncts, so it is here. // 34 //
And because it is logical:

such a connection alone is appropriate here, and no other; for [the text], "He becomes merged in his own Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), teaches this connection as one of essential nature (*svarūpa*), and because that essential nature is imperishable.
A relationship according to the analogy of a man and his city is not tenable;
however, because its own nature is concealed by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the statement "he becomes merged in his own self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1) is logically consistent.
Likewise, a difference of any other kind is not possible, because it would contradict the well-established doctrine of the oneness of the Lord found in numerous scriptural passages.
Thus, scripture explains that even for the single ether, a designation of difference based on location is justified: "That which is the ether outside the person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.8).
"That which is this space within the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.9). // 35 //
Likewise, because of the negation of others (tathānyapratiṣedhāt).
Having thus demolished the arguments of the opposing side regarding the designations of a "bridge" and so forth, he now concludes his own position with another reason:
likewise, from the negation of others, it is understood that there is no other entity beyond Brahman.
For instance: "He alone is below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1),
"I alone am below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1),
and "The Self alone is below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2).
"Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6);
"Brahman alone is all this; the Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"There is not the slightest diversity here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1).

Since there is nothing whatsoever higher than this (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9), and since such scriptural passages as "This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19)— which belong to their own respective contexts— cannot be interpreted as having any other meaning, they exclude the existence of any other entity distinct from Brahman.
And because of the scriptural statement that [the Self] is within all, it is determined that there is no inner self other than the Supreme Self. // 36 //
By this [means], through the words "extent" (*āyāma*) and so forth, its omnipresence is established.
By this refutation of designations such as "bridge" and by resorting to the negation of anything else, the omnipresence of the Self is also proven;
otherwise, it would not be proven.
For if the designations such as "bridge" and so forth were accepted in their primary sense, it would follow that the Self is limited, since the bridge and the like would constitute its very nature.
Likewise, even if there were no negation of other things, the fact that one object is distinguished from another object would still result in the consequence that the Self is limited.
Furthermore, its omnipresence is understood from the word "extent" (āyāma) and other scriptural passages.

The word *āyāma* signifies pervasion; for example: "As far as this space extends, so far does this space within the heart extend" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3); "All-pervading and eternal like space" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.7); "Greater than heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3);
"Greater than space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3); and "Eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.24).
For such scriptural passages, traditional texts, and logical arguments as these demonstrate that the Self is omnipresent. // 37 //
7. The Section on the Fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 38–41: "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (BBs 3.2.38).
Another nature of that very Brahman is described in its empirical state, characterized by the distinction between the ruler and the ruled.

Regarding the threefold fruit of action—consisting of the desirable, the undesirable, and the mixed—which is well known among living beings as belonging to the sphere of *saṃsāra*, there arises an inquiry: does this result from action, or rather from the Lord (*īśvara*)?
In this regard, it is first established that the fruit must indeed proceed from the Lord.
Why? Because it is logically consistent (*upapatti*).

For he, as the universal supervisor, performing the manifold acts of creation, maintenance, and destruction, brings about for the agents of action fruits corresponding to their deeds, which is logical because he possesses knowledge of the specific details of place and time.
However, it is illogical that an action— which perishes moment by moment— should have a fruit occurring at a later time, because an effect cannot arise from non-existence.
It might be argued: "An action, while perishing, produces its own corresponding fruit at its very time of occurrence and then perishes; that fruit will be experienced by the agent at a later time.
This too is not tenable, because until there is a prior connection with an experiencer, it cannot logically be established as a "fruit."
For it is well known in the world that whatever pleasure or pain is experienced by oneself at a particular time belongs to that very [self] as its fruit;
indeed, worldly people do not recognize the status of being a fruit for a pleasure or pain that is unrelated to the self.
Now, it might be argued: "Let there not be the production of a fruit immediately after the action."
The claim that the fruit will arise from the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the action is also untenable;
for it is impossible for the *apūrva*, being insentient and equivalent to wood or a clod of earth, to act unless it is impelled by a sentient being.
And because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.

If it is argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the valid means of cognition, we say no; for once God is established [by other means], the necessity for presumptive testimony ceases. // 38 //
FN: Desired [karma] leads to heaven; undesired [karma] is suitable for states such as the Avīci hell;
and mixed [karma] results in the experiences of human beings.
*Samsāra* is that which has as its basis the stream of birth and death;
and because it is taught in scripture (*śrutatvāt*).

Not only do we postulate God as the cause of the fruit based on logical reasoning (*upapatti*), but rather, we consider God alone to be the cause of the fruit because it is taught in scripture as well.
And thus there is a scriptural passage: "He indeed is that great, unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24), and others of a similar kind. [FN:
He is called the "eater of food" (annāda) because he gives food (anna) completely (āsamantāt) to all living beings.]
"Vasudāna" means a giver of wealth. "Dharma" [is so called] because of this very reason; the teacher Jaimini, however, considers Dharma to be the giver of the fruit.
For this very reason, both on account of scripture (*śruti*) and logical consistency (*upapatti*):
first, this meaning is heard in such scriptural passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*).
And in that context, because the injunction (*vidhi-śruti*) accepts the sacrifice as its object, it is understood that the sacrifice is the producer of heaven.
Otherwise, the sacrifice would result in being one that lacks a performer, and in that case, its instruction would be rendered purposeless.
Now, it may be argued that since the ritual act perishes moment by moment, a fruit cannot logically arise from it; thus, this position has been abandoned.
This is not a valid objection.
Because the authority of scripture [is decisive].
If scripture is the authority, then this connection between action and its fruit, as it is heard in scripture, must be understood in such a way that it is logically consistent.
And an action, perishing without first producing some "unseen potency" (*apūrva*), is not capable of yielding a fruit that is temporally remote.
Therefore, it is inferred that there exists a certain subtle subsequent state of the action, or a prior state of the fruit, which is termed "the unseen" (*apūrva*).
This meaning is established by the manner already explained.
However, the claim that God bestows the fruit is untenable.

Because it is impossible for a non-variegated cause to produce a variegated effect, as that would entail the faults of partiality and cruelty, and because it would result in the futility of ritual performance;
therefore, the fruit arises from dharma alone. // 40 //
"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord is the cause] because of the designation of a cause.
However, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers the previously mentioned Lord alone to be the cause of the fruit.
The view that the fruit arises from action alone or from the *apūrva* alone is set aside by the word "but" (*tu*).
The established conclusion is that the fruit [of action] arises from God, whether it be through dependence on *apūrva* (unseen merit/demerit) or through dependence on *karman* itself.
Why? Because of the designation of Him as the cause.

For God is designated as the cause of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) by virtue of being their instigator, and as the giver of the fruit. As it is said: "For He indeed causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds."
"He indeed causes him to perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward.
And this same meaning is recorded in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Whatever form a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his unshakable."
"Endowed with that faith, he strives for His propitiation and thereby obtains the desired objects, which are indeed ordained by Me alone" (7.21).
Furthermore, in all the Vedāntas, creations are declared to have the Lord as their sole cause.
And that very fact—that the Lord creates offspring in accordance with their own past actions—is precisely what constitutes His being the cause of their fruits.
Furthermore, defects such as the impossibility of diverse effects do not apply to the Lord, because He takes into account the efforts previously exerted by beings. // 41 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
**Third Quarter of the Third Chapter** [In this section, there is an exposition on the integration of qualities in the knowledge of the higher and lower Brahman.]
1. The Section on the Uniformity of Knowledge in All Vedāntas. Sūtra 1.4:
There is uniformity of knowledge regarding Brahman in all Vedāntas, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
The true nature of Brahman, which is to be known, has been explained.
Now, however, it is investigated whether the cognitions (*vijñāna*) differ from one Vedānta text to another or not.

But surely, Brahman—the object of cognition—has been determined to be devoid of distinctions such as before and after, uniform in essence like a mass of salt; how, then, can there be any introduction of an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of cognitions?
For it cannot be said that, as in the case of the multiplicity of ritual acts (*karman*), a multiplicity of Brahmans is intended to be taught in the Vedāntas.
Because Brahman is a single entity and possesses a single nature,
and because multiple forms of cognition cannot coexist within a single Brahman;
for it is not the case that when the object is one way, the cognition is another way, and yet it be non-erroneous.

If, however, many cognitions of Brahman were intended to be taught in various Vedānta texts concerning a single Brahman, then one of them would be non-erroneous while the others would be erroneous; this would lead to a lack of confidence in the Vedāntas.

Therefore, it is not possible to suspect a difference in the cognition of Brahman for each respective Vedānta text. Nor can its non-difference be asserted on the grounds of the non-distinction of injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth.
Because the knowledge of Brahman is not characterized by injunction (*codanā*).

For the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] stated in the sūtra, "But that [is established] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*, Brahma-sūtra 1.1.4), that the knowledge of Brahman is produced by the statements concerning Brahman—which terminate in the reality of the thing itself—and which have as their primary purport not injunctions.
How then does he undertake this inquiry into difference and non-difference?

To this it is replied: there is no fault here, for this discussion regarding the difference or non-difference of cognitions concerns both the qualified Brahman and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

For in this context, difference and non-difference of meditations (*upāsanā*) are possible just as they are of ritual acts (*karman*); and like ritual acts, these meditations are said to have either visible results or the result of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by way of the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding these [Upanishads], the following reflection arises:
is there a difference in the consciousness (vijñāna) taught in each Vedānta, or is it not so?
In this regard, the arguments for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) are first set forth.
First of all, it is well known that a name serves as a cause for the cognition of difference, as seen in the case of "light" (*jyotis*) and other such terms.

Furthermore, in this context, there are various distinct names for the cognitions enjoined in different Vedānta texts, such as the *Taittirīyaka*, the *Vājasaneyaka*, the *Kauthumaka*, the *Śāṭyāyanaka*, and so forth.

Likewise, a difference in form (*rūpa*) is also well known to establish a difference in ritual action (*karman*), as in the case of "the curd for the Viśvedevas" and "the whey for the Vājins," and so on.
Moreover, there is a difference in form here;
for example—some followers of the Vedic branches prescribe a sixth additional fire in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), while others recite only five.
Likewise, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth, some record speech and the other organs as fewer in number, while others record them as more.
Likewise, a specific feature of the ritual (*dharmaviśeṣa*) has been suspected as an indicator of a difference in action (*karmabheda*) in the case of the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others;
and such a specific feature exists here,
namely, the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) of the Atharvaṇikas.
Furthermore, other grounds for differentiation, such as repetition and so forth, should likewise be applied to the various Vedānta texts as far as possible.
Therefore, it follows that there is a difference in the cognitions (vijñāna) according to each Vedānta text.
This being the position reached, we reply: the cognitions taught in all the Vedānta texts must be one and the same in each respective Vedānta text.
Why? Because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.

By the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), the reasons for non-difference set forth in the *Siddhānta-sūtra* of the section on different Vedic branches (*Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*) are drawn in here; the meaning is: "because there is no difference in the connection, form, injunction, and name."

Just as in the case of a single Agnihotra sacrifice, even though there are differences in the Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the same human effort is enjoined by the injunction "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*);

likewise, in the passages "He who knows the eldest and the best" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.1.1; *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.1.1), the injunction is exactly the same for both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas.
The connection with the purpose is also indeed the same, as stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.1.1): "He becomes the eldest and the best among his own people.
The form in both cases is also the very same for the knowledge—that is, the reality of Prāṇa endowed with specific qualities such as being the eldest and the best.

And just as the substance and the deity constitute the form of a sacrifice, so should the object of knowledge be understood as the form of this knowledge; for by that [object], the knowledge is defined.
The designation itself is also the same, namely "the science of the vital breath" (*prāṇavidyā*).
Therefore, the cognitions [of Brahman] are based on all the Vedāntas.
In this same way, it should be applied to the science of the five fires, the Vaiśvānara science, the Śāṇḍilya science, and so forth.

However, those apparent causes of differentiation such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth have already been refuted in the very first section, beginning with the words: "It would not exist by name, because it is not designated by an injunction" (*codanā*). [The author] now raises a specific objection regarding this point and refutes it: (Note: An *codanā* is that which impels; it is human effort, for it is an activity of the person.
Here too, having raised a certain specific doubt, he provides a refutation.)
If it is argued that [the knowledge derived from different Upanishads] is not identical because of differences [in qualities], we say no; for this would apply even to a single [Upanishad].
It might be thought:
the identity of the cognitions arising from all Vedānta texts is not tenable due to the difference in their qualities (*guṇabheda*).

For instance, the Vājasaneyins, having introduced the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), mention a sixth fire as another [fire] in the passage beginning with, "For him, fire itself becomes the fire" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.2.14).
The Chandogas, however, do not mention that [sixth fire], but conclude [the teaching] with the number five alone, saying, "Now, he who thus knows these five fires" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.10).
Since this quality exists for some and does not exist for others, how can a single knowledge (*vidyā*) be possible for both?
Furthermore, the combination of qualities cannot be understood here, because it would contradict the number five.
Likewise, in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the Chandogas mention four other breaths besides the chief one: speech, sight, hearing, and mind.
The Vājasaneyins, however, record even a fifth [meditation]: "Prajāpati is indeed semen; he who knows this is procreated with offspring and cattle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.6).

If it is argued that there is a difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) due to the difference in insertion and omission (*āvāpodvāpa*), and consequently a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*)—just as there is a difference in sacrifice due to the difference in substance and deity—this is not a valid objection.
Since such a difference in qualities is possible even within a single Vidyā—

despite the fact that the inclusion of a sixth fire is not possible— nevertheless, because the five fires beginning with Heaven (dyu) are recognized as identical in both places, there can be no difference in the Vidyās; for the Aṭirātra sacrifice is not divided by the taking or non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Moreover, the sixth fire is recited by the Chāndogyas: "When he has departed from here, they carry that deceased person, as destined, to the fires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.2).

However, the Vājasaneyins, for the purpose of terminating the conceptualization of fuel, smoke, and so forth—which had been applied to the five fires in their preparatory meditation—state: "For him, fire indeed becomes fire; fuel, fuel" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.14).
Such passages as these are constant restatements (*nityānuvāda*).
Even if this statement is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), nevertheless that quality can be combined even by the Chāndogyas;
nor should any contradiction with the number five be suspected here.
For this number five, intended to refer to the fires of the *sāṃpādika* meditation, is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) and not an integral part of the injunction; thus there is no fault.
In the same way, even in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the inclusion of an additional quality elsewhere is not contradictory.
Nor should one suspect a difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*) or a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) due to the variation of addition and subtraction (*āvāpodvāpa*).
Because, even when certain portions of the object of knowledge are added or subtracted, one perceives no difference in the vast mass of that which is to be known;
therefore, there is indeed only a single science. [Note:
"Diṣṭam" means having departed from this world to another world; "haranti" means the kinsmen carry [the deceased] to the fire.]
"Because of the nature of the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya), because of the qualification for the Samācāra [section], and because of the rule regarding it being like the Sava sacrifice.
This is said in response to the claim that there is a difference in knowledge (vidyā) because the followers of the Atharva-veda require the "head-vow" (śirovrata) and others do not.
That is a property of the study of one's own Veda, not of the knowledge itself.
How is this understood?

Because, in the *Samācāra*—a text devoted to the instruction of Vedic observances (*vedavrata*)—the followers of the Atharvaveda record that this [practice] as well has been explained as a Vedic observance, stating: "One who has not performed the vow does not study this" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.11). It is understood as such because it possesses the nature of a duty to be tasted (*svādya*) in its true state.

Thus, from the word *iti* referring to the subject matter of the original author, and from the words *adhyaya* and *adhyayana*, it is determined that this is indeed a duty pertaining specifically to the study of one's own Upanishad.

But, one might object: since the text "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow (*śirovrata*) has been performed according to rule" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.10) mentions a connection with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and since the knowledge of Brahman is one and the same everywhere, would this duty not be conflated [with all such teachings]? No.
In that case as well, because there is no reference back to the subject matter by the word "this" (*etām*),
and because the state of being manifest (*prakatatvam*) of the knowledge of Brahman depends upon a specific text, this duty is connected only with that specific text.
The phrase "and like the *sava* sacrifice, its restriction [is fixed]" is an indication of an illustrative example.

Just as the seven sacrifices beginning with the Saura and ending with the Audana are restricted to the Atharvaṇikas alone—because they are not connected with the three fires mentioned in other Vedas, but are connected with the single fire mentioned in the Atharva Veda—so too this duty (dharma) is restricted to that [Atharva Veda] because of its connection with a specific study of that text.
Therefore, the oneness of the knowledge (vidyaikatva) remains beyond reproach. // 3 //
And it is also shown [by scripture].

The Veda too shows the unity of knowledge, because all Vedāntas teach the unity of the object of knowledge, as in: "That which all the Vedas proclaim" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15). Likewise: "For the Bahvṛcas investigate this very one in the great Uktha; the Adhvaryus [investigate] this in the fire; the Chandogas [investigate] this in the Mahāvrata. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17)

Likewise, in the Taittirīyaka, there is seen a reference to the quality of fear-causality belonging to the Lord—which was stated in the Kaṭhaka as "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt" (Ka. 6.2)—for the purpose of censuring the perception of difference: "For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him. (Taitt. Up. 2.7)
"In that very [state] there is fear for the one who knows [it] but does not reflect" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).

Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka, Vaiśvānara—who has been established as being the size of a span—is referred to in the Chāndogya as an established fact: "But he who meditates on this very self, Vaiśvānara, as of the measure of a span and as all-pervading" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).

Likewise, because the *uktha* and other elements enjoined elsewhere are taken up for the purpose of enjoining meditation (*upāsana*) in another context, it is established by the principle of "observation of the majority" (*prāyadarśananyāya*) that meditations also possess the character of being recognized across all Vedāntas.

**The Section on Synthesis (Upasaṃhārādhikaraṇa)** Sūtra 5: And there is synthesis [of details] when [the meditation] is the same, because the object is non-different, as in the case of the supplements to injunctions. (BBs 3.3.5)
This is the aphorism concerning the purpose.

And since it is thus established that all Vedānta texts have the same purport, there occurs a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the qualities of the knowledge mentioned in one place within the same knowledge elsewhere as well,
because there is no difference in the object.
For that very purpose served by those qualities in one instance— which is to assist a specific cognition— is the same in the other as well;
since in both cases it is that single cognition [which is assisted], there is therefore a transfer [of the qualities],
just like the remainder of a ritual injunction (*vidhiśeṣavat*).

Just as there is a combination of the subsidiary elements of the *agnihotra* and other rites—since the single act of the *agnihotra* and so forth remains the same everywhere due to the non-difference in their meaning—so it is here as well.

For if there were a difference in the cognitions (*vijñāna*), then because the qualities would be bound to different cognitions and because there would be no relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), there could be no combination.
But since the cognition is one, this is not the case.
However, an elaboration of this very sūtra concerning the purpose will follow, beginning with the words "Because of the non-difference of all. (5)

3. The Section on Change (Anyathātvādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 6–8. "If it be argued that there is a difference [in the Udgītha] because of the scriptural word, we say no, because there is no distinction. (Brahmasūtra 3.3.6) In the Vājasaneyaka [it is said]: "Those gods said, 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1)

Having begun with the passage, "They said to Speech: 'Chant for us'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2), and having censured the vital breaths beginning with Speech as being pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the acceptance of the principal breath is recorded:
"Then they said to this breath in the mouth: 'Chant for us'; 'So be it,' [said] that breath to them."
"Then he rose up" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.7).

Likewise, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as well, after introducing the passage—"The gods then approached the Udgītha, thinking, 'By this we shall overcome them'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.1)—and having censured the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*) for being pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the selection of the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is likewise recorded: "Then they meditated upon that which is this principal breath as the Udgītha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7)
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7).
In both cases, it is determined that there is an injunction for the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā) through the praise of the vital breath.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is there a difference between these two knowledges here, or rather, is there oneness of knowledge?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That the unity of the knowledge follows from the aforementioned reasoning.

But is it not improper to maintain the unity of the knowledge because of the difference in the introductory contexts? For the Vājasaneyins begin in one way, while the Chandogas begin in another: "Do thou sing for us" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2).

Thus, the Vājasaneyins enjoin the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the agent of the *udgītha*, whereas the Chandogas enjoin it as the *udgītha* itself, stating: "They meditated upon that *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7). If it be asked how there can be identity of the two meditations (*vidyā*) in such a case:
This is not a fault;
for the unity of the knowledge does not depart merely because of this distinction,
since a much greater degree of non-distinction is also perceived.

For instance— the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras, the intention regarding the destruction of the asuras, the introduction of the Udgītha, the mention of speech and the other [organs], the censure thereof, the taking refuge in the chief vital breath (prāṇa), and the destruction of the asuras by its power through the illustration of the clod of earth and the stone—
all these many matters are perceived as being identical in both [chapters].
In the Vājasaneyaka as well, the co-referentiality of the *udgītha* with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is heard: "This, indeed, is the *udgītha*" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.23).
Therefore, even in the Chāndogya, agency must be understood as indicated; and from that, the identity of the two meditations follows. // 6 //
FN: "Āsanyam" means that which exists in the mouth (*āsya*).
This dialogue is intended for the overcoming of the Asuras, for the purpose of conquering them.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and other such passages. (BBs 3.3.7)
Nor is it logical that there is merely oneness of knowledge; rather, in this case, a difference in knowledge is what is logical.
Why?
Because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*).
The meaning is "due to a difference in the introductory context.
For instance, here a difference in the introductory context is observed.
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, for example: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya 1.1.1).

Having thus introduced the fact that the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, is to be meditated upon, and having provided an explanatory exposition of its qualities such as being the "most savory" (*rasatama*), [the text] continues: "Now, indeed, there follows an explanatory exposition of this very syllable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1).

Then, following once again that same *oṃ* which is a constituent of the *udgītha*, it says: "By means of the narrative of the Devas and Asuras, they meditated upon that *prāṇa* as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.2).

In this context, if the word *udgītha* were intended to signify the entire liturgical section (*bhakti*), then since its performer is the *udgātṛ* priest, the initial statement would be contradicted and a figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) would have to be resorted to.
Furthermore, there must be a conclusion in accordance with the beginning within a single passage;
therefore, in this context, the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—is being taught.
In the Vājasaneyaka, however, because there is no reason for taking the word *udgītha* to refer to a mere part, the entire liturgical portion (*bhakti*) is indicated.

In the passage, "Do thou sing for us" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2), the agent of that [singing] is likewise described as the vital breath (prāṇa) by way of being the Udgātṛ priest; thus, this constitutes a different method of exposition.

Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the vital breath with the *udgītha* there is intended solely to demonstrate that the vital breath—which is sought to be shown as the Udgātṛ—is the Self of all; therefore, it does not bring about the identity of the two meditations (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, there is a difference [between the two cases] because in that [other case] as well, the word *udgītha* refers exclusively to the entire act of devotion (*bhakti*).

Nor can the status of the *udgātṛ* (chanter) be discarded from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on the grounds of impossibility; for just like its state as the *udgītha*, its state as the *udgātṛ* is taught as being for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*).
And since the *udgātṛ* performs the function of the *udgātṛ* solely through the power of the vital breath, there is no such impossibility.
And so it has been declared in that very same place: "With speech and with breath he sang the udgītha" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.24).
Furthermore, when a difference in the intended meaning is clearly perceived, it is not proper to determine identity of meaning based merely on the imitation of the phrasing of the sentence.

For instance, in the *abhyudaya-vākya* and the *paśukāma-vākya*, [the injunction] "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts; those which are medium-sized, those one should offer to Agni... [is repeated].

Although there is a similarity in the injunctions such as "one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Dātṛ," because of the difference in the introductory context (*upakrama*), it is determined that in the *abhyudaya* passage there is a removal of the deities,
whereas in the passage concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), there is an injunction for a sacrifice.
Likewise here too, there is a difference in knowledge due to a difference in the introductory context (*upakrama*), as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and so forth.

For example, even though there is a commonality in the superimposition of the vision of the Supreme Self, [it is said]: "The ether is indeed greater than these; the ether is the ultimate resort" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
"This very Udgītha is higher than the high, it is infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2).

Thus, the meditation on the Udgītha as characterized by the quality of being "higher than the high" is distinct from the meditation on the Udgītha as characterized by qualities such as having golden hair and a golden beard located in the eye, the sun, and so forth.
And just as there is no mutual combination of qualities within even a single Śākhā, the same applies to meditations of this kind situated in different Śākhās. // 7 //
FN: "Difference" (*vaiṣamya*) refers to the diversity of the sciences in both cases.
"Removal" (*apanaya*) means separation.
"Higher than the high" (*parovarīyān*) means more excellent than the most excellent.
If it is argued that [the unity of the science] is established by name— that is, "But even that [name] exists" (BBs 3.3.8)—
and it is further stated that because the names are identical, the unity of the science is logical here, since the name "Udgītha-vidyā" is one and the same for both,
that too is not tenable.
For this has been stated: "Or rather [it is not so], because of the difference in context, as in the case of the 'higher than the high' and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.7).

That alone is more reasonable here, for it follows the literal sense of the scripture; whereas the identity of name is outside the literal sense of the scripture and is merely a figurative usage by worldly speakers based on the employment of the word *udgītha* alone.
And this identity of name exists even in the case of meditations such as the "higher than the high," where the distinction is well-known, yet both are designated as the "Udgītha-vidyā."

Likewise, even for those rites such as the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are well-known to have distinct forms, the designation "Kāṭhaka" is observed when they are recited in the single text of the Kaṭhas; so it will be here as well.
However, where there is no such cause for distinction, let there be identity of knowledge due to the unity of the name, as in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā and others. // 8 //
4. The Section on Pervasion (Vyāptyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 9:
"And because of pervasion, [the meditation on the syllable *Om*] is appropriate.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1): "One should meditate upon this syllable *Om* as the *Udgītha*."

Thus, since the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words *akṣara* and *udgītha* is heard here, and because the alternatives of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), sublation (*apavāda*), identity (*ekatva*), and qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) present themselves, an inquiry arises as to which of these positions is logical. Among them, "superimposition" means that when the cognition of one of two things has not yet been set aside, the cognition of the other is superimposed upon it; and in that case, even when the cognition of the other has been superimposed, the original cognition of the former thing continues to persist.
Just as when the cognition of Brahman is superposed upon a name, the cognition of the name continues to persist and is not removed by the cognition of Brahman;

or as the superposition of the cognition of Viṣṇu and others upon images and the like— so too here, the cognition of the syllable *akṣara* is superposed upon the *udgītha*, and the cognition of the *udgītha* upon the syllable *akṣara*.

Sublation (*apavāda*) is that wherein, when a false cognition previously established regarding some object has become certain, a subsequently arising cognition conforming to reality serves as the remover of that previously established false cognition.

For example, the notion of a self with respect to the aggregate of the body and senses is removed by the subsequent cognition of the Self itself, namely, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7)
Thus, by means of this cognition of reality, [the error] is removed;
just as the cognition of a disorientation regarding direction is removed by the cognition of the true nature of direction.
Or, just as the cognition of a disorientation regarding direction is removed by the cognition of the true nature of direction.
In the same way here as well, the notion of the syllable is set aside by the notion of the *udgītha*, and the notion of the syllable is set aside by the notion of the *udgītha*.
However, the identity between the words "syllable" (*akṣara*) and "*udgītha*" consists in their referring to an object that is not distinct from one another,
just as [the terms] "best of the twice-born," "Brāhmaṇa," and "god on earth" [refer to the same person].

Furthermore, the qualification serves to assign a specific portion of the Sāmavedic chant (audgātra) to the syllable "Om," which pervades all the Vedas, lest there be the contingency of grasping the syllable in its entirety.
Just as one says, "Bring that lotus which is blue," so too here it means: "One should meditate upon that syllable Om which is the Udgītha."

When this sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is thus examined, these alternative positions appear; since there is no cause for determining any one among them, and a lack of determination has ensued, this is stated: "And because of pervasion, [the view] is consistent. This word "and" (*ca*) is placed in the position of the word "but" (*tu*), with the purpose of excluding the three other positions.
Thus, in this context, the positions involving [literal] destruction are excluded as being faulty;
only the position of qualification is accepted as faultless.

Regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*) first: if a cognition were superimposed upon one thing while belonging to another, it would follow that the word functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and its result would have to be postulated.
If it is argued that the fruit is indeed heard [in scripture], as in "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7) and so forth, we say no; for that has a different fruit.
For that is the fruit of the view [of identity] with Āpti and so forth; it is not the fruit of superimposing [the qualities of] the Udgītha.
Even in the case of negation (apavāda), the absence of a fruit is the same.
If it is argued that the fruit is the cessation of false knowledge, we say no.
This is because no utility for human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is perceived [in such an identification].
Furthermore, the cognition of "Oṃ" in the syllable *oṃ* never ceases, nor does the cognition of "Udgītha" in the Udgītha;
moreover, this sentence is not intended to establish the true nature of reality.
This is because [the text] is devoted to the injunction for worship (*upāsanā-vidhi*).
Nor does the position of identity (*ekatva-pakṣa*) hold together; for in that case, the utterance of two words would be purposeless, since the intended meaning is conveyed by one alone.
Furthermore, there is no established usage of the word *udgītha* for the syllable *oṃ* in the context of the office of the Hotṛ or the office of the Adhvaryu;
nor is there an established usage of the word *udgītha* for the entire second division (*bhakti*) of the Sāman;

nor is there an established usage of the word *oṃ* for that which is denoted by the word *udgītha*—namely, the entire second division of the Sāman—by virtue of which they could be considered identical in meaning.
By process of elimination, the view that it is a qualifier is accepted,

because pervasion is common to all the Vedas. Lest the syllable (akṣara) that pervades everything be [inappropriately] implied here, the syllable is qualified by the word "udgītha," so that the syllable *oṃ*— which is a constituent part of the udgītha— might not be understood.
"But is it not the case that even in this view, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is equally present,
since the word 'udgītha' has the sense of indicating a part [of the whole]?
True, this is so.
However, even in the case of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), there indeed exists a distinction between proximity and remoteness.

For in the view of superimposition (adhyāsa), the cognition of one object is projected onto another object; thus, this secondary indication is remote. On the other hand, words functioning under the view of qualification (viśeṣaṇa) are observed to apply to their constituent parts as well, as in the cases of "cloth" or "village."
And therefore, because of this pervasion, it is logical and faultless that "this syllable Om" is a qualification of "the Udgītha"; such is the meaning. // 9 //
5. The Section on Non-Difference of All (Sarvābhedādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 10:
"In other [texts], [the same] because of the non-difference of all.

In the dialogue concerning the vital breath (prāṇa) among both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is stated that the vital breath, endowed with the quality of preeminence, is the object of meditation.

For speech and the other organs are also described there as being endowed with qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), and these are then restored back into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of passages such as, "Insofar as I am the most excellent, you are that most excellence" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14). Furthermore, in the dialogues concerning the vital breath among other recensionists, such as the Kauṣītakins, it is said: "Now, therefore, the attainment of the highest good; these deities, indeed, were disputing over who was the best" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.14).

In such passages as these, the pre-eminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) is stated, but these qualities such as being the most excellent (vasiṣṭhatva) and so forth are not mentioned. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: should these qualities such as being the most excellent, which are mentioned in one place, be extended to other places as well, or should they not be extended? On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they should not be extended.
Why? Because of the connection with the word "thus" (evam).
In various passages, such as "Now, he who, knowing thus, having recognized the highest good in prāṇa," the object to be known is presented by means of the word "thus.
And the word "thus" refers to what is proximate; it cannot present a collection of qualities of that kind which is recited in another branch of the Veda.
Therefore, [it might be argued that] the state of having no further expectancy is fulfilled by the qualities mentioned only within its own specific context.
This being the position reached, the author replies: "In this restrictive rule, qualities such as being the best (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, though mentioned in one place, apply elsewhere as well.
Why? Because of the non-difference of all [the Upanishads]."
For in every instance, that very same single knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is recognized as undivided,
due to its similarity in form with the dialogue concerning the vital breath and so forth.
And since there is no difference in the knowledge itself, how could these qualities mentioned in one place not be accepted elsewhere?
But has it not been stated that, in various places, the word "thus" (evam) presents a collection of qualities of this kind for the purpose of being known?

To this it is replied: although the collection of qualities found in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa is not explicitly mentioned by the word "thus" in the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa because it is not proximate, nevertheless, within that very same cognition, it is indeed mentioned by the word "thus" in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa; thus, even what belongs to another recension is included when it is encompassed by a non-differentiated cognition.
The collection of qualities is distinguished from that which belongs to one's own branch;
yet this being so, there is neither the abandonment of what is heard nor the assumption of what is not heard.
For even within a single branch, the qualities heard there are indeed heard everywhere, because there is no difference in the possessor of those qualities.

For Devadatta, though famous in his own country for qualities such as heroism, does not cease to possess those qualities when he goes to another country simply because they are not perceived by the inhabitants of that other land.
And just as in that case, through a particular familiarity, Devadatta’s qualities are perceived even in another country,
so too, through a particular application, the qualities to be meditated upon in one recensional text (śākhā) may be extended to another recensional text as well.
Therefore, those properties connected with a single primary purpose, even when stated in only one place, must be applied everywhere. [10] [Note:
*Niḥśreyasa* means the attainment or determination of excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*). *Ahaṃśreyase* means for one's own excellence.]
6. Section on Bliss and Other Attributes. Sūtras 11–13:
Bliss and other attributes belong to the Principal [Brahman].

(BBs 3.3.11) In those scriptural passages intended to establish the essential nature of Brahman, certain attributes of Brahman—such as its being of the nature of bliss, its being a mass of consciousness, its omnipresence, and its being the self of all—are mentioned in various places.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are the attributes of Brahman, such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, to be understood in each instance only as many as are heard in that particular context, or are all of them to be understood everywhere?

Since it might be concluded that the attributes are to be understood according to the specific division of the scriptural texts, this is said in reply: the attributes of the primary reality, Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, are all to be understood everywhere.
Why?
Precisely because of the non-difference of all [texts].
For everywhere, that same one Pradhāna—the qualified Brahman—is not divided.
Therefore, the attributes of Brahman are universal, by virtue of that very example of Devadatta’s heroism mentioned in the preceding section. 11.
But if this were so, would not attributes such as "having joy as its head" also become confused across all [texts]?
For instance, in the Taittirīyaka, with reference to the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is recorded: "Joy indeed is its head;
delight is its right wing."
"Bliss is the highest part; joy is the self; Brahman is the tail, the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
To this, he recites the following:
"There is no attainment of [qualities] such as 'having pleasure as the head' and so forth, because increase and decrease exist only where there is difference.
(BBs 3.3.12) There is no attainment elsewhere of those attributes such as "having pleasure as the head" which are recorded in the Taittirīyaka.

For the reasons that pleasure (*priya*), joy (*moda*), delight (*pramoda*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are perceived as having degrees of intensity— whether in relation to one another or in relation to different experiencers—
and since increase and decrease are possible only where there is difference,
Brahman is indeed without differentiation, being "one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, these qualities—having joy as the head and so forth—are not attributes of Brahman;
rather, we have already taught in the sūtra "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.12) that these are attributes of the sheaths (kośa).
Moreover, these [attributes] are postulated merely as means for directing the mind toward the supreme Brahman, and not as things to be perceived [in Brahman itself].
Even so, it is all the more impossible for [qualities] such as "having pleasure as its head" to apply elsewhere [than to the individual soul].

However, having treated these as attributes of Brahman, the Teacher has merely demonstrated this logical principle: that [qualities] such as "having pleasure as its head" do not apply [to the individual soul].

And that same principle is to be applied to other ascertained attributes of Brahman taught for the purpose of meditation, such as "having all things gathered" (*saṃyadvāma*) and so forth, and "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) and so forth.

For even though the Brahman to be meditated upon is one and the same, since there is a difference in the meditations due to the difference in the introductory contexts, there is no transfer of the attributes of one to the other.

Just as two women may serve a single king—one with an umbrella and the other with a fly-whisk—wherein, despite the oneness of the object of service, there is a difference in their service and a fixed arrangement of their respective duties, so it is here as well.

For the quality of being augmented or diminished is possible only in the case of Brahman possessing qualities (saguṇa) when there is the conventional usage of distinction, but not in the case of the supreme Brahman which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, the meaning is that attributes such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva), though heard in certain places, do not apply everywhere. // 12 //
"But the others, on account of the identity of their meaning.

(BBs 3.3.13) But the other attributes, such as bliss and so forth, which are mentioned solely for the purpose of establishing the nature of Brahman, should be understood everywhere because of the identity of the subject, Brahman, to whom they belong; thus there is a difference [from the former case], for they serve the sole purpose of bringing about comprehension. // 13 //
7. The Section on Contemplation (Ādhyānādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 14–15:
"For the sake of contemplation, because there is no other purpose.
(BBs 3.3.14) For it is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind."
Beginning with "The intellect is higher than the mind" (Ka. 3.10) and ending with "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" (Ka.

3.11), there arises a doubt: Are all these objects, beginning with the earth, each taught as being higher than the preceding one, or is it the Person alone who is taught as being higher than all of them?
In this regard, the view arises that all of these are indeed presented as being superior;
for it is heard [in scripture]:
"This is superior to this," and "This is superior to this."
But surely, if many meanings are intended to be conveyed as being primary, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
This is not a fault,
because the existence of multiple sentences is logically justified.
Indeed, these many statements are capable of establishing various objects endowed with supremacy;
therefore, each of them establishes supremacy individually.
This being the position reached, we reply: it is logical that the Person alone is to be established as supreme by all of these, and not that supremacy is established for each of them individually.
Why?
Because there is no purpose.
For when the others are understood as being "other," no purpose is seen; the purpose is the accomplishment of liberation.
And so says the Śruti: "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death" (Kaṭha 3.15).

Furthermore, by means of the negation of anything else and by using the word *kāṣṭhā* (the ultimate limit), it shows respect for the Puruṣa as the subject; thus it demonstrates that the discourse concerning the preceding and succeeding currents is intended solely for the realization of the Puruṣa.
The phrase "for the sake of meditation" (*ādhyānāya*) means for the sake of perfect knowledge preceded by meditation.
For in this context, meditation is taught solely for the purpose of right vision; meditation itself is not the primary goal. // 14 //
And because of the word "self" (ātman).
For this reason as well, this discourse on the stream of the senses and so forth is intended solely for the purpose of understanding the Person (puruṣa);
because [it says]: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."
"However, it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, with a sharp and subtle intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.12);
thus the text refers to the Puruṣa under discussion as the Self (ātman).
From this, it is understood that the intention is to show that all others are non-Self (anātman).
And he demonstrates that very [Self] is difficult to know and is to be reached through the measure of the conditioned;
for the sake of knowing it, he prescribes meditation in such passages as, "The wise man should restrain speech and mind" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.13).
This has been explained under the sūtra, "Even that which is based on inference [is Brahman], for some [scriptures] mention even one" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.1).
Thus, in various ways, an extraordinary abundance of intention regarding the Person is observed in the Śruti, and not in others.
Furthermore: "He reaches the end of the journey; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.9).

When this has been said, in response to the inquiry, "What is that further shore of the path? It is Viṣṇu’s supreme abode," it is determined from the sequence beginning with the senses that this progression is indeed for the sake of attaining the supreme abode. Section on the Comprehension of the Self (Ātmagṛhītyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 16–17: "The comprehension of the Self [is established] as in the other case, because of what follows. (BBs 3.3.16)

In the Aitareyaka it is heard: "Verily, in the beginning, this was the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Ai. 1.1); and "He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and Āpas" (Ai. 1.2), and so forth. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the Supreme [Brahman] alone denoted by the word "Self," or is it some other [entity]?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the Supreme Self cannot be denoted by the word "Self" here.
Why?
Because we observe the consistency of the context of the passage.

But is it not the case that the syntactical connection of the passage is clearly seen to have the Supreme Self as its subject, because it establishes the oneness of the Self prior to creation and because it speaks of a creator preceded by reflection? No, it is replied.
Because of the mention of the creation of the worlds (*loka*).

For if the Supreme Self were intended as the creator, the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) would have to be mentioned first; however, here the creation of the worlds is mentioned at the outset.
And the worlds are specific arrangements of the great elements.
And likewise, [the text] explains water and the other elements as being worlds themselves, in such passages as: "That which is beyond the sky is water" (Ai. 1.2).

Furthermore, the creation of the worlds was carried out by another lord presided over by the Supreme Lord, as seen in such texts as: "He became a person" (Bṛ. 1.4.1). Smṛti also states: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called Puruṣa."
"He was the first creator of beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning.

The followers of the Aitareya also, in the preceding section of the passage "Now, therefore, from semen [arose] Prajāpati; from the semen of Prajāpati, the gods," record a manifold creation having Prajāpati as its agent.
Furthermore, the word *ātman* is seen used for him: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1).
The determination of oneness prior to creation is also logically consistent with respect to its own modifications;
likewise, its act of "seeing" is justified by the admission of its sentience.

Furthermore, numerous specific activities of this kind—such as "bring a cow for them," "bring a horse for them," "bring a man for them," and "they said"—are well known in the case of worldly individuals who possess distinct characteristics.
Here, [the opponent] follows [the argument]:
"Therefore, the self here must be some particular [limited] entity.
This being the position reached, we reply: "The supreme Self alone is grasped here by the word 'Self,' just as in other cases."
Just as in other scriptural passages concerning creation, such as "From that very Self, indeed, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the Supreme Self is understood;

and just as in other worldly usage of the word "Self," the inner self alone is primarily grasped by the term "Self," so too should it be here. However, where [it says], "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad...);
In such passages as these, other qualifiers such as "of human form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1) are heard, and there the Self might indeed be understood specifically;
however, in this case, a subsequent qualifier is found that is entirely consistent with the understanding of the Supreme Self: "He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1).
"He created these worlds" (Ai. 1.2), and so forth.
Therefore, it is logical that he alone [the Self] is being referred to. // 16 //
FN: Ambhas is heaven;
Marīcis is the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka);
Mara is the world of mortals (martyaloka).
The waters are the world of Pātāla.
"Puruṣavidhaḥ" means having the form of a man;
"ātman" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha;
"retas" means the product of semen.
If it is argued that [the Supreme Self is meant] because of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*), then [we reply]: it would be so because of the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).
That which was stated previously—that the Supreme Self is not being grasped here because we observe the syntactical connection of the sentence—must now be refuted.
To this, it is said:
It might be so because of the restriction;
that is, the apprehension of the supreme self would be logical.
Why?
Because of the definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).
For if the Supreme Self is grasped, the definitive determination of the oneness of the Self prior to creation is appropriately understood as direct;
otherwise, it would have to be conceived as indirect.
As for the statement regarding the creation of the world, I shall interpret it as occurring after the creation of the gross elements well-known from other scriptural passages;

just as I have interpreted the passage "That [Self] created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3) as occurring after the creation of space and air well-known from other scriptural passages, so it is here as well.
For a specific detail well-known from another scriptural passage (śruti) that pertains to the same subject must be integrated into other scriptural passages.
Furthermore, this sequence of specific activities, such as "He brought a cow from them," must also be understood only insofar as it accords with the determination of the intended meaning.
Indeed, it cannot be said that this entire narrative sequence is what is intended to be expressed.
Because there would be no human purpose in practicing that [merely as a ritual act],
whereas it is the identity with Brahman that is intended here.
For thus, after teaching the creation of the worlds beginning with water and the world-protectors beginning with Agni, [the text teaches] the organs.

Having taught that the body is the locus of the instruments of action, the same Creator, having reflected—"How indeed might this exist without me?"—is shown to have entered this body in the passage: "He, having split open this very crown of the head, entered through this door" (Ai. 3.12).

Furthermore, after first discerning the functions of the organs through such passages as, "If it is uttered by speech, if it is breathed by the vital breath" (Ai. 3.12), and having investigated with the thought, "Now, who am I? (Ai.
3.11), he beheld this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman (Ai. 3.13).
Thus, he establishes the realization of Brahman as the Self.

Likewise, later on, in the passage beginning with "This is Brahman, this is Indra" (Ai. 5.3), having sublated the entire range of differentiated entities along with the great elements, [the text declares]: "All that has consciousness as its leader, is established in consciousness; consciousness is the leader of the world, consciousness is the foundation; consciousness is [Brahman]."
The passage, "Brahman" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.3),
specifically determines that it is the vision of the identity of the self with Brahman;
therefore, the apprehension of the Self here is beyond dispute.
Another interpretation: "The grasping of the Self [is Brahman], as in the other cases, because of what follows.

In the Vājasaneyaka, having begun with the word "Self" in the passage, "Which is the Self? He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the person" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), the text establishes that this very Self is Brahman by demonstrating its state of being entirely free from all attachments.
For thus he concludes: "That indeed is this great unborn Self, undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).

In the Chāndogya, however, having commenced without even the word "Self" in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), it concludes at the end: "That is the Self; That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Thus, he teaches identity.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: do these two scriptural recensions have the same meaning, or do they have different meanings?
First, it is argued that they must have different meanings, because the two recensions are dissimilar.
For it is not reasonable to assume an identity of meaning when there is a discrepancy in the scriptural texts, since the determination of meaning is dependent upon the specific wording of the text.
In the Vājasaneyaka, because the discourse begins with the word "Self" (ātman), it is understood that the instruction concerns the reality of the Self;
however, in the Chāndogya, due to the reversal of the opening statement, there is a reversal of the instruction.
"But was it not said that even among the Chandogas there is an instruction of identity in the concluding portion?
True, this was said;
however, because the conclusion is dependent upon the opening, he considers that [instruction] to be merely the attainment of identity.

This being the case, it is replied: "The apprehension of the Self must also apply to the Chandogas in the passage, 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), just as in other cases;
for example, [the question] 'Which is the Self? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7)."
In this regard, for the Vājasaneyins, the Self is likewise grasped;
why?
Because of the subsequent teaching of identity.
If it is argued that [the self is not grasped] because of the connection with what precedes, we reply: "It would be so because of the restriction.

If it is asked, "What is the rebuttal to the claim that the self is not grasped because of its connection with what precedes, and because the word 'self' is not heard in the opening passage?"—that is now stated: "It would be so because of the restriction. It is indeed reasonable here that the self is grasped.
Because of the restriction [implied by the context].

For instance, having established through the restriction that "by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1)—that is, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—the text says, "Being alone... with the desire to bring that [knowledge] to fulfillment.
And that [universal knowledge] is accomplished when there is the grasping of the Self;
for otherwise, since this individual self (*mīmāṃsya*) would not be known as the Self, universal knowledge itself would not be accomplished.

Likewise, the determination of oneness prior to creation, the reference to the living being (*jīva*) by means of the word "Self," and the statement regarding the attainment of its own nature during the state of deep sleep—these are further explained following an objection.

Furthermore, the emphatic declaration "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), as well as everything else [in this context], is intelligible only for the purpose of establishing identity (*tādātmya*), not for the purpose of bringing about identity.
Nor is it reasonable to introduce the argument that the text is dependent on the perspective of an ignorant person.

For there is no introductory statement either proclaiming selfhood or proclaiming non-selfhood. Furthermore, an introduction in general terms is not contradicted by a specific detail found in the remainder of the passage, because the general requires a specification. Moreover, when the meaning of the word "Being" (sat) is carefully considered, nothing other than the primary Self is possible; for all other categories of entities are established as unreal on the basis of such terms as "merely a fabrication" (ārambhaṇa-śabda).
Even a discrepancy in traditional recitation does not necessarily entail a discrepancy in meaning;
for this is observed in cases such as "Bring the vessel" and "The vessel, bring it," where there is identity of meaning despite the difference.
Therefore, it is established that in sentences of this kind, although there is a difference in the mode of presentation, there is no difference in the object to be presented. // 17 //
FN: *Tatamaṃ* means most pervasive; the elision of the letter *t* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Udarka* means conclusion.
9. Section on the Description of the Task (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 18:
"Because of the description of the task, it is not something new.

(BBs 3.3.18) The Chandogas and the Vājasaneyins, in the dialogue concerning the vital breath (prāṇa)—specifically the dialogue with the dog and others—record that the food of the vital breath extends as far as dogs, and they further record that water is its clothing.

And immediately thereafter, the Chandogas record: "Therefore, those who are about to eat surround it with water both before and after [the meal]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.2). The Vājasaneyins, however, record: "Knowing this, learned Śrotriyas sip water before eating and sip water after eating; they think that they are thereby making this very breath-breathless (anagna)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14); and, "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating; he thereby makes this very breath-breathless."

In this regard, it is considered whether both the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and the meditation on the non-nakedness of the breath (*prāṇa*) are enjoined, or only the rinsing of the mouth, or only the meditation on the non-nakedness of the breath; for since both are not previously established (*apūrva*), they are both worthy of being enjoined.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
Both of these are worthy of being enjoined because they are not already known from other sources.
Alternatively, only the sipping of water (ācamana) is enjoined;
for in that case, the injunctive suffix is clearly present, as in the text: "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating.
The mention of being "not naked" (anagnatā) is merely for the purpose of praising that very act.
This being the case, we reply: the injunction of sipping water (ācamana) is not tenable, because it is a restatement of an already established action.
For this sipping of water, which serves the purpose of purification, is already well-known from the Smṛti as something to be performed; it is merely restated here.
[Objection: But surely this Śruti text must be the source for that Smṛti?
This is not so; it is said that this is because their objects are different.
For recollection has a general object, whereas the sipping of water (ācamana) enjoined for the sake of purification pertains specifically to the individual person.
However, the Śruti text, being read within the context of the Prāṇavidyā, would enjoin the act of sipping water (ācamana) specifically with reference to that [knowledge].
Furthermore, it is not possible for a relationship of source and derivative to exist between a Śruti and a Smṛti that have different subjects.
Nor can it be maintained that this Śruti text enjoins a previously unknown act of sipping water as something connected to the Prāṇavidyā.
Because the very same act of sipping water (ācamana), which was previously connected with the person as a whole, is recognized here;
for this very reason, there is no injunction of both.
And if both were enjoined, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (vākyabheda).

Therefore, since the sipping of water has already been established for both those who have eaten and those who intend to eat, this sentence— "Thinking, 'We are thus making him (Prāṇa) not naked'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14)— teaches as something new, in connection with the knowledge of Prāṇa, the mental resolve to keep Prāṇa from being naked while using the water intended for sipping.
