Nor is it reasonable to hold that this statement regarding non-nakedness is merely for the purpose of praising the act of sipping.
Because rinsing the mouth (ācamana) is not something to be enjoined,
whereas it is understood that the mental resolve for nakedness itself is what is to be enjoined;
and thus, in this case, a single act of rinsing the mouth does not result in the acceptance of a dual purpose— namely, both for the sake of purification and for the sake of clothing.

Since it is admitted that they are distinct actions, it is accepted that the act called *ācamana* (sipping water) is indeed a separate action for the purpose of purification (*prāyatya*) of the person; likewise, the act called the "conception of clothing" (*vāsasaṃkalpana*) with respect to those waters is accepted as a distinct action for the purpose of providing a garment (*paridhāna*) for the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, there is no fault.
Furthermore: "Whatever exists here, even down to a dog, down to worms, down to insects and moths—that is your food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14).
In this context, it cannot be said that the consumption of all food is enjoined, because such a thing is neither expressed by the words nor possible.

Rather, the injunction is for the meditation on food—that "everything is the food of the vital breath" (prāṇa). And because of its association with that, even in the passage "water is his garment," the sipping of water is not enjoined; rather, since the water for sipping is already well-known, the injunction is for the meditation on wearing [the water] as a garment.
This is logical, for a partial contradiction is not possible. Moreover, the word "ācāmanti" (they sip water) is a statement in the present tense, and such a word is incapable of being an injunction.
[Objection: But is it not the case that the status of being a statement in the present tense is the same for the phrase "they think" as well?
[Reply: True, this is so.

However, since one of the two must necessarily be enjoined, and because rinsing the mouth (ācamana) is already established as before, it is the mental resolve regarding water as clothing—which is called the "performance of the act of clothing"—that is enjoined as something new; rinsing the mouth is not enjoined, as has been demonstrated.

As for what was said—that there is a clear injunctive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*) regarding the sipping of water (*ācamana*)—that too has already been refuted by the fact that the sipping is merely a restatement (*pūrvavat*).

Precisely because the sipping is not intended to be enjoined, the Kāṇvas conclude right here with the words, "they think that they thus make him not naked," and do not recite the subsequent portion beginning with "one who knows thus.

Therefore, even in the reading of the Mādhyandinas, it must be understood that, following the restatement of the sipping, the state of being "one who knows thus" is enjoined as the knowledge of the garment of the aforementioned Prāṇa.
Furthermore, this position—that in some instances rinsing the mouth is enjoined while in others the perception of [water as] clothing is enjoined—is also not correct.

Since the application of the scriptural passage beginning with "Water is clothing" is uniform in all cases, it is logical that here the perception of clothing alone is enjoined, and not the rinsing of the mouth. // 18 //
10. Common substratum. Sūtra 19:
"And likewise, because there is no difference in the common [substratum].
(BBs 3.3.19) In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyi-śākhā, the knowledge designated by the name Śāṇḍilya is recognized.
And in that regard, qualities are heard: "One should meditate upon that Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, and having light for its form," and so forth.
In that very same scripture, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, it is further read: "This person consists of mind; he is light within this true heart.
As a grain of rice or a grain of barley, so is he. He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, who governs all this, whatever exists."
"And what [is it]? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.6.1).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this a single meditation in which the qualities from the *Agnirahasya* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* are to be combined, or are these two meditations distinct with no combination of qualities?
What, then, is the initial position?
[The difference consists in] the distinction of the knowledge and the arrangement of the qualities.
Why? Because otherwise there would be the consequence of redundancy (*paunaruktya*).

For, having observed that in different branches (*śākhā*) redundancy is avoided due to the difference of students, and having determined the unity of the knowledge, it has already been stated that in cases such as the "Dialogue of the Vital Breaths" (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the qualities that are redundant in one place are combined in the other.

Furthermore, since there is no difference between the students and knowers when it comes to a single branch of the Veda, repetition—which cannot be avoided—is unavoidable; therefore, a single knowledge (vidyā) cannot reside in two locations separated by distance.
Nor is it possible here to make a distinction such that one recension is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge itself while the other is for the purpose of enjoining its attributes.

For if that were the case, only those attributes not already mentioned elsewhere would be recited in each location; however, qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomayatva) and so forth are recited identically in both places.
Therefore, there is no mutual combination of qualities [between different recensions].

This being the position reached, we reply: Just as the unity of knowledge and the combination of qualities occur across different recensions (śākhās), so too should they occur within a single recension.
Because the object of meditation is non-different, we recognize that very same Brahman—characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind—as the identical object of meditation in both places.
And the form is that which is to be meditated upon for the knowledge;
nor can we determine a difference in knowledge when there is no difference in its form,
nor can there be a fixed distribution of qualities when there is a difference in knowledge.
Is it not the case that a distinction between the two knowledges is established due to the consequence of tautology?
No, it is said,
because a distinction in their respective purposes is logically possible.
For one recension is for the purpose of enjoining knowledge and ignorance, while the other is for the purpose of enjoining qualities; thus, nothing is untenable.
But if this were so, then that which is recited in the *Agnirahasya*—namely, "He is the lord of all," and so forth—should also be recited in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.
As for that which has already been recited, such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, it should not be recited [again].
This is not a fault;
for it is precisely by the power of that [text] that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the same knowledge (*vidyā*) as one recited in another place.

Indeed, by the mention of qualities belonging to the *maṇḍala*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā located at a distant place is recognized, and within that [vidyā], lordship (*īśānatva*) and other attributes are taught.

Otherwise, how could this injunction regarding qualities be stated with respect to that [meditation]? Furthermore, once the sentence has become meaningful through the instruction of an unestablished portion, its reference to an already established portion can be justified as a constant restatement (nityānuvāda); therefore, it is not possible to establish recognition on the strength of that.
Consequently, even though the branch (śākhā) is the same, the unity of the knowledge and the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) are both logically established. // 19 //
11. The Section on Connection (Saṃbandhādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 20–21:
"In the same way, [the connection] exists elsewhere as well because of the connection.
Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.1: "Brahman is Truth."

Having thus proceeded, [the text] teaches two secret names (*upaniṣad*) for that very same Brahman, which is Truth, after having taught its specific abodes in the divine sphere (*adhidaivata*) and the self-sphere (*adhyātma*)— namely, "That which is Truth is this person in that orb and this person in the right eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2)—
and after establishing that its body consists of the *vyāhṛtis*. Its secret name in the divine sphere is "Hari."
Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "I" with respect to the self (adhyātma).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should both secret names be applied to both [the divine and the self] without distinction, or should they be applied separately—one to the divine and one to the self?
On this point, he begins with the aphorism itself.

Just as in the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, where it has been stated that there is a combination of qualities even though the vidyā is studied separately, so it must also be in other cases of this kind,
because of the connection with a single vidyā; for this Satya-vidyā is indeed one and the same, being studied both with reference to the deities (adhidaiva) and with reference to the self (adhyātma).
Because the introductory context is undivided and because of the interconnected recitation,
how could a duty enjoined in that [context] not apply to that very same [person]?
For whatever conduct, such as following behind, has been enjoined for a teacher, it applies when he has gone to the village.
And it is exactly the same when one has gone to the forest;
therefore, both secret doctrines (upaniṣads) are applicable in both places. // 20 //
This being the case, he provides the following rebuttal:
"Or rather, it is not so, because of the distinction" (BBs 3.3.21).
That is to say, there is no application of both [rules] to both [cases].
Why?
Because of distinction;
that is to say, because of being bound by the specific continuity of meditation.

How is it said that there is a connection with specific locations? For, having introduced the person pertaining to the divine sphere with the words, "This person who is in this orb" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3), the scripture declares, "His secret name is Ahar.
And [it speaks of] "this person who is in the right eye" (5.5.4).
Thus, having introduced the internal person with the words "his secret name (upaniṣad)," the pronoun "his" refers to that which is immediately proximate;
therefore, these two secret names are taught specifically by relying upon those particular abodes.
How can both [the two forms] be applicable to both [the divine and the internal]?
Is it not the case that this is indeed one and the same *puruṣa* with respect to the divine and the internal, since it is the presentation of two abodes for the single, true Brahman?
True, that is so.
However, because a specific Upaniṣadic instruction is given by taking up a particular state of even a single person, that [instruction] must belong to that person only in that state.
There is indeed this illustration: even though there is no change in the teacher's essential nature, what is prescribed as following the teacher when he is seated does not apply when he is standing;
and what is prescribed for him when he is standing does not apply when he is seated.

However, because the nature of the teacher does not change whether he is in a village or a forest, and because there is no distinction made by the village or the forest regarding the Dharma realized through that very nature, the Dharma exists equally in both places; thus, that [comparison] is not a valid example.
Therefore, this applies to the two systems of the Upaniṣads. // 21 //
And it is further shown:

moreover, there is a scriptural indication regarding the establishment of such categories of dharmas, namely: "Of this [person], that very form is the same as that [sun's]; whatever two ears he has, those are the two ears; whatever name he has, that is the name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
How is this [the eye] a sign? That is now explained:

observing that the attributes distinguished by their various fixed locations, such as the eyes and so forth, are not to be combined with one another, the text here—by means of an extended application (*atideśa*)—attributes the form and other qualities belonging to the person in the sun to the person in the eye, starting with the words, "The form of this very one is that same form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
Therefore, the conclusion is that these two Upaniṣads are indeed established as distinct. // 22 //

12. The Section on the Accumulation (Saṃbhṛtyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 23: "And therefore [the qualities of] accumulation, pervading the heaven, and so forth [belong to Brahman]. In the *Khilas* of the Rāṇāyanīyas, there are passages such as: "The powers have been accumulated with Brahman as the eldest; in the beginning, Brahman stretched out the eldest heaven. Thus, the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of Brahman, beginning with the accumulation of power and the entering into the heaven, are described.
They are recited [in various places],
and in their very Upanishads, Brahma-vidyās such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others are also recited.

In the deliberation as to whether those manifestations of Brahman (brahmavibhūti) should be combined within those Brahma-vidyās or not, since the combination would initially follow from the connection with Brahman, the author writes as follows:
The manifestations such as the accumulation [of food], pervasion of heaven, and so forth, are not to be combined in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and other meditations.
This is precisely because of the association with specific abodes;
for instance, in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Brahman is stated to have the heart as its abode: "This is my Self within the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
In the same way, in the Dahara-vidyā as well, it is said: "In the small lotus-palace there is a small inner space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).
In the Upakośala-vidyā, however, the eye is the abode: "This person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1).
Thus, in those respective instances, an internal abode is perceived in these meditations.
But these manifestations—such as "being gathered," "shining forth," and "pervading"—belong to the divine realm (*ādhidaivika*). How, then, could they be attained in these [human] states?
Is it not the case that divine manifestations are also heard of in connection with these very states? For instance: "Greater than heaven, greater than these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3);
and "He indeed is the light-bringer, for he shines in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.4).
"As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3).
There are also other Brahma-vidyās mentioned here, such as that of the sixteen parts, which do not specify a particular abode.
This is true;
nevertheless, there exists here a specific reason for not combining [the qualities], beginning with the fact that they have been accumulated [in different places].

For it is logical that when meditations located in distant places are brought to mind through the mention of identical qualities, the qualities belonging to those distant locations should also be combined.

However, it is stated that qualities such as "being composed of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth— which are the objects of the *Śāṇḍilya-vidyā* and other passages— do not bring to mind a meditation existing in another location, because their essential natures are mutually distinct.
This is possible even when there is a difference between meditations,
for it is an established principle that even the one Brahman is worshipped in many ways through various manifestations (*vibhūti*).

Because a perception of difference is observed—as in the case of the *parovarīyastva* (the "higher-than-higher") meditation and others—therefore, there is no combination (*anupasaṃhāra*) of the accumulation of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbhṛti*) and other such qualities within the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and similar meditations. [FN:
*Brahmajyeṣṭhā brahmajyeṣṭhāni*; the elision of the final vowel is Vedic.]
Vīryas are types of heroic effort. 13. The section concerning the person and so forth. Sūtra 24: Because the others are not mentioned, as in the case of the Puruṣa-vidyā. (BBs 3.3.24)
In the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* of the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins, there is a "Knowledge of the Person" (*puruṣavidyā*). Therein, the person is conceived as a sacrifice;
his lifespan is divided into three parts, which are conceived as the three daily libations (*savana*).
Furthermore, [acts] such as the desire to eat are conceived as the consecration (*dīkṣā*) and so forth;
other properties (*dharma*) are also attained therein, such as the employment of benedictory mantras (*āśīr-mantra*).

The followers of the *Taittirīya* school also conceive of a certain "sacrifice of the person" (*puruṣayajña*), stating: "For one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife... (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).

By means of this section (anuvāka), a doubt arises there: should those characteristics of the "Sacrifice of Man" (puruṣayajña) that are mentioned elsewhere be combined with the Taittirīyakas, or should they not be combined? Since the status as a "Sacrifice of Man" is common to both, the prima facie view suggests they should be combined; however, we declare that they should not be combined.
Why?
Because there is no recognition of that same form.
Thus the Teacher said: "As in the case of the Puruṣa-vidyā."

Just as there is a scriptural recitation regarding the "knowledge of the person" (*puruṣavidyā*) among certain branches—such as the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins—there is no such recitation for others, namely the Taittirīyas.

For them, the accomplishment of the sacrifice is seen to be entirely different, due to the sequential enumeration of the wife, the sacrificer, the Vedas, the altar, the sacrificial grass, the sacrificial post, the clarified butter, the horse, the officiating priests, and so forth.

Even that accomplishment of the *savana* rites is likewise distinct from others, as it is said: "That which [is performed] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, those [are the three]" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).

Even whatever slight similarity there may be—such as [the ritual] being a final bath at death (*maraṇāvabhṛtha*) and so forth—is overwhelmed by a greater dissimilarity and is thus incapable of effecting recognition.
Furthermore, in the Taittirīyaka, the person (*puruṣa*) is not heard of as being the sacrifice;
for in the phrase "of the wise one, the sacrifice" (*viduṣo yajñasya*), these two genitives are not in apposition (i.e., it does not mean "of that which is both the wise one and the sacrifice").
For the person does not possess primary sacrificial status;
rather, these two genitives are in different grammatical cases, meaning "the sacrifice which belongs to the wise man.
Indeed, there exists a primary connection between the person and the sacrifice.
And when a primary sense is possible, one must resort to that very meaning rather than a figurative one.

Furthermore, by explaining the person's status as the sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) through the statement "the Self is the sacrificer," [the text] shows his connection to the sacrifice precisely through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Moreover, since there is the scriptural restatement "for him who knows thus" as an established fact, if one were to seek to understand both the person’s state of being the sacrifice and the Self's and others' state of being the sacrificer and so forth, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Moreover, since the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā) was taught previously with the words "having renounced," and immediately thereafter the sequence beginning with "of one who knows thus" (tasyaivaṃvidaḥ) follows as a conclusion, this scriptural tradition is clearly a supplement to what precedes and not an independent section;
for we perceive that the fruit of both these sections is indeed one and the same: "He attains the greatness of Brahman" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).
However, for others, the scriptural teaching on the Puruṣavidyā is not a supplement to anything else.
For this [knowledge] has the fruit of the increase of lifespan, as indicated by the statement: "He who knows thus lives for a hundred and sixteen years" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.16.7).
Therefore, the qualities of the Puruṣavidyā, such as the benedictory mantras and so forth, which are studied in other recensions, do not apply to the Taittirīyaka.
14. The Section on Piercing and so forth (Vedhādyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 25:
Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth (vedhādyarthabheda).

In the beginning of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaṇikas, there is a traditional recitation of mantras: "Piercing everything, piercing the heart, cutting open the vessels, cutting open the head—divided threefold."
And so forth.
For the Tāṇḍins, it begins with: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice," and so on. For the Śāṭhyāyanins, it begins with: "You are the white-horsed, green-blue one," and so on.
For the Kaṭhas and the Taittirīyas, there is the passage beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious to us" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.1).
For the Vājasaneyins, however, at the beginning of their Upaniṣad, the Pravargya Brāhmaṇa is recited, beginning with "The gods, indeed, sat down.

For the Kauṣītakins as well, there is the Agniṣṭoma Brāhmaṇa: "The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman; that day is Brahman itself. By means of Brahman they approach Brahman; those who approach that day attain immortality."
Thus [it is said].

We now investigate whether all these mantras, beginning with the *pravidhya*, and the rituals, beginning with the *pravargya*, are to be combined with the meditations (*vidyā*), or whether they are not to be so combined. What first occurs to us is that they are indeed to be combined with the meditations.
Why?
Because they are recited in proximity to the Upaniṣadic texts, which have knowledge as their primary subject matter.
But do we not perceive an injunction for these [rites] as being for the sake of knowledge?
"Certainly;
even though we do not perceive it directly, we shall infer it from the force of proximity.
For when the meaningfulness of proximity is possible, it is not right to assume it to be accidental."
[Objection: "But we do not perceive any power of these mantras with respect to the subject matter of knowledge (*vidyā*).
And how can we understand that rituals such as the *pravargya*, which are enjoined for other purposes, also serve the purpose of knowledge?
[Response: This is not a fault."
First of all, some efficacy of the mantras even within the sphere of knowledge (*vidyā*) can be postulated, because of the mention of the "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth.

For the heart and other such parts are generally taught in meditations (*upāsana*) as being the abodes (*āyatana*) and so on; and by means of those, it is appropriate that mantras of this kind—such as "pierce the heart"—should serve as auxiliary members of meditation.
Furthermore, the application of mantras in meditations is observed, for example: "I take refuge in Bhūḥ, with [this name], with [that name], with [that name]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.15.3).
And so forth.

Likewise, there is no contradiction in employing rites such as the Pravargya—which have already been enjoined for other purposes—within the context of meditative knowledges (vidyās), just as the Bṛhaspatisava is employed within the Vājapeya sacrifice.
This being the position reached, we reply:
There is no application of these [rules] to the sciences (vidyās).
Why?
Because of the difference in purpose regarding the piercing [of the heart].
For in the case of mantras such as "Pierce the heart," the meanings—such as the piercing of the heart and so forth—are distinct and unconnected with the knowledges (vidyās) taught in the Upaniṣads;
they have no capacity to be joined with those [knowledges].
Now, it might be argued that since the heart is employed even in meditations (upāsanās), a connection with meditation through that medium has been proposed.
This is not so;
for while the mention of the "heart" alone might somehow be imagined to have such a purpose, the heart alone is not the meaning of the mantra here.
Indeed, the entire meaning of the mantra—such as "having pierced the heart, having cut open the vessels"—is not connected with the [other] sciences.
For this subject matter pertains to malevolent rites (*ābhicārika*); therefore, the connection of this mantra—"one should pierce everything with the malevolent rite"—is established.
However, its specific application must be pursued through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In the same way, regarding other mantras as well—some applied to different purposes by means of their indicative mark (*liṅga*), some by explicit statement (*vacana*), and some by other means of valid knowledge—even though they are recited in secret [in the Veda], [their application is determined].

The status of being a subsidiary to knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*). For it has been stated in the first *Tantra* [the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras]—specifically at *Jaimini Sūtra* 3.3.14: "When there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose"—that proximity is indeed weak compared to direct statement and the others.
Likewise, it is not possible for ritual acts such as the *pravargya*, which have been assigned elsewhere, to be subsidiary to knowledge (*vidyā*);
for there is no commonality of purpose whatsoever between these and the meditations.
In the case of the *vājapeya*, however, there is a clearly stated separate application for the *bṛhaspatisava*: "Having sacrificed with the *vājapeya*, one should sacrifice with the *bṛhaspatisava*."

Moreover, this single *pravargya* rite, having been produced once and assigned elsewhere by a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), does not deserve to be assigned elsewhere even by a weaker means of knowledge.

For this would be the case only if there were no perceived distinction between two means of knowledge; however, it is impossible for there to be no perceived distinction between a strong and a weak means of knowledge, precisely because of their difference in strength.
Therefore, one should not suspect that such mantras or rites become subordinate to a *vidyā* merely by virtue of being recited in its proximity.
However, one should be satisfied with the fact that they are recited in proximity due to the commonality of their dharmas, such as the recitation in the forest (araṇyānuvacana) and so forth. // 25 //
15. Section on Loss (Hāny-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 26:
But in the case of loss, because the word "attaining" (upāyana) is supplementary [to it], as in the cases of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; this has been stated.

(BBs 3.3.26) There is a scriptural text among the Tāṇḍins: "Shaking off evil like a horse its hairs, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, shaking off the body, I, having perfected my self, attain the uncreated world of Brahman."
Thus [it is said in] Chāndogya 8.13.1.
Likewise, for the Atharvaṇikas: "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.8).
Similarly, the Śāṭyāyanins recite: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds."
Similarly, the Kauṣītakins [state]: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take up his good deeds, and his non-dear ones his evil deeds" (KauṣU 1.4).

Thus, in some places the abandonment of good and evil deeds is heard, in others the taking up of those very same deeds by the dear and the non-dear through division, and in yet others both the abandonment and the taking up. Regarding that case where both are heard, there is nothing at all to be said.
Even where only the taking over (*upāyana*) is heard and not the abandoning (*hāna*), the abandoning is nonetheless included by implication;
for when the good and evil deeds belonging to oneself are being taken over by others, their abandonment is a necessary consequence.

However, where only the abandoning is heard and not the taking over, there arises a doubt as to whether the taking over should be included or not; in such a case, it is not included because it is not explicitly heard.
Furthermore, because the hearing of the text belonging to another recension falls within the scope of a different branch of knowledge (*vidyā*), [it cannot be assumed].

Moreover, since the abandonment (*hāna*) of good and evil deeds has the self as its agent, whereas the taking up (*upāyana*) of those same deeds has another as its agent, and since there is no necessary connection between these two, how could the act of taking up be implied by the act of abandonment?
Therefore, there is no conjunction of the taking up with the abandonment.
Regarding this attainment, he recites: "But in the case of loss.
For even when this [attainment] alone is heard, the taking up [of qualities] must necessarily be combined with it, because it is supplementary to that.
For it has been established in the Kauṣītaki-rahasya that the word "attainment" (upāyana) remains implied even where the word "abandonment" (hāna) alone is heard;
therefore, even when only the word for abandonment is heard elsewhere, the process of attainment follows by implication.

As for the argument that there is no conjunction [of the two] because of the lack of explicit mention, because it pertains to the scope of other knowledges, and because it is not mandatory—this is refuted as follows:
To this it is said:
This formal distinction would hold if they were proclaimed as things to be performed;
however, their mention here is for the purpose of praising knowledge.

Thus, this is a highly exalted knowledge, by the power of which the good and evil deeds of this wise man—which constitute the cause of transmigratory existence—are shaken off; and these [deeds] enter into his friends and enemies respectively.

Since this mention [of the shaking off] is for the purpose of praise, and because it is heard in some places that the "attainment" (upāyana) follows immediately after the "shaking off" (hāna), one considers that the mention of attainment should also follow wherever the shaking off is mentioned, in order to achieve the excellence of the praise.

Furthermore, the application of one explanatory passage (arthavāda) with reference to another explanatory passage is well known—for instance: "This sun over there is indeed the twenty-first" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.10.5).

In such passages as these, how indeed could the number twenty-one of the Ādityas be stated here without depending on another explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), namely: "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder Āditya as the twenty-first"? Likewise, in such statements as "There are two *triṣṭubh* verses for the sake of possessing the sense organs," a dependence on other explanatory passages is observed, such as: "The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the sense organ."

Furthermore, since this statement regarding the "attaining" (upāyana) is for the purpose of praising knowledge (vidyā), one should not be overly insistent on how the good and evil deeds belonging to one person could be attained by others.

By explicitly pronouncing the word "word" (śabda) in the phrase "because it is supplementary to the word 'attaining' (upāyana)," [the author] indicates that the mention of attaining follows from the act of abandonment (hāni) solely for the sake of praise.
For if the intention were to enjoin the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra), he would have stated that the meaning of attaining itself recurs in the context of abandonment.
Therefore, this Sūtra is intended to demonstrate the inclusion of praise (stuti) by way of the discussion on the inclusion of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra).

The employment of the analogy—"as in the case of the *kuśā* grass, the meters (*chandas*), the praise, and the singing" (*kuśācchandastutyupagānavat*)—is as follows: in the Vedic recitation (*nigama*) of the Bhāllavins, "O *kuśā* grass, you are of the nature of trees; protect me," there is no specific distinction made regarding the *kuśā* grass.

When there is a scriptural mention of being born from a tree (*vanaspati*), the specific statement of the Śāṭyāyanins, "The *kuśa* grasses are made of *udumbara* wood," leads one to adopt *audumbara* *kuśa* grasses.

Just as in some cases, when there is no distinction between the meters of the gods and the asuras and a sequence of priority might arise, they are understood to be the "prior meters of the gods" based on the recitation of the Paiṅgin school;
and just as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra, when a lack of specific time might apply for some, the specific time is understood from the Vedic text of the Ārcikas: "When the sun has half-risen."

Just as some transmit the "approaching" (upagāna) without qualification, while the Bhāllavins transmit it with specific qualification— just as in these cases of the *kuśa* grass and so forth, there is indeed a connection (*anvaya*) with the specific details found in other scriptural passages— so too in the case of "leaving behind" (*hāni*), there is a connection with "taking up" (*upāyana*).
For if one were not to accept the specific detail established in one scriptural passage within another scriptural passage, there would necessarily be an option (*vikalpa*) in every instance.
And that [interpretation] is unjustified when another way is possible;

as it was stated in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇā*: "But rather, because it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion of the others; for if it were a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*).
Alternatively, this very point should be considered with respect to these very scriptural passages concerning the shaking off (*vidhūnana*) by means of this Sūtra.
Does this statement regarding "shaking off" (vidhūnana) denote the abandonment of good and evil deeds, or does it signify something else? In this regard, the following position must be established:
"shaking off" does not denote abandonment, because of the traditional grammatical rule (smaraṇa) that the root *dhū* with the suffix *adhañ* signifies trembling (*kampana*).
Since we observe the usage of the term "shaking" (*vidhūnana*) in the sense of movement— as in the phrase "the tips of the banners are shaken" when the banner-tips are being moved by the wind—
it follows that "shaking" denotes motion.
Having established this— that motion refers to the temporary obstruction of the fruition of good and evil deeds— one must respond as follows:
This word "vidhūya" (shaking off) must indeed be understood as denoting abandonment (*hāna*),
because it is supplementary to the word "upāyana" (attaining).
For it is not possible for others to attain good and evil deeds that have been acquired by another and have not yet been abandoned.

Although this "taking up" (*upāyana*) of the good and evil deeds belonging to others by others cannot be conceived as literal, nevertheless, because it is mentioned in connection with that [shaking off], it can be determined that what is called "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) is actually "abandonment" (*hāna*) in accordance with it. Furthermore, this "taking up," when heard in proximity to "shaking off" in some instances— like the *kuśa* grass, meters, hymns, and singing— is required everywhere by the scriptural mention of "shaking off," and thus serves as a universal basis for determination.
It is accomplished;
however, a literal shaking like the tip of a banner is not possible for good and evil deeds as their primary mode of action,
because they lack substantiality.

And just as a horse, shaking its hairs, casts off dust along with them, it likewise causes even the worn-out hairs to fall away; for there is a Brāhmaṇa text stating, "Having shaken off evil like a horse its hairs" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1).
Furthermore, since it is accepted that verbal roots have multiple meanings, there is no contradiction with the traditional grammatical memory (smṛti).
"That has been explained" thus concludes the commentary.
16. The Section on the Time of Death (Sāṃparāyādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 27–28:
"At the time of death [the soul departs with its subtle body], because there is nothing else to be crossed over; for so it is with others. (BBs 3.3.27)

The Kauṣītakins record in the Paryaṅka-vidyā that for one who has set out upon the path of the gods and is seated on the couch, the division of good and evil deeds occurs midway; beginning with "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni" (Kauṣ.
1.3), they continue: "He comes to the river Virajā and crosses it by mind alone; there he shakes off his good and evil deeds" (Kauṣ. 1.4).

In this regard, when the question arises whether the statement regarding the separation [from good and evil deeds] is to be understood as occurring only during the journey (*vyadhvan*), or rather at the very beginning upon departing from the body, and when the conclusion that one must follow the literal scriptural statement follows from the authority of the *Śruti*, the author reads:
"At the time of departure" (*sāmparāye*).
He asserts that this abandonment of good and evil deeds through the power of knowledge occurs precisely at the time of departure—that is, at the very moment of leaving the body.
And he states the reason for this as "because there is nothing further to be crossed.

For one who is wise, who has passed away and is seeking to reach Brahman through knowledge, there is nothing at all to be attained in the interval by means of good and evil deeds for the sake of which those two might be imagined to remain undestroyed for some moments.

Rather, because their fruits are contrary to knowledge, their destruction must occur through the power of knowledge; and that [destruction] must happen precisely when the knowledge is about to manifest its fruit.
Therefore, this destruction of good and evil deeds, which actually occurs earlier, is described later [in the text].

For likewise, other schools—the Śikhins, the Tāṇḍins, and the Śāṭyāyanins—declare the casting off of good and evil deeds precisely at the prior stage: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes off its hairs" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1), and "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2). // 27 //
According to one's preference, because both [views] are not contradictory.

(BBs 3.3.28) For if it were admitted that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs halfway along the path of the gods for one who has departed from the body and set out on that journey, then— once the body has fallen away— the cause of the destruction of good and evil deeds, consisting of self-restraint, observances, and the practice of knowledge, would have ceased to exist.
Since the performance [of actions] by human effort cannot occur through mere desire, the destruction of good and evil deeds caused by that [effort] would likewise be impossible.

Therefore, it should be understood that the performance [of actions] according to one's will must have occurred previously, during the stage of the seeker; and preceded by that, comes the abandonment of good and evil deeds.
Thus, the logical connection between the sign and that which is indicated by it, as well as the consistency with the Śrutis of Tāṇḍi and Śāṭyāyani, is established. // 28 //
Section 17: The Topic on the Purposefulness of the Path (Gater-arthavattva-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 29–30.
"The purposefulness of the path exists in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
(BBs 3.3.29) In some places, the path of the gods (devayāna) is mentioned in proximity to the destruction of merit and demerit, while in others it is not.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the path of the gods apply without distinction to all who depart [from the body], or does it apply only in some cases and not in others?

Just as it was stated that the "approaching" (upāyana) applies without distinction to all those who depart, so too it might be argued that the application of the path of the gods should likewise be without distinction. To this we reply: the purposefulness of the journey on the path of the gods must exist in both ways—that is, by way of distinction—such that the journey is purposeful in some cases and not in others, rather than being without distinction.
For otherwise, if this going were accepted without distinction, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural text:
"Having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, he attains the highest equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3),
wherein a movement leading to another location is contradicted.
For how could one who is stainless go to another place?
Moreover, since the supreme state of equality to be reached does not depend upon reaching another location, we consider that movement here is entirely purposeless.
This is established because the object characterized by that [nature] is perceived, as is the case in the world.
And this dual existence— that in some cases movement has a purpose and in others it does not—
is established because the object characterized by that [nature] is perceived.
For movement is found to be purposeful in the case of the Paryaṅka-vidyās and in meditations on the qualified Brahman (saguṇopāsanas).

Indeed, in those instances where the mounting of the couch, conversing with that Brahman, and the attainment of special fragrances and so forth are heard of as fruits dependent upon reaching another place—
there, movement is meaningful.
For there is no perception of the goal characterized by that [liberation] in the case of right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

Indeed, for those who perceive the oneness of the Self, whose desires are fulfilled, and for whom the seeds of all afflictions have been burnt away even here, there is nothing further to be expected other than the exhaustion of the residual impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*) that have begun to bear fruit; therefore, the journey to that state is useless.

This distinction should be understood as being like the worldly usage: just as in the world, upon reaching a village, a path leading to another place is required, but not so for the attainment of health, so it is here as well.
Furthermore, we shall establish this division more precisely in the fourth chapter. // 30 //
18. The Section on Non-Restriction. Sūtra 31:
There is no restriction [regarding the destination] for all [meditations], because there is no contradiction with scripture and inference.

It has been stated that the journey (gati) is meaningful in the case of meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vidyā*), but not in the case of the meditation on the supreme Self (*nirguṇa-paramātma-vidyā*).

Even among those meditations (*vidyā*) that possess attributes (*saguṇa*), a [specific] departure (*gati*) is heard of in some, such as in the Paryaṅka-vidyā, the Upakośala-vidyā, the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and the Dahara-vidyā;
but not in others, such as the Madhu-vidyā, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Ṣoḍaśakala-vidyā, and the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is this departure restricted only to those meditations in which it is explicitly heard, or is it connected by way of non-restriction with all meditations of this kind?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that there is a restriction; it must apply only where it is explicitly heard, because the context serves as the regulator.

If a path, even when heard in one context, were to apply to another branch of knowledge (*vidyā*), the authority of the sacred texts (*śruti*) and other means of proof would be undermined, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that everything applies to everything.

Furthermore, the single path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) is mentioned identically in both the Upakośala-knowledge and the Pañcāgni-knowledge; if it were intended for all, this repeated mention would be purposeless.
Therefore, the conclusion being reached is that there is a restriction (*niyama*). To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: "There is no restriction" (*aniyama*).
This path called *devayāna* ought to be the destination for all qualified knowledges (*vidyā*) that have the attainment of exaltation as their fruit, without distinction.
Now, it was argued that if no such restriction is accepted, there would be a contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*).
This contradiction does not exist, because it is established by both scripture and inference—that is, by *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

For instance, the Śruti— introducing the path of the gods for those who possess the knowledge of the five fires with the words, "Now, those who know thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1)— and then stating, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1), shows that even those devoted to other forms of knowledge share the same path as those who know the five-fire doctrine.
But how is it understood that this destination belongs to those who practice other branches of knowledge?
Is it not the case that it should belong only to those devoted to faith and austerity, since that alone is heard [in the texts]?
This is not a fault.

For this goal cannot be attained by faith and austerity alone, without the power of knowledge, as another scriptural passage states: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have vanished; neither do those who give sacrificial gifts go there, nor do the ignorant who practice austerity.
Therefore, in this context, faith and austerity serve as indicators for other forms of knowledge.

The Vājasaneyins, however, study this in the section concerning the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*): "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship faith (*śraddhā*) as the Real (*satya*)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
In that context, it should be explained that those who possess faith are they who worship the Real, which is Brahman;
for the word *satya* has been used repeatedly with reference to Brahman.

Furthermore, since those who know the science of the five fires are already included by virtue of their knowledge itself, it is logical that this [mention] refers only to those devoted to other sciences. Moreover, the Śruti passage, "But those who do not know these two paths become moths and what is here that bites" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16), which indicates a miserable downward course for those who have strayed from the two paths, includes them precisely within the Devayāna and Pitṛyāṇa paths.
Even in that case, their attainment of the path of the gods (*devayāna*) results from a particular distinction in their knowledge.
Smṛti also states: "These two paths of the world, white and black, are considered eternal;
by one a person goes to non-return, by the other he returns again" (Bhagavad Gītā 8.26).
Furthermore, as for the twofold mention of the path of the gods (*devayāna*) in both the Upakośala-vidyā and the Pañcāgni-vidyā, that is for the purpose of meditation upon it in both instances.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule [regarding the order]. (31) [Note:
They meditate upon Brahman, characterized by faith and austerity.]
A *daṇḍaśūka* is a snake.
19. Up to the completion of their office (yāvad-adhikāra-adhikaraṇam). Sūtra 32: "The continuance of those who hold office lasts as long as their office. (BBs 3.3.32)
It is now considered whether or not another body arises for the knower after the fall of the present body.
One might object: "Once the perfection of knowledge, which is the means, has been attained, will there be the attainment of liberation or not?
This doubt is not tenable.
For it does not occur to one that "will the rice become cooked and ready for eating, or will it not? nor is it thought by one who is eating, "will I be satiated, or will I not?
However, this doubt does arise even for some knowers of Brahman, because the Itihāsas and Purāṇas show the production of another body [after death].
For instance, they remember that the ancient seer and Vedic teacher named Apāntaratamas was born as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages by the command of Viṣṇu.
And Vasiṣṭha, though a mind-born son of Brahmā whose former body had been lost due to the curse of Nimi, was born again from Mitra and Varuṇa by the direction of Brahmā.
Likewise, the rebirth of Bhṛgu and others—who were also mind-born sons of Brahmā—at the sacrifice of Varuṇa is heard in the scriptures.
Sanatkumāra, too, who was the mind-born son of Brahmā himself, manifested as Skanda through the granting of a boon by Rudra.
In this very same way, the repeated production of new bodies for Dakṣa, Nārada, and others is recounted in the Smṛti with various causes;
it is also frequently found in the Śruti, within the mantras and arthavādas.

Some of them, upon the falling away of their previous body, assume another body, while others, by virtue of the power of yoga, assume multiple bodies even while that [original] body remains, according to the principle of taking on many forms.
All of these are recorded as having mastered the entire meaning of the Vedas.

Therefore, since the production of another body is observed in these cases, it follows that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) might be only an occasional cause of liberation, or perhaps not a cause at all.
To this, the following is said: No;

for those such as Apāntaratamas and others, who have been appointed to offices that are causes for the maintenance of the world—such as the promulgation of the Vedas—their status remains dependent upon those very offices.
Just as that blessed Sun, having performed his office for the world until the end of a thousand yugas, at its conclusion becomes free from rising and setting.
"He experiences isolation (kaivalya); then, having risen above that, he neither rises nor sets, but remains alone in the middle"—so says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.1).
And just as the living knowers of Brahman experience isolation upon the exhaustion of their commenced karma (ārabdha-bhoga), so too does this one.
This is because of the scriptural text: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

In this way, even those who are lords, such as Apāntaratamas and others, being appointed by the Supreme Lord to various offices, remain in their positions until the end of their term—even though they possess perfect knowledge, which is the cause of liberation—because their residual karma has not yet been exhausted;
and at the conclusion of that period, they attain final release. Thus, there is no contradiction.

For they, having exhausted their store of karma (karmāśaya) which was set in motion only once for the sake of yielding its fruit, move from one body to another— just as from one house to another— independently; with their memory unimpaired, they assume bodies either simultaneously or in succession through their mastery over the body, the senses, and primordial nature (prakṛti), in order to complete their specific office.
Nor are these called "rememberers of former births" (jātismara) simply because of the traditional recollection expressed as "these are those very same [beings]";

for instance, it is recorded in tradition that a female exponent of Brahman named Sulabhā, desiring to debate with Janaka, cast off her own body, entered the body of Janaka, engaged with him, and subsequently re-entered her own body.
For if another action, which is the cause for the commencement of a new body, were to manifest while an action already set in motion has not yet been exhausted, then...

Otherwise, it would follow that other unburnt seeds of karma would remain just like those [already burnt], and one might suspect that the knowledge of Brahman is either an occasional cause of liberation or not a cause at all;
however, such a suspicion is not reasonable, because the burning of the seeds of karma by knowledge is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.
For thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
And: "Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the complete liberation from all knots" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
And there are such [scriptural passages] as these.
Smṛti also says: "Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37).

And as it is said in such passages: "Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too the self is not produced again when the afflictions have been burnt away by knowledge. Furthermore, once the afflictions such as ignorance have been consumed by fire, it is logically impossible for there to be both the burning of one part of the seed—the latent disposition (*saṃskāra*)—and the sprouting of another part.
For it is never observed that a grain of rice burnt by fire sprouts even in part;
however, the latent impression of karma whose fruit has already begun proceeds until its cessation, like an arrow whose momentum is exhausted—according to the text:
"For him, there is delay only so long" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
Thus, because there is a projection [of karma] until the fall of the body,
it is therefore established that those who hold office remain in their positions for as long as their term of authority lasts;
nor is the fruit of knowledge uncertain.

And thus, scripture shows that liberation results from knowledge for all without distinction: "Therefore, whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he indeed became that; likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Furthermore, it is possible that the great seers might have been attached to other forms of knowledge whose fruits are sovereignty and the like.

It is logical that they, becoming disillusioned by the subsequent observation of the decay of their sovereignty and becoming firmly established in the knowledge of the Supreme Self, attained liberation (*kaivalya*);

for there is a traditional text (*smṛti*) stating: "When the dissolution occurs, at the end of the highest [Brahmā], all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā."
Furthermore, because knowledge has direct perception as its fruit, the suspicion that it might lack a fruit is untenable.
For regarding the fruit of ritual action, such as heaven and the like—which is not established in experience—one might suspect whether it exists or not;
but the fruit of knowledge is established in experience, as stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.4.1): "That Brahman which is immediate and direct."
This is because of such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), which teaches as an established fact;
for the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" cannot be interpreted as "Thou shalt become That after death."

Furthermore, the text "Seeing this very thing, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I became Manu and the Sun'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10) shows that the fruit of knowledge—namely, the state of being the Self of all—is attained at the very moment of perfect realization.
Therefore, the attainment of absolute liberation for the knower is certain.
FN: Having risen up as one who is distinct and of the nature of Brahman, he engaged in debate— that is, conducted a dispute— with that Janaka.
Disgusted and detached;
withdrawal is lamentation.
20. The section on the twenty-six letters. Sūtra 33.

"But there is an inclusion of those [meditations] involving syllables, on account of the commonality and the presence of that [Brahman]; it is like the Aupasadamantras; so it has been stated. (BS 3.3.33).

In the Vājasaneyaka it is heard: "This indeed, O Gārgī, is that imperishable (akṣara); the Brāhmaṇas declare it to be neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily," and so forth.
Likewise, in the Atharvaṇa it is heard: "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that imperishable is apprehended..."
"That which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5), and so forth;
likewise, in other places as well, the supreme Brahman is proclaimed as the Imperishable (akṣara) by means of the negation of specific attributes.
And in those [passages], in some instances, certain additional specific attributes are presented.

Regarding these cognitions of specific negations, when a doubt arises as to whether they apply everywhere or are restricted to specific contexts, and since a restriction might be inferred from the division of the scriptural passages, it is said: all cognitions of specific negations concerning the Imperishable (akṣara) must be included everywhere,
on account of both their commonality and the existence of that [Imperishable]— for the form consisting of the negation of specific attributes is the same everywhere.
This is the manner of establishing Brahman;
and that very Brahman which is to be established everywhere is recognized as non-different [from itself].
In that case, why should cognitions produced in one place not apply to another?
And so it has been explained in the sūtra, "Bliss and the rest belong to the Principal" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.11).
The distinction here is that while in that [previous] context the qualifying attributes were considered in their affirmative form, here they are considered in their negative form.
This distinction in reflection is for the sake of detailed exposition;
"like the Aupasadah" is the illustration.

Just as when the Upasads accompanied by sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are enjoined in the *Ahīna* sacrifice of Jamadagni, the mantras for offering the cake—such as "O Agni, protect the work, protect the sacrifice"—though originating in the Udgātṛ-veda, are nevertheless connected with the Adhvaryus.

It occurs as follows: because the offering of that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has the Adhvaryu as its agent, and because the subordinate elements (aṅga) are dependent upon the primary element (pradhāna);
so too here, since the qualifiers are dependent upon the syllable (akṣara), the meaning is that those [qualifiers] produced anywhere at all are connected everywhere with the syllable.

This has been stated in the first book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "In the case of a conflict between the subordinate and the primary, because the purpose is for that [primary], the connection with the Veda is determined by the primary" (*Jaiminisūtra* 3.3.8). // 33 //
21. This much is the subject matter. Sūtra 34:
"On account of the scriptural declaration of this much.
(BBs 3.3.34) "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."
"In one of them, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).

This mantra, belonging to the Atharva Veda, the Kaṭhas, and the Śvetāśvataras, is recited in the context of the supreme self (*adhyātma*). Likewise, the Kaṭhas [recite]: "Drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest heaven... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.1).
"Those who know Brahman speak of shade and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and have thrice performed the Nāciketa sacrifice" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.1).
Here a doubt arises: is there unity of the knowledge taught here, or is there a plurality of knowledges?
What, then, is the prima facie view?
"Regarding the diversity of knowledge:
why?
Because of the perception of distinctions."
In the verse "Two birds," one is seen to be the enjoyer and the other is seen to be the non-enjoyer;

however, in the verse "The two drinking the *ṛta*," both are seen to be enjoyers. Since the object of knowledge (*vedya*) appears different, it might be argued that the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) must differ accordingly. To this, the author replies: "The unity of the knowledge."
Why? Because they declare that for both of these mantras, the object of knowledge is non-different, being limited to a specific measure and endowed with duality.
[Objection: But was not a difference in form shown? [Reply: No, it is said.
Both of these mantras establish the Lord who has the individual soul as His companion; they do not convey different meanings.
In the verse "Two birds," for instance, the Supreme Self—who transcends hunger and other such needs—is established by the words "the other, not eating, looks on.
Furthermore, in the remainder of that passage, He alone is seen to be the subject of exposition.
"When he sees the other, the Lord, and His greatness" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.7).

However, in the passage "the two who drink the Truth" (Katha Upaniṣad 3.1), while it is the individual soul that drinks, the Supreme Self—who transcends hunger and so forth—is also figuratively said to drink due to association, according to the maxim of the "umbrella-bearer.
For this is a context concerning the Supreme Self, as seen in: "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Katha Upaniṣad 2.14).

Because of this introductory statement, the complementary portion of the passage here also refers to that very same subject: "The bridge for those who sacrifice, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.2).
Furthermore, [the Sūtra] states: "For the two selves have entered the cave" (Brahma-sūtra 1.2.11).
This has been explained in detail in this context.

Therefore, there is no difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*), and consequently, there is unity of the knowledge (*vidya*). Furthermore, upon examining the sequence of these three Vedānta passages, it is understood that they concern only the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); the mention of the individual self (*jīva*) is intended solely to express identity with It, not to suggest any other meaning.

And it has been stated that there is no occasion for an inquiry into difference and non-difference within the knowledge of the Supreme Self. Therefore, this application (yoga) is solely for the purpose of elaboration; and from that follows the inclusion of additional attributes. // 34 //
22. The Section on Non-interruption. Sūtras 35–36:
[The Self] is within the aggregate of elements, like [the self within the body];
"That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1–3.5.1).
Thus, the Vājasaneyins record the two questions of Uṣasta and Kahola in immediate succession.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is there identity of knowledge (*vidyaikatva*) or diversity of knowledge (*vidyānānātva*)?
For the moment, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is diversity of knowledge.
[This is] due to the power of repetition (*abhyāsa*).
For otherwise, a double recitation regarding a meaning that is neither deficient nor redundant would be entirely purposeless.

Therefore, just as there is a difference in ritual acts (*karma*) due to repetition, so too there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to repetition—this being the position reached, [the author] replies: "Because there is no distinction in the intermediate recitation, there is oneness of knowledge with respect to one's own self."
For one's own Self, which is the innermost of all, is indistinguishable in both cases; it is both questioned about and answered regarding.
Indeed, two Selves cannot both be the innermost within a single body;
for if that were so, the status of being the innermost of all would only be conceivable for one of them.
But for one [entity], there can be no "being within all" (sarvāntaratva) in the same way as in the case of the aggregate of elements (bhūtagrāma).

The meaning is that just as in the body, which is a collection of the five elements, earth is within water, and fire is within water—even though there is a relative "being within," this does not constitute the primary sense of being within all—so it is here as well. Alternatively, the phrase "like the aggregate of elements" cites another scriptural passage as an illustration.

Just as in this mantra, "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11), the single inner Self of all is declared to exist within the entire aggregate of beings;
such is the meaning here regarding these two Brāhmaṇas as well.
Therefore, because the object of knowledge is one, the knowledge is one. // 35 //
If it is argued that otherwise the distinction [between the meditations] would be untenable, we say: no, for it is like other instructions (upadeśa).

Now, as for what was stated—that if the difference between the two knowledges (*vidyā*) is not admitted, the difference in their scriptural recitation (*āmnāna*) would be untenable—that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault.
This is because it is logical, as in the case of other instructions.

Just as in the sixth chapter of the *Tāṇḍya Upaniṣad*—wherein it is said, "That is the Self; thou art That, Śvetaketu"—there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) despite the instruction being given nine times, so it will be here as well.
How is it that there is no difference in the knowledge even though the instruction was given nine times?
Because the single meaning is understood through the beginning and the conclusion [of the passage], as in:
"Please, venerable sir, instruct me further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).
And because this very same single subject is introduced for the purpose of being explained again and again, and because repeated instruction is justified by the removal of successive doubts;
so too here, since there is no difference in the form of the questions, [the text says]: "Other than this, everything is perishable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2–3.5.1).
Thus, because there is no difference in their completion, the opening and the conclusion are seen to refer to a single subject matter.

By employing the particle *eva* in the second question— “That which is Brahman, immediate and direct” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1)— the author shows that the very same subject matter contained in the preceding question is being carried forward into the subsequent one.
In the former [section], the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and the organs is stated;
in the latter, however, that very same Self is described as transcending the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth.
Thus, the consistency of their having a single meaning is established.
Therefore, knowledge is one. // 36 //
23. Section on the Exchange (Vyatihārādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 37:
"There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [them] as in the other case.
Likewise, with reference to the Person in the Sun, the followers of the Aitareya recension record: "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I," and so forth.
Likewise, the Jābālas [state]: "O venerable one, you indeed am I, O deity; I indeed am you.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should the cognition here be formed in both ways through mutual transposition, or in only one way?
For now, he states that it should be in only one way.
For in this context, there is nothing else to be contemplated except the oneness of the self with the Lord.

If one were to imagine such a distinction as something to be contemplated— namely, that the transmigrating being possesses the nature of the Lord's self, or that the Lord possesses the nature of the transmigrating being—

then while the transmigrating being might attain excellence by having the nature of the Lord, how could there be any degradation for the Lord if he were to have the nature of the transmigrating being?
Therefore, the cognition has indeed a single form;
however, the scriptural teaching on mutual exchange is for the purpose of strengthening the realization of unity.
This being the position reached, he replies: "This mutual exchange is taught for the sake of meditation, as in other cases."
Just as other qualities, such as being the self of all and so forth, are recorded in the scriptures for the purpose of meditative reflection, so it is here;
for the reciters distinguish themselves by uttering both [identifications] in the form: "I am thou" and "Thou art I.
And that [distinction] becomes meaningful when a cognition of a dual form is to be produced.
Otherwise, this specific dual mention would be purposeless,
since the purpose would already have been accomplished by one alone.

Now, it was argued that if a specific meaning were postulated for the dual mention, it would entail the degradation of the deity by leading to the conclusion that the deity possesses the nature of a transmigrating soul.
This is not a fault,
because it is precisely the unity of the self that is being contemplated in this manner. But if that is so, does it not follow that this results in a mere reinforcement of the notion of oneness?

We do not deny the strengthening of the idea of oneness; rather, we establish only this much: that by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, the cognition here must be formed in two ways through mutual exchange, and not in a single way alone.
As a result, however, even oneness becomes firmly established.

Just as even when the purpose is meditation (*adhyāna*), the Lord is established as possessing those qualities through the instruction of attributes such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) and so forth, so it is here. Therefore, this reciprocal exchange (*vyatihāra*)—which consists of the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord—is to be meditated upon and should be integrated into the common subject matter. (37) *Note: Reciprocal exchange (*vyatihāra*) is the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul and the Lord.*
24. Section on Truth and the Others (Satyādyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 38:
"For that [same meditation] indeed consists of Truth and the others.
(BBs 3.3.38) "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as Brahman... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.4.1).

In the Vājasaneyaka, after enjoining the knowledge of Truth (*satyavidyā*)—the meditation on the syllables of its name—the following is recorded: "That which is this Truth is that Āditya, who is the person in this orb, and he who is the person in the right eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2), and so forth.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: Are these two distinct knowledges of Truth, or are they one and the same?
First, it is established that there are two; for there is a connection with distinct results mentioned earlier: "He conquers these worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.4.12).
"He destroys evil and leaves it behind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3, 4), as stated later on;
however, the reference back to the subject at hand is due to the identity of the object of meditation.
This being the case, we reply: this is indeed one and the same knowledge of Truth.
Why? Because of the reference back to the subject under discussion in the passage, "That which is that Truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2).
But has it not been stated that even when there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*), the attraction of what is under discussion is justified because the object of meditation (*upāsya*) is one?
This is not so;
for this would indeed be the case only where a difference in knowledge is perceived from some other clear cause.

In this case, however, since there is no possibility of [two] separate meditations due to the attraction of what was previously introduced as "That which is the Truth," the very same Truth connected with the preceding meditation is attracted into the subsequent one; thus, the certainty of their being a single meditation is established.

As for the argument that they are different meditations because a different fruit is heard, it is replied: this hearing of a different fruit is merely a commendation of the instruction on another auxiliary element—namely, "His secret name (upaniṣad) is 'aharaham'"—and therefore there is no fault.

Furthermore, since the fruit must be inferred from the explanatory passage (arthavāda) itself, and since the knowledge is one, even though many fruits are heard mentioned for its constituent parts, they must all be combined within the knowledge as a whole.

Therefore, this very same single knowledge of the True (Satya-vidyā) is taught as endowed with various specific attributes; consequently, all qualities such as "the True" (satya) and so forth must be combined in a single performance.
Some, however, [hold that] in this sūtra, this Vājasaneyaka passage concerning the Person in the eye and the sun—

And in the Chāndogya, having cited the passages, "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun" (Chā. 1.6.6) and "Now, this person who is seen in the eye" (Chā. 4.15.1), they consider that since this very same knowledge concerning the person in the eye and the person in the sun is one and the same in both places, the qualities such as Truth (satya) and the rest must be combined by the Chāndogyas from the Vājasaneyins.
That does not appear correct;

for in the Chāndogya, this knowledge based on the *udgītha* is understood as being connected with the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, since there are signs of connection with the ritual at its beginning, middle, and end, such as: "This [earth] is indeed the Ṛc, fire is the Sāman" (Chā. 1.6.1).
Thus at the beginning;

in the middle, "The sun and the Sāman are his two shoulders; therefore it is called the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8); and [at the end], "He who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.9).
Thus it is in the concluding summary.
In the Vājasaneyaka, however, there is no such mark connected with ritual action at all.

Since there is a difference in the introductory context (*prakrama*), and consequently a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*), it is logical that the qualities (*guṇa*) should remain in their respective states. 38.
FN: *Geṣṇau* means singers. Therefore, because they have the Ṛg and Sāman as their singers (*geṣṇa*).
Section 25: On the Authority of Wishes and so forth. Sūtra 39.
[The qualities such as] desire and so forth [belong] elsewhere, and not to those [qualities] such as the sense-bases.

Now, having introduced the topic with the words, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1), the Chandogas study the passage beginning: "This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger, without thirst, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).

Likewise, the Vājasaneyins [state]: "This indeed is that great unborn Self, who consists of cognition among the vital breaths; he rests in that space which is within the heart; he is the ruler of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Regarding this, when a doubt arises as to whether there is identity of knowledge and a mutual connection of qualities, or not, the conclusion is that there is identity of knowledge.
To this, it is said: "Because of desire and so forth."
The meaning is "one whose desires are true" (satyakāma), just as Devadatta is called simply Datta, or Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā.

That collection of qualities such as having true desires which is found in the Chāndogya with respect to the space within the heart is also found elsewhere in the Vājasaneyaka as mastery and so forth; and that [mastery] is also found elsewhere in the Chāndogya in the passage: "This Self is free from evil... (eṣa ātmāpahatapāpmā).
This is connected here [in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5].
Why? Because of the commonality of the abode and so forth.

For in this case as well, much commonality is observed: both have the heart as their locus; the Lord is the object of knowledge in both; and His nature as a bridge, with the purpose of preventing the confusion of worlds, is the same—thus many such similarities are seen.

Is it not the case that differences are also seen? In the Chāndogya, qualities are attributed to the space within the heart, whereas in the Vājasaneyaka, they belong to Brahman who has space as His support. No.

Because in the passage "The small [self] on account of the subsequent [arguments]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.14), it was established even in the Chāndogya that the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to Brahman alone;
however, this specific distinction exists here.

For in the Chāndogya, the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahmavidyā*) is taught, because there is a scriptural statement regarding the objects of desire being objects of knowledge just like the Self: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires" (Chā.
8.1.6). In the Vājasaneyaka, however, only the supreme Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa*) is seen being taught: "Speak further for the sake of liberation" (Bṛ. 4.3.14).
For this is established by the consistency of the question and answer beginning with "This person is indeed unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15);
as for the collection of qualities such as mastery and so forth, they are mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka solely for the purpose of praising that [Self].
And likewise, later on, the text concludes that Brahman is indeed devoid of attributes with the passage beginning, "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).

It should be understood, however, that this compendium of qualities is formulated in the Sūtra for the purpose of demonstrating the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the qualified Brahman due to its unity, and not for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). // 39 //
26. The Section on Reverence (Ādarādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 40–41:
On account of reverence, there is no omission.

(BBs 3.3.40) In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, with reference to the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it is heard: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice. Whatever first oblation he should offer, let him offer it to Prāṇa..."
"svāhā" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19.1), and so forth.

In that context, five offerings to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis) are prescribed; and regarding them, the term "agnihotra" is employed later on: "He who, knowing this thus, performs the agnihotra... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.2).

Thus [it is said]: "Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother, so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.5). Regarding this, the following is considered: Is the Prāṇāgnihotra omitted when eating is omitted, or is it not omitted?

Thus, since it is heard that there is a connection between the arrival of the devotee and [the performance of the rite], and since the arrival of the devotee is for the purpose of eating, it follows that when eating is omitted, the Prāṇāgnihotra is also omitted.
This being the position reached, he says first: "It should not be omitted.
Why?
Out of respect [for this].
For instance, in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā itself, the Jābāla Śruti says: "One should eat before the guests;
