for that would be as if one were to offer the Agnihotra for another without having offered it oneself"—thus, by censuring the priority of the guests' meal, it establishes the master's meal as first, thereby [prescribing] the Prāṇāgnihotra.
He shows respect [for this rule].

For he considers that while one [the *agnihotra*] cannot tolerate the omission of its priority, the other [the *bali*] certainly can; thus, it is thought that the latter can tolerate the omission of the *agnihotra*, which possesses that priority.
But is it not well known that, because of the connection with the arrival of the food intended for eating, there is an omission [of the *bali*] when the eating is omitted? No.
Because this [sentence] is intended to prescribe a specific substance for that [rite]:

since in the archetypal Agnihotra substances such as milk and so forth are fixed, and since here too the word "Agnihotra" brings about the extension of those same properties— just as in the case of the Kauṇḍapāyināmayaṇa sacrifice— this sentence, "That which is rice-gruel," is for the purpose of prescribing the specific quality of having rice-gruel as the sole substance.
Therefore, it follows that when a secondary quality is omitted, the primary act is not lost.
Thus, even upon the omission of food, the Prāṇāgnihotra should be performed by means of water or some other non-contradictory substance, according to the principle of substitution. // 40 //
To this, he recites the following:
"Because of the scriptural statement regarding what is present" (BBs 3.3.41).
When food is present, the *prāṇāgnihotra* is to be performed from that very substance of food which happens to be first available.
Why?
Because of that statement; for it says: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19.1).
By referring to the arrival of a devotee as if it were already established, the text prescribes that the oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) are to be accomplished with substances intended for others.
Since these [oblations] have acquired the characteristic of being non-obligatory (*aprayojaka*), how could they cause another substance to be substituted in the event of the omission of the meal?
Furthermore, there is no extension here of the ritual details (*dharma*) belonging to the original *agnihotra*.

In the case of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana sacrifice, because the word "Agnihotra" occurs within the injunctive statement—"He offers the Māsāgnihotra"—it is logical that it should cause the application of those [original] properties, and thus the acquisition of those properties is appropriate.
Here, however, the word "Agnihotra" occurs within an arthavāda (laudatory passage) and cannot cause the application of those properties.
Furthermore, if the acquisition of those properties were admitted, then even the fetching of the fires (*agnyuddharana*) and other such details would have to be performed.
And this is not possible:
first, the extraction of fire is for the purpose of providing a locus for the oblation;
nor can this be an oblation in the fire, because that would entail the contradiction of its being intended for the purpose of eating.
Moreover, this is indeed a *homa* because it is connected with substances brought forward for the purpose of eating.
Thus, the Jābāla Śruti—"One should eat before the guests"—shows that this performance of the *homa* has the mouth as its substratum.

For this very reason, even here [in the Chāndogya], it shows that the members of the Agnihotra are merely figurative: "The chest is the altar, the hairs are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2).
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the mention of the *vedi* (altar) here should be understood as an indication for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) alone,
because there is no altar in the primary *agnihotra*.
Furthermore, because the constituent parts of that [fire sacrifice] are intended to be accomplished here,
and because it is connected with the time specifically determined by the meal itself, there is no possibility of it obstructing the time for the *agnihotra*.
In this way, other duties as well, such as the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and so forth, are in some way or another incompatible [with the new moon sacrifice].
Therefore, these five oblations, through the conjunction of mantra, substance, and deity, must be performed only in the case of eating.
As for the statement regarding the observation of respect, that is intended to prescribe primacy in the case of eating;
for there is no such thing as an overburdening of a scriptural injunction.
But permanence cannot be demonstrated for this [fire-sacrifice] by means of that [eating];
therefore, there is simply an omission of the Prāṇāgnihotra when eating is absent. // 41 //
27. The Section on the Determination of That [Sūtra 42]: "There is no rule regarding the determination of that, because it is seen; for it is separate, and its fruit is the absence of obstruction.
(BBs 3.3.42) There exist meditations based upon the constituent parts of ritual action, such as: "One should meditate upon this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1).
Such are the [passages] beginning with these words.
We now investigate whether these are indeed eternal, like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood in sacrificial acts, or whether they are non-eternal, like the *godohana* vessel and similar items.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That they are eternal.
Why? Because they are encompassed by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*).

For even though these [meditations] are taught as unattached (*anārabhya-adhīta*), they are connected to the sacrifice through the *udgītha* and other such elements; thus, like other subsidiaries (*aṅga*), they are touched by the very injunction of the sacrificial performance.
As for the hearing of fruits in their own sentences—such as, "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7)—[this is not the primary result].

Because such passages take the form of descriptions of present facts, they are merely *arthavādas* (eulogistic statements), like the mention of "not hearing evil verses," and do not bestow a fruit. Therefore, just as in the case of [passages] such as, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood hears no evil verse," which— though read outside of a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇa*)— enter into the sacrifice by way of the *juhū*, and thus possess the character of being obligatory (*nitya*) like those read within a context, so too it is with the meditations (*upāsanās*) on the *udgītha* and other such elements.
This being the case, we reply: "The restriction is for the purpose of determining that.

Those determinations regarding the true nature of the qualities of ritual acts such as the *udgītha*—namely, [the meditations on] the "most savory," "attainment," "prosperity," the "chief vital breath" (*mukhya-prāṇa*), the "sun," and so forth—are not to be restricted as permanent parts of the rituals.
Why? Because of the observation of that [in the scriptures].

For thus the Śruti shows the non-necessity of such [knowledge], by permitting the performance of the action even for one who does not know: "Therefore both perform it—he who knows this thus, and he who does not know" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10). Furthermore, we observe that the Prastotṛ and others, though devoid of knowledge regarding the deities of the Prastāva and so forth, nevertheless resolve upon officiating at the sacrifice: "O Prastotṛ, if you shall chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.9).
"If you chant the udgītha not knowing that," (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.10),
and "If you respond with the pratihāra not knowing that," (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.11).
Moreover, a fruit of consciousness that relies upon such action is perceived as distinct from the action itself;
it is the accomplishment of the fruit of action, an unimpeded success, a certain excellence or distinction. "Therefore, both perform [the sacrifice]:
he who knows this thus, and he who does not know."
"But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different; whatever one performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).

In this passage, because of the separation of the performance of rites by the knower and the non-knower expressed by the word "different," and because of the use of the comparative suffix *-tara* in the word "more powerful" (*vīryavattaram*), it is understood that even ritual action devoid of knowledge possesses power.
And this is logically consistent only if knowledge is impermanent.
But if [the soul] were eternal, how could it be admitted that an action devoid of that [soul] could be efficacious?
For the established rule is that an action is efficacious only when all its constituent parts are brought together.

Likewise, in the case of the *loka-sāman* and other such rites, specific fruits are taught for each individual meditation: "The worlds, both ascending and descending, are prepared for him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3).
Regarding such passages as these, it is not reasonable to consider this mention of the fruit as being merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise);
for if that were so, it would result in [the scripture] being a mere figurative statement (*guṇavāda*).
In the case of the instruction regarding the fruit (*phalopadeśa*), however, the interpretation as a primary statement (*mukhyavāda*) is justified.

But in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, since the sacrifice—which has a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣa*)—is already under discussion (*prakṛta*), it is appropriate that the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), given that [the offerings] serve that purpose.
The same applies to such things as being made of *parṇa*-wood, which are taught as unconnected [*anārabhyādhīta*] [to any specific rite].
For non-ritualistic properties such as being made of *parṇa* wood cannot be connected to a result without a substrate.

Indeed, in the case of the *godohana* vessel and the like, the injunction of a result is appropriate because they obtain a substrate in the form of the *praṇayana* (water-carrying) which is under discussion in the context.

Similarly, for the *bilva* wood and the like, the injunction of a result is also appropriate because they obtain a substrate in the form of the *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and so forth, which are under discussion in the context.
However, in the case of [the injunctions regarding] being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth, there is no such substrate (*āśraya*) mentioned in the context;

since one would have to intend the *juhū* and other vessels as the substrate by means of a separate sentence while also intending an injunction for the fruit, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would occur.

But because meditations (*upāsanā*) are of the nature of action, it is possible to enjoin them with specific qualifications; therefore, there is no contradiction in enjoining those based on the *udgītha* and so forth for the sake of a fruit.

Therefore, just as the *godohana* vessel and other such items, although dependent on a sacrifice, are non-permanent due to their connection with specific results, so too should it be understood that meditations (*upāsanā*) on the *udgītha* and other elements are likewise non-permanent.
For this very reason, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* did not include such meditations within the ritual procedures of the sacrifices.
28. The Section on Bestowal. Sūtra 43:
"That has been explained as being like the bestowal.
In the Vājasaneyaka it is said: "I shall indeed speak—thus did Speech resolve" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).

Thus, in this context, Vāyu has been determined as the best among fire and the other deities with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*), while Speech and the others have been determined as the best among themselves with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Similarly, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—"Vāyu indeed is the absorber" (Chā.
4.3.1)—Vāyu is determined as the absorber of fire and the other deities with respect to the divine; and in "Prāṇa indeed is the absorber" (Chā.
4.3.2), Prāṇa is [determined] as the absorber of speech and the other organs with respect to the self.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: should these two, the vital air (vāyu) and the prāṇa, be understood as distinct, or as non-distinct?
For now, the initial position is that they are non-distinct, because there is no difference in their essential nature;
for it is not logical to contemplate as distinct that which is not different in its essence.

Moreover, Śruti demonstrates the non-difference of the essential nature (*tattva*) with respect to both the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine realm (*adhidaivata*), beginning with: "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth" (Ai.
2.4). Likewise: "Therefore, all these are indeed equal; all are infinite" (Bṛ. 1.5.13).
Thus, he shows that the divine manifestation is the very self of the internal vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Likewise, in various other places, there is a manifold presentation of the distinctions between reality regarding the internal (*ādhyātmika*) and the divine (*ādhidaivika*).
And in some instances, as in the statement "that which is the *prāṇa* is Vāyu," he clearly makes Vāyu and *prāṇa* one and the same.

Likewise, even though this Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa has been cited, in the concluding verse—"whence the sun rises"—it shows this very point by concluding with "breath alone," stating: "Verily, he rises from breath and sets in breath. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23)

Furthermore, the text, "Therefore, one should observe only one vow—both while breathing out and while breathing in" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23), confirms this by concluding with the single vow of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Similarly, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as well, it is stated later: "The great-souled one, the four, and the one God—who is he that awakens, the guardian of the world? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.6).
Thus, [the text] leads [the seeker] to a single absorber alone; it does not state that for some one among the four is the absorber and for others another is the absorber.
Therefore, the approach is non-distinct.
This being the position reached, we reply: Vāyu and Prāṇa are indeed to be approached separately.
Why?
Because of their separate instruction.

For this instruction concerning the division between the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva) is for the purpose of meditation; if there were no distinctness in meditation, it would be entirely purposeless.
But was it not said that there is no separate meditation because of the non-difference of the reality?
This is not a fault;
for even though there is non-difference of reality, a difference in meditation is possible due to the difference in states, by virtue of the difference in instruction.

Furthermore, since the citation of the verse can be understood even as intending no difference in essence, it lacks the capacity to refute the previously mentioned distinction between objects of meditation;

this is also because of the employment of a comparison and its object in the passage: "As the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22).
By this, the instruction regarding the vow is explained.

Furthermore, in the passage "The vow is indeed one" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23), the particle *eva* ("indeed") is intended to establish the vow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the exclusion of the vows of speech and the other senses.
For speech and the other organs are said to have broken their vows, according to the Śruti: "Death, having become weariness, overcame them" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).

Nor does [the subsequent passage] aim at the cessation of Vāyu's vow; for, having introduced the subject with "Now, therefore, the investigation of the vow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21), it determines that both Vāyu and Prāṇa equally possess unbroken vows.

Having stated, "One should observe only one vow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23), the text further declares, "By that, he wins union with and the same world as this deity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23);
by thus declaring the attainment of Vāyu as the fruit, it shows that the vow of Vāyu is not to be abandoned.

In the phrase "dvata," it must be Vāyu, because the state of having an unlimited nature is what is desired to be attained, and because of the preceding application [of this term]: "This deity, namely Vāyu, is never-setting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22).
Likewise: "These two are indeed the two absorbers—Vāyu among the deities and Prāṇa among the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.4).

Thus he designates them by way of distinction; and in the passage, "These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the Kṛta" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.8), he concludes by means of that very distinction.
Therefore, the approach [to the fires] is indeed separate.

It is like the case of the offering (*pradāna*). For example, in this sacrifice consisting of three sacrificial cakes (*tripuroḍāśinī iṣṭi*)—namely, "To Indra the King, a cake on eleven potsherds; to Indra the Overlord; to Indra the Self-Ruler"—there arises a suspicion that the offerings are made together because of the scriptural statement, "He cuts off [the portions] while bringing them all together so as not to cause a failure," and because there is no distinction between the Indras. However, due to the difference in qualities such as "King" and so forth, and because of the injunction for the transposition of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, just as in other cases, there is a distinctness of the offerings (*pradāna-pṛthaktva*) because of the distinctness of the deities (*devatā-pṛthaktva*).

It is so; thus, even though there is no difference in reality (*tattva*), there is a distinction in meditation (*ādhyāna*) because of the distinctness of the portions to be meditated upon (*ādhyeyāṃśa*).
This has been stated in the *Saṃkarṣa*: "Or the deity is not manifold, because of the knowledge [of it] as distinct."
In that case, however, a distinction between sacrifices exists due to differences in substance and deity; here, such a distinction between the meditations does not exist.

This is because, from both the introduction and the conclusion, it is understood that a single meditation is being enjoined throughout the teachings concerning the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva).

Even though the meditation is one and the same, a difference in practice arises due to the distinction between the internal and the divine, just as there is a difference in the performance of the *agnihotra* due to the distinction between evening and morning times.
Having intended this much, it was stated: "like the giving away" (pradānavat). // 43 //

29. The Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 44–52. Sūtra 44: "On account of the abundance of indicative marks; for that is more powerful, and that [is also] there.

In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyins, in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning, "In the beginning, this was not existent," the following is taught concerning the mind (*manas*): "He beheld thirty-six thousand Arka-fires of his own self, consisting of mind, built of mind."
And so forth.

In the same way, they record various fires to be meditated upon (*sāṃpādika*), such as "the fire built of speech, the fire built of breath, the fire built of sight, the fire built of hearing, the fire built of action, and the fire built of the sacrificial altar" (*vākcitaḥ prāṇacitaścakṣuścitaḥ śrotracitaḥ karmacito 'gnicitaḥ*).

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are these fires, beginning with that built of mind (*manaścit*), subordinate to ritual action and entering into it as its auxiliaries, or are they independent, consisting solely of knowledge (*vidyā*)?

In this regard, since the possibility of entering into the performance of ritual acts (prakaraṇa-kriyā) might arise, he first asserts their independence on the grounds that "there is fear of [contradicting] the indicative marks" (liṅga-bhaya-stvāt).

For in this Brāhmaṇa, many indicative marks are seen which strengthen the view that these [fires] consist solely of knowledge (vidyā); for example: "Whatever these beings conceive with the mind, that is indeed their making," and "All beings always build these [fires] for one who knows thus, even while he sleeps," and other passages of a similar kind.
For that indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This has also been stated in the previous section: "In the case of a conflict between direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the meaning" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.13).
[The opponent argues: "It should be an alternative to the preceding [rite] on account of the context, like the mental [sacrifice]. (BBs 3.3.45)
It has not been stated that these fires are independent (*svatantra*) and not subsidiary to anything else;

rather, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the previously mentioned fire consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*), this instruction regarding a specific option must pertain to that very subject and cannot be independent.
[Objection: But surely, indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than context.
This is true;
however, even an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this kind does not possess greater force than the context (*prakaraṇa*),
for this is merely an observation of something intended for another purpose.
Because this [passage] consists of praise for the fires as they are superimposed [upon the body],

and because a "perception of another purpose" (anyārthadarśana) is compatible even as a figurative statement (guṇavāda) when no other application is established, it is not able to subvert the context (prakaraṇa).
Therefore, these fires, though superimposed, must indeed enter into the ritual action due to the context.
It is like the case of the *mānasa* [offering].

For instance, on the tenth day of the ten-night sacrifice, which is the *avivākya*, the taking up, placing, offering, bringing forward, invitation, and consumption of the Soma— concealed from the deity Prajāpati as the ocean within the vessel of the earth—
are prescribed as being purely mental (*mānasa*).

And that mental construction of a grasper, because it occurs within the context of ritual action, is indeed a supplement to that action; thus, the meaning is that this [fire] is also like fire. (45) [Note:
*Avivākyam* is the name of the tenth day; and because of the extended application (*atideśa*). (BBs 3.3.46)

Furthermore, this extended application (*atideśa*) of these fires reinforces their entry into the ritual action: "There are thirty-six thousand fires; each one of them is as large as that former [fire].
For an extended application proceeds only when there is a commonality.

Thus, by extending the fires that are produced through the bricks—which have already entered the ritual action—to these other fires, the text indicates that these too must indeed enter into the ritual action. // 46 //
"But it is knowledge alone, because of the determination.
The word "but" sets aside the previous position.
These fires, such as the mind-fire (*manaścita*) and others, must consist of knowledge alone and be independent; they are not subordinate elements of ritual action.
For it determines thus: "These, indeed, are built of knowledge alone," and "By knowledge alone are these built for those who know thus. // 47 //
And because of the scriptural evidence.
Furthermore, a mark indicating their independence is observed;
this was demonstrated previously in the sūtra, "On account of the abundance of marks" (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.44). // 48 //

[Objection: But surely, even an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of establishing any meaning when another [means] is available; therefore, having set that aside, its status as a supplement to ritual action (*kriyāśeṣatva*) was determined by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*). To this, he recites the reply:

"And because of the greater strength of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, there is no sublation" (BBs 3.3.49). It is not the case that the position of independence should be sublated by determining its status as a supplement to ritual action through the force of the context.
This is because direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof are more powerful.
For it is established in the *Śrutiliṅga* Sūtra that direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are indeed stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*).
And these [means of proof] are seen here to establish the position of independence (*svātantrya*).
How so?
First, there is the direct scriptural statement (śruti): "These [fires] are indeed built by knowledge alone.
Likewise, there is the indicative mark (liṅga): "All beings always build them, even while they sleep."
Likewise, there is the statement: "By knowledge alone these [fires] are thus resorted to by one who knows thus.
For this scriptural text, which contains a restrictive particle (*eva*), would be contradicted if their entry into ritual action were admitted.
Now, it might be argued that this restriction is intended to show that they have no external means of accomplishment.
This is not so;

for if [the text] were intended to mean that [knowledge] is appropriate for that [state], then the restriction would be redundant, since the purpose would have been accomplished by the mere mention of their essential nature (svarūpa) itself.
For their very essence is such that they require no external means.

However, even though there are no external means [of performance], when a doubt arises as to whether these might enter into the ritual action—just like the mental [sacrifices]—the restrictive particle (*eva*) will be meaningful as having the purpose of excluding that possibility.

Likewise, the observation of their continuity in the passage, "For one who knows thus, whether sleeping or waking, all beings at all times pile these fires for him," is possible only if they possess independence.

This is just as in the case of the constructed Agnihotra consisting of speech and breath, where it is said: "Then he offers the breath in speech; then he offers speech in breath" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5).
Having said this, it is further stated: "These two infinite oblations he constantly offers while waking and while sleeping" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5).
It is just like that;
for if they were to enter into [the sphere of] ritual action, their performance could not be considered constant, since the application of ritual action occupies only a short period of time.
It is not logical to claim that this is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

For where a clear injunctive suffix or other such marker is perceived, it is appropriate that a mere mention constitutes an arthavāda. Here, however, since no other distinct injunction is found, one must assume that the injunction for the knowledge of these [elements] arises from the very mention itself.
And since that [agency] can only be postulated in accordance with what has been mentioned, it is postulated as being exactly of that nature because it is observed to be continuous.
Consequently, their independence is established by implication.
By this, such passages as "Whatever these beings conceive with the mind, that is indeed their creation" and so forth, have been explained.
Likewise, the scriptural statement "to one who knows thus" (evaṃvide), by declaring a connection with a specific person, does not tolerate a connection with a ritual sacrifice.
Therefore, the position of independence alone is superior. // 49 //
"Because of the connection [with ritual acts] and other reasons, as seen in the case of the distinctness of other cognitions; and that has been stated.

(BBs 3.3.50) For this reason as well, setting aside the context, the independence of the *manascit* and the others must be understood, because [the text] connects the parts of the ritual action with the operations of the mind and so forth, stating: "They were studied by the mind alone, they were piled up by the mind alone... and so on.

"The planets were seized by the mind; they praised with the mind; they recited with the mind. Whatever ritual act is performed in the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that is performed as consisting of mind alone, in those [beings] which consist of mind and are conscious of the mind. Thus it is said.
For this connection has prosperity as its fruit.
Furthermore, the constituent parts of an action, being perceptible, are not to be sought after through meditative identification (*saṃpad*).

Nor should it be suspected here that they enter into the action due to a connection with its parts—as is the case with the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—because the scriptural statement is of a different nature.
For the scripture does not say here that one should take some part of the action and superimpose the name "Agni" upon it.

Taking up thirty-six thousand varieties of mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*), it conceives of them as fire and so forth, as well as the cups (*graha*) and other ritual elements, just as in the case of the person (*puruṣa*) and the year.
This number should be understood as being observed in the days of a human lifespan and then superimposed upon the mental fluctuations associated with that lifespan.
Thus, due to this connection, the fires consisting of mind (*manaścit*) and the others possess independence.
The word "and so forth" (ādi) implies that extension (*atideśa*) and other such principles should also be applied as appropriate.

For instance, by stating, "Each one of those [fires] is indeed as great as the preceding one taken together," the text extends the greatness of the fire consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*) to each individual fire consisting of knowledge (*jñānamaya*), thereby demonstrating a lack of regard for mere ritual action.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the former and the latter fires only when a connection with ritual action actually exists.
For it is not possible for subsequent [elements] to assist in the action through that same operation— such as the carrying of the firewood— that the preceding one assists;

as for what was said in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that the extended application (atideśa) serves as a supporting argument because an extended application proceeds only when there is a commonality, that has been refuted by our position, since the extended application is possible here on the basis of the commonality of "fire-ness" (agnitva),
for even the fires that are merely metaphorical possess the nature of fire.
Furthermore, the scriptural passages and other grounds have been shown.
Thus, on account of these grounds— beginning with the connection— the mind-altars (*manaścita*) and so forth possess independence,
just as in the case of the distinctness of other cognitions (*prajñā*).

Just as other forms of knowledge, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, being connected with their own respective [injunctions], exist as independent of ritual actions and other forms of knowledge; so it is here.

Furthermore, it is observed that the *āveṣṭi* sacrifice, though recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya, is extracted from that context because it is connected with the three castes and because the Rājasūya is a sacrifice performed by a king alone.

This was stated in the first section (*kāṇḍa*) [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]: "If it is argued that it is for the sake of the sacrifice, no, because of the connection with the three castes" (Jaimini-sūtra 11.4.7).
FN: The *aveṣṭi* is a sacrifice bearing this name.
[The objection] that it is like death because of a commonality is not valid, for there is no attainment of the worlds [in this case].
This is said in response to what was stated regarding the *mānasa* [cup].
Nor can the status of the mental fires (manaścidādi) as subordinate to ritual action be inferred merely from their commonality with the physical fires,
because it is observed— on account of the previously mentioned reasons such as direct scriptural statement— that they serve solely the purpose of the person.
Indeed, there is nothing that does not share some degree of similarity with something else.
And by that much alone, the inequality does not cease to be as it truly is, just like death; for example:
"That person who is in this orb is indeed death," and "Agni, indeed, is death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10).
Thus, even though the term "death" (*mṛtyu*) is applied equally to the person in the fire and to the person in the sun, there is no attainment of absolute identity between them.

And just as in the passage, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; its fuel is the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1), the world does not actually become fire merely because of the commonality of the fuel and other attributes, so it is here as well. // 51 //
And the same nature of the word [is seen] later as well; however, due to its abundance, it is a continuous connection.

Even further on, in the immediately following Brāhmaṇa passage, "This world indeed is this fire-altar built of thought," the purpose of the word is observed to be solely the injunction of knowledge (*vidyā*), and not the injunction of a mere subsidiary element of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). For there [it says]: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have gone to rest."

By this verse—"Neither sacrificial gifts go there, nor those who are ignorant though ascetic"—the text, by censuring mere ritual action and praising knowledge, leads one to this understanding. Likewise, in the preceding Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "That orb which shines," it is clearly observed that knowledge alone is primary;
for it concludes with the fruit of knowledge itself, stating, "He becomes immortal, for Death becomes his very Self," and thus there is no primacy of ritual action.

Because of that similarity, it is the same here as well. However, the reason the fire-altar is associated with the knowledge (*vidyā*) is because a great many components of the fire-altar are to be accomplished within that knowledge; it is not because the fire-altar is a constituent part of ritual action (*karma*).
Therefore, it is established that the mind-built altars (*manaścita*) and so forth consist solely of knowledge.
30. The Section on the Unity of the Self (Aikātmyādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 53–54:

"The self is one, because it exists in the body. (BBs 3.3.53) Here, the existence of a self distinct from the body is established for the purpose of determining the eligibility for bondage and liberation.
For if there were no self distinct from the body, the injunctions regarding the next world would not be possible, nor could the state of being Brahman be taught to anyone.

[Objection: But was it not stated at the very beginning of the scripture, in the first section (pāda), that the self which experiences the fruit of the scripture exists as something distinct from the body?
[Reply: It is true that this was stated by the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra), but there is no sūtra there concerning the existence of the self.
In this context, however, the author of the Sūtras himself established its existence by means of a preliminary objection (*ākṣepa*).
It was precisely from this [work] that the teacher Śabarasvāmin drew [the argument] to describe it in his *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*.

For this very reason, the venerable Upavarṣa, when the occasion arose for stating the existence of the self (*ātman*) in the first book (*tantra*), made the following reference: "It will be explained in the *Śārīraka*."

And here, while these meditations characterized by scriptural injunctions (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*) are being investigated, the existence of the Self (*ātman*) is examined in order to demonstrate that this constitutes a supplement to the entire scripture. Furthermore, in the preceding section, by accepting the displacement of the context, it was described how the "mind-altars" (*manaścit* etc. serve the purpose of the person; now, when the question arises as to who that person is for whose sake these mind-altars exist, the existence of a Self distinct from the body is stated.

This first Sūtra is intended to raise an objection regarding its existence; for a refutation preceded by an objection produces a firm conviction regarding the intended meaning, according to the maxim of driving in a pillar. In this regard, some—the Lokāyatikas, who hold the view that the self is merely the body—consider that there is no self distinct from the body.

Even though consciousness is not observed in external elements such as earth, either individually or collectively, they imagine that it might exist in the elements when transformed into the form of a body;
thus, they assert that consciousness arises from these elements like the power of intoxication, and maintain that the person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by consciousness.
They hold that there is no self distinct from the body capable of going to heaven or attaining liberation (*apavarga*).
And they state the reason: "Because [these qualities] exist when the body exists.

For whatever exists when something else exists, and does not exist when that thing is absent, is determined to have that as its inherent property (*dharmatva*), just as heat and light are properties of fire.

Furthermore, for those who maintain the existence of a self (*ātmavādin*), vital breath, movement, consciousness, and memory are accepted as properties of the self; yet these too exist only within the body.

Since [the self] is perceived [as existing] externally yet is not perceived [as such], and since a substratum (dharmin) distinct from the body has not been established, it must necessarily be a property of the body alone.
Therefore, the self is non-distinct from the body. // 53 // [FN:
*Uddhāraḥ* means cessation.]
This being the case, we reply:
there is a distinction [between the self and the body] because [the cognition of the self] exists when that [body] exists; it is not, however, as in the case of perception.
It is not the case that what was stated—that there is no distinction between the self and the body—is correct.
Its distinction from the body must indeed exist, because it exists only when that [body] exists.

If one were to think that the attributes of the self belong to the body because they exist when the body exists, then why not likewise consider them not to be its attributes because they do not exist even when the body exists?
This is because they differ in nature from the attributes of the body.
Those bodily attributes such as form and so forth exist as long as the body exists;
however, vital functions, movements, and the like do not exist in the state of death even though the body is present.
Furthermore, bodily attributes such as form and so forth are perceived by others, but self-attributes such as consciousness and memory are not.
Moreover, while the body exists, it is possible to determine the presence of these [qualities] during the state of life, but not their absence when it is no longer present.
Even after this body has fallen, the attributes of the self might continue by migrating into another body.
Even on the basis of mere doubt, the opposing position is refuted.
Furthermore, the opponent must be questioned as to what he considers this consciousness (*caitanya*) to consist of, for which he desires an origination from the elements;
for the materialist (*lokāyatika*) does not admit any reality apart from the four elements.
If it is argued that consciousness is simply the experience of the primary elements and their derivatives, [we reply:]...
In that case, because they are objects, those [cognitions] cannot possess that [nature of being a subject], due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
For fire, though hot, does not burn itself;
nor will an actor, though well-trained, ever mount his own shoulders.
For it is not the case that the elements and elemental derivatives could be made objects by consciousness— which itself is of the nature of the elements and elemental derivatives—
since neither its own form nor the form of another is made an object by color-form (*rūpa*) and the like.
Rather, external and internal elements and elemental derivatives are indeed made objects by consciousness.
Therefore, just as the existence of this perception— which has as its objects the primary elements and their derivatives— must be admitted,
so too must the self be distinct from the body, since the self is not the very nature of perception;
and the self is eternal because perception is uniform in its nature.

Furthermore, because there is recognition [of the self] as the perceiver even when associated with different states, expressed as "I saw this," and because memory and other such functions are possible,
that which was argued— that perception is a property of the body because it exists only when the body is present— is refuted by the manner already described.
Furthermore, perception occurs when instruments such as a lamp are present and does not occur when they are absent;
yet, perception does not thereby become a property of the lamp and so forth.
In the same way, although perception occurs when the body is present and does not occur when it is absent, it cannot therefore be a property of the body.
For it is possible for the body to serve as an instrument for perception, just like a lamp or other tools;
yet, even the absolute necessity of the body's utility for perception is not observed, since various kinds of perceptions are seen in dreams even while this body is motionless.
Therefore, the existence of a self distinct from the body is beyond reproach. // 54 //
31. The Section on Those Bound to the Subsidiary Parts (Aṅgāvabaddha). Sūtras 55–56:
"But those bound to the subsidiary parts are not [restricted] to the branches, for they pertain to each Veda. (BBs 3.3.55) The incidental discussion is concluded.
But now we shall follow the subject at hand: "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1);
"One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
and "People say, 'The hymn, the hymn'; that very thing is indeed the hymn."
"‘This very earth,’ ‘this world indeed is this piled fire-altar’— such meditative realizations (pratyayas) connected with the members of rites such as the Udgītha,
which are enjoined in each Veda across various recensional branches (śākhā), would they apply only to the Udgītha and so forth belonging to those respective branches, or rather [to all]?"
The doubt concerns those [meditations] occurring in all the Vedic branches:
should they not be enjoined for the Udgītha and so forth in each individual branch because of differences in accent and the like?
Why? Because of proximity.

For when there is a requirement for specification regarding those things enjoined in general terms, such as "one should meditate on the udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), that requirement for specification is satisfied by the proximate details belonging to one's own Vedic branch alone;
therefore, there is no reason to bypass those and adopt specifications enjoined in another Vedic branch.
Therefore, it follows that there is a fixed rule for each Vedic school (*śākhā*).
To this position, [the author] says: "But those connected with the subsidiaries (*aṅgāvabaddhāḥ*). The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous view.

These [meditations] do not remain restricted to their own branches for each Veda; rather, they recur in all branches. Why? Because there is no distinction in the scriptural mention of the *udgītha* and so forth.

For if one were to restrict [the meditation] to one's own Vedic branch (svaśākhā), the scriptural statement (śruti) "one should meditate on the udgītha," which is general in nature and applies without distinction, would be strained when it is restricted to a specific instance by virtue of proximity (saṃnidhāna).
And this is not logical;
for scripture is more powerful than proximity.
Nor is it the case that a cognition based on a universal is untenable;

therefore, even though there are differences such as the specific tones (svaras), because the nature of being the *udgītha* and so forth remains undifferentiated, such cognitions must apply to the *udgītha* and other elements found in all Vedic branches.
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like.
Alternatively, one should not even suspect a contradiction here, such as:
"How could meditations prescribed in one Vedic branch apply to the *udgītha* and other elements belonging to another Vedic branch?"
Because there is no contradiction in the application of mantras and so forth;
for it is observed that mantras, rituals, and accessories, even when produced in one Vedic branch (*śākhā*), are incorporated into another branch.
Indeed, even for those followers of a branch who do not have the mantra "kuṭarur asi" prescribed for the taking up of the stone, its application is nonetheless seen.

The mantra for taking up the stone, "Thou art a cock," is not recited [in some schools], yet its application is seen even among them: "He takes up the stone with [the mantra] 'Thou art a cock' or 'Thou art a ram.

Furthermore, even for those [schools] where the *samits* and other *prayāja* offerings are not recited, an injunction regarding their quality is handed down: "The *prayājas* are indeed the seasons; they are to be offered together.

Likewise, even for those who have no instruction regarding a specific genus, such as "The *agnīṣomīya* animal is a goat," a portion of a mantra concerning that subject is found: "Recite the invitatory verse for the omentum and fat of a goat."
Likewise, the inclusion of mantras originating in one Veda within another Veda is observed, such as the mantras beginning with "agnerveḥ hotram veradhvaram.
Similarly, the inclusion of the hymn recited by the Bahvṛcas, "yo jāta eva prathamo manasvān" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.6.7), within the Adhvaryu ritual in the passage "sajanīyaṃ śasyam," is observed.

Therefore, just as there is a universal persistence of the constituent parts of the ritual (karmāṅga) which serve as the bases, so too is there such persistence of the conditions (pratyaya) which depend upon them; thus, there is no contradiction. // 56 //

32. The Section on the Superiority of the Whole (Bhūman). Sūtra 57: The superiority of the Whole [is established] like that of the sacrifice; for thus the scripture shows. "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.1).
In this narrative, the meditation upon Vaiśvānara both distributively and collectively is heard.

First, regarding the distributive meditation: "O Aupamanyava, whom do you meditate upon as the Self? "The god alone, O venerable King," he replied. [The King said: "This indeed is the highly resplendent Self, Vaiśvānara, whom you meditate upon as the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.1), and so forth.

Likewise, there is also meditation on the whole, as in: "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brightly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (the multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (the one whose paths are separate), the trunk is *bahula* (the vast), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are the earth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should there be meditation in both ways—on the divided [parts] and on the whole—or only on the whole?
What, then, is the initial position?

Since the verbal action "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) is heard in connection with each individual member, such as *sutejas* and the rest, and since distinct fruits are heard in passages such as, "Therefore, Soma-pressing, continuous pressing, and constant pressing are seen in your family" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.1), it follows that the meditations may indeed be performed separately.

To this, it is replied: In this passage, what is intended to be expressed is the superiority and primacy of the entire Vaiśvānara meditation— which consists of the accumulation of many constituent elements— not the individual meditations on each of its parts,
as is the case with a sacrificial rite (*kratu*).

Just as in sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, it is intended that the performance of the principal rite together with all its subsidiaries (*sāṅga-pradhāna*) is to be carried out as a whole, and not the performance of the subsidiaries like the *prayāja* offerings individually, nor the principal rite joined with only a portion of its subsidiaries—likewise [it is so here]. Why is this? Because the abundance [of means] alone is superior.
For thus scripture shows the superiority of the *bhūman* (the Infinite), because we perceive a single unified statement [in this context].
Indeed, by considering the preceding and following passages, one recognizes that this is a single sentence concerning the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.
To explain: six sages, beginning with Prācīnaśāla and ending with Uddālaka, were unable to attain full certainty regarding the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.

Having begun with the statement, "They approached King Aśvapati Kaikeya," and having caused each of the sages to hear one by one [the names] beginning with Dyus— who were to be worshipped— it prescribes their status as the head and so forth through the passage, "But he is indeed the head of the self," and so on (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2).
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2), [the text] censures meditating on the parts separately.
Then, having again set aside meditation on the parts and continued with meditation on the whole, it says: "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).
Thus, he shows that the fruit indeed rests upon the *bhūman* (the Infinite) alone.

As for the mention of distinct fruits for each [meditation] beginning with "Sutejas" and so forth, this should be understood as follows: since this is the case, the fruits of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are actually accepted as belonging to the principal part (*pradhāna*) itself.

Likewise, the hearing of the verb in the past tense (*ākhyāta*) for every single member, such as "He meditated" (*upāsā cakre*), is for the purpose of restating the opponent's view, not for the purpose of enjoining separate meditations on each individual part.
Therefore, the position that meditation on the whole alone is superior.

However, some maintain that having established the position of meditation on the whole as superior here, the author of the Sūtras must also approve of the position of meditation on the parts, precisely because of that statement regarding its superiority; this is incorrect, for when a single coherent meaning is understood, it is improper to assume a split in the sentence.
Furthermore, this contradicts such censure statements as, "Your head would have fallen off" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2).
Moreover, since the conclusion clearly indicates that all [attributes] are to be meditated upon, it would be impossible to maintain the opponent's prima facie view regarding their absence.
And because the statement regarding the superiority of the Sautrāntika position is also tenable when understood as intending that it possesses valid authority. // 57 //
33. The Section on the Difference of Words and so forth. Sūtra 58:
"They are different because of the difference of words and so forth.

(BBs 3.3.58) In the preceding section, it was stated that even though there are scriptural mentions of different fruits for those beginning with *Sutejas*, the meditation upon them as a whole is superior. However, [in the present case], they are different because of the difference of words and so forth.
Therefore, it follows that other meditations with different scriptural texts, having been attained, would be combined and practiced together.
Moreover, when there is no difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*), a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot be recognized;
for the object of knowledge is the very form of the knowledge, just as the material substance and the deity are the form of a sacrifice.

Moreover, the Lord who is to be known is understood to be one alone, even though there is a diversity of scriptural passages, such as: "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2),
"Bliss is Brahman, space is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5),
and "He whose desires are true, whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).
In such passages as these, as well as:
"The vital breath alone is the absorber; the vital breath indeed is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.3), and "The vital breath indeed is the eldest and the best" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1).
In such passages as "Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is the mother" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1),
because the knower is one, the knowledge is one.

Even the diversity of scriptural statements (*śruti-nānātva*) in this view does not imply a multiplicity of meanings, because they refer to different subordinate qualities (*guṇāntara*). Therefore, the collection of qualities prescribed in one's own and other branches, which rest upon a single substance, must be combined for the sake of the completeness of the knowledge (*vidyā-kārtsnya*). This being the position reached, the author states the conclusion: "Not so; [there is] diversity."
Even though the object of knowledge is non-different, ignorance of this kind must nevertheless be distinct.
Why? Because of the difference in words and so forth.
For there is indeed a difference in words: "one should know," "one should meditate," "he forms a resolve" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
This is the beginning [of the argument].

It has been established previously that a difference in words is a cause for a difference in ritual acts, according to the principle: "In the case of another word, there is a difference in the act because of the connection with a different [verbal] root.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), other factors such as qualities (guṇa) and so forth should also be applied as causes of differentiation, as far as applicable.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the passages beginning with "He knows" (*veda*), only a difference in words is perceived, and not a difference in meaning as in the case of "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and so forth? For all these [verbs] have no difference in their meaning, since they all refer to a mental activity (*manovṛtti*), and because no other meaning is possible. Therefore, how can there be a difference in knowledge (*vidyābheda*) based on a difference in words?
[Response: This is not a fault.

Even though there is no difference in the fact that both have mental activity as their purpose, a distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*) is established because there is a distinction in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) due to a difference in their adjuncts (*anubandha*).
For even in the case of the one Lord who is the object of worship, distinct qualities are taught in each respective section.

Likewise, although the Prāṇa who is the object of worship is the same, in one place it is to be worshipped with one set of qualities, and in another place with a different set of qualities; thus, since there is a distinction in the objects of knowledge due to a difference in adjuncts, there is a distinction between the meditations.
It is understood that it is not possible to say here that one is an injunction of knowledge (*vidhi*) while the others are injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*),
because there is no reason for such a distinction in their application (*viniyoga*).
Furthermore, because the qualities are distinct in each section, it is impossible to enjoin them by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a previously established knowledge (*vidyā*).
Moreover, on this view, the common qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) would not need to be repeated [in every section].

And since, in each section, one understands a state of self-sufficiency through the realization that "this is to be meditated upon by one desiring this, and that by one desiring that," there is no resulting loss of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Furthermore, in this case, as in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is no overarching injunction (*samasta-codanā*) by whose force the meditations on the individual parts contained within each respective section could attain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

And if the unity of the meditation were asserted everywhere without restriction on the grounds of the identity of the meditation itself, then it would be impossible to assert the combination of all qualities.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "They are distinct, because of the difference in words and so forth."
And while this subject matter remains, it should be understood that [the principle] "all Vedānta texts convey the same cognition" and so forth applies here as well. // 58 //

34. Section on Option (Vikalpa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 59: There is an option, because the fruit is not distinguished. (BBs 3.3.59) Having established the difference between the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is now considered whether there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) among them according to one's desire.
Alternatively, [one might argue] that there is a rule of optionality (*vikalpa*) alone.
In that case, since the distinction between the types of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established, there is no reason whatsoever for a rule of mandatory combination (*samuccaya*).
But surely, even for distinct rites such as the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, a rule of mandatory combination is observed?
This is not a fault;
for in that case, the scriptural statement regarding eternality is the reason, whereas there is no such scriptural statement regarding the eternality of the vidyās.
Therefore, there is no rule of obligatory combination.
Nor is there a restriction regarding the specific meditative knowledge (*vidyā*);
for one who is engaged in one *vidyā* is not prohibited from another. By the principle of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that one may proceed according to one's own preference.
But surely, since their fruits are indistinguishable, it is logical that they should be treated as optional alternatives;
for instance: "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2), and "Bliss is Brahman, the ether is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5).
[Objection: Passages such as "He whose desire is truth, whose resolve is truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5) appear to indicate that the fruit is the attainment of the Lord in all cases alike.
[Reply: This is not a fault.
Even among those ritual acts that lead to the same fruit, such as the attainment of heaven, since we observe that they may be performed according to one's desire,
therefore, when there is the possibility of acting according to desire, it must be understood that these acts are subject to option (*vikalpa*) and not to combination (*samuccaya*).
Why?
Because their fruit is not distinct.
For the fruit of these [meditations] is indeed the same: the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object of worship.
Once the object of worship, such as the Lord (*Īśvara*), has been directly realized through one meditation, a second meditation would be purposeless.
Moreover, there is the impossibility [of simultaneous realization] because,
in the case of a combination [of means], it would cause distraction of the mind;
and the scriptures show that the fruit of knowledge is the attainment of direct realization.
"Whoever has this [knowledge], for him there is truly no doubt" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4),
and "Having become a god, he goes to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2)— such passages as these [are evidence].

Therefore, having selected any one of those meditations which yield non-distinct results, one should be devoted to it until that result is attained through the direct realization of the object of meditation. // 59 //

35. The Section on Optional Rites (Kāmyādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 60: But the optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not, because the previous reason [for non-combination] is absent.
This is a counter-example to the argument that [the rites] have indistinguishable fruits.

Furthermore, in those optional sciences (*kāmyā vidyā*) such as "He who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters does not weep for a son" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.15.2), and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman— so far as Name extends, there he has free movement according to his will" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5)— which accomplish their respective fruits through an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) inherent in the action itself, there is no requirement for direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Therefore, they may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not be combined, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason;
for there is an absence of that alternative reason [namely], "because the preceding [practice] has an undifferentiated fruit. // 60 //
36. The rule regarding the nature of the substratum, etc. (Sūtras 61–66):
"The nature of the substratum applies to the auxiliary parts" (BBs 3.3.61).

Regarding the doubt as to whether the meditative realizations (*pratyaya*) prescribed in the three Vedas that are based upon the auxiliary parts of ritual action—such as the *udgītha* and so forth—should be combined or may be performed according to one's preference, the Sūtra states: "The nature of the substratum [applies]."
Just as their bases, such as the hymns (*stotra*) and so forth, exist collectively, so too do the conditions (*pratyaya*), because conditions are dependent upon their bases. // 61 //
And because they are taught together (śiṣṭeś ca).
Just as the bases, such as the *stotra* hymns, are taught in all three [Vedas], so too are the suffixes (*pratyaya*) that depend upon them.
The meaning is that there is no distinction created by the instruction regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the suffixes that depend upon them. // 62 //
Because of the bringing together [of the two].
And from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.5.5): "Even from the Hotṛ’s seat, he repairs a poorly sung udgītha.
Thus, through the greatness of the knowledge of the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, the singer (*udgātṛ*) repairs the damage incurred in his own ritual act from the act of the Hotṛ.

By stating "he restores," it indicates the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) that suggests the inclusion of a sacrificial element taught in one Veda based on the commonality of its connection with the ritual elements taught in another Veda. // 63 //
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities:

in the context of knowledge (*vidyā*), the scripture declares that the syllable *oṃ*, which is the substratum of knowledge, is common to all three Vedas—“By means of this, this triple knowledge proceeds; one intones ‘Oṃ,’ one recites ‘Oṃ,’ one chants the *udgītha* ‘Oṃ’” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
Consequently, because the substratum is common, that which depends upon it is also common; this is merely the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Alternatively, it is because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the qualities (*guṇa-sādhāraṇya*).

If these ritual qualities, such as the *udgītha* and so forth, were not common to all performances, then there would be no simultaneous occurrence of the meditative realizations (*pratyaya*) based upon them.

However, those [limbs] such as the *udgītha* and so forth are heard through the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) which encompasses all limbs; thus, they are common to the entire performance.
And in this way, because of the coexistence of their substrates, there is a coexistence of the mental cognitions (*pratyaya*). // 64 //
Or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture].
The word "or rather" (na vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
It is not possible for the meditations (*upāsanā*) that depend [on a substrate] to exist in the same manner as the substrate itself.
Why? Because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture].

For whereas the coexistence of the auxiliary elements such as the *stotra* (chants), which are prescribed in the three Vedas, is indeed heard—e.g., "Having taken up the cup (*graha*), or having drawn out the *camasa*, he begins the *stotra*; he recites after the *stotra*; O Prastotṛ, sing the *Sāman*; O Hotṛ, recite this offering-verse," and so forth—[no such rule exists for the meditations].
There is no such scriptural statement regarding the simultaneous performance of these meditations.
But would it not be the case that the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) would necessitate their simultaneity?
We say: no, because these meditations have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
For the injunctive statement would bring about the coexistence of the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) such as the *udgītha* and others, which serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

We have already stated in the commentary on *Brahmasūtra* 3.3.42—that "the fruit is separate because there is no obstruction"—that meditations (*upāsanā*) on the *udgītha* and so forth, although based on elements serving the purpose of the sacrifice, are for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), like the *godohana* vessel.

This very distinction based on the scriptural instruction is what differentiates the subsidiaries from the meditations that take them as their support: namely, that some are for the purpose of the sacrifice while others are for the purpose of the person.
Furthermore, the two marks [of gender] are not a cause for the coexistence of meditations, because there is neither scriptural authority nor logical reasoning for it.

Nor can it be understood that the meditations themselves must likewise be combined with every performance [of the rite], on the grounds that the entire substratum is to be employed in each performance;
for such meditations have already been refuted by that [refutation of the combination of subsidiaries].

For even meditations that depend on a substrate may indeed cease to exist in the absence of a substrate; however, they do not require a rule of coexistence based on the coexistence of the substrate, precisely because there is no scriptural statement regarding such coexistence.
Therefore, the meditations should be performed according to one's own desire. // 65 //
And because it is seen [in scripture].
For scripture shows that the conditions are co-existent with hearing: "Thus indeed does Brahmā protect the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.10).
For if all conditions were brought together, everyone would be omniscient; thus, it would not be proclaimed that others are to be protected by the omniscient Brahman.
Therefore, according to one's desire, there may be either a combination or an option among the meditations. // 66 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Third Chapter, Fourth Section.
Herein is the investigation of the internal and external means for the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.
1. The Section on the Goal of Human Life (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–17.
"From this [knowledge] results the human goal, according to the Word; thus says Bādarāyaṇa.

Now, investigating whether the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads enters into ritual action by way of a specific qualification, or whether it is an independent means for accomplishing the human goal, he begins with the established conclusion: "From this results the human goal."
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the human goal is accomplished through the knowledge of the Self as enjoined by our Vedānta, which is independent [of ritual action].
From what is this understood? He says: "From the Word" (śabdāt).
For instance: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3).
"He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9);
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
"The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
Thus [it is said]:

"Having begun with, 'That Self which is free from evil' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), [the text continues]: 'He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1)."

Beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6) and concluding with "This much, indeed, my dear, is immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), scripture of this kind declares that knowledge alone is the cause of the human goal. // 1 //
Now, an objection is raised here:
"Because it is subordinate [to ritual action], it is a statement of human purpose (*puruṣārthavāda*), as in other cases," says Jaimini.

Since the self's status as an agent is subordinate to the ritual action, the knowledge of that [self] is also connected to the ritual action by way of its object—just like the sprinkling of rice grains (*vrīhiprokṣaṇa*) and so forth; therefore, when its purpose has been understood...

The teacher Jaimini maintains that the scriptural declaration of results regarding the knowledge of the Self is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), just as in the case of other rites involving substances, purificatory acts, and ritual actions— for example:
"He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," and "When one anoints his eyes, he thereby appropriates the very sight of his rival."

"The fact that the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed constitutes an armor for the sacrifice, a rite for the sacrificer's overcoming of his enemies"—such scriptural mentions of results (*phalaśruti*) are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
It is similar in this case.

But how can it be suspected that this knowledge of the Self, which is taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), enters into the sacrificial ritual in the absence of any basis such as a specific context (*prakaraṇa*)?
If it is argued that the connection of the knowledge of that [mantra] with the sacrifice occurs through the sentence by way of the agent, we say no;
for its application [to the sacrifice] cannot be established on the basis of the sentence alone.
For even in the case of those [passages] studied as unattached (anārabhyādhīta), a connection with the sacrifice based on the sentence is possible only through some non-deviating medium.
But the agent is an inconsistent means, because it is common to both worldly and Vedic actions;
therefore, the connection of the knowledge of the Self with the sacrifice is not established through that means. [Reply:
No, because the realization of the distinction [between the Self and the body] has no application other than for Vedic actions.
Knowledge of a self distinct from the body is not of use in worldly activities, since engagement in them is possible in every way through perceived ends.

However, in the case of Vedic rites whose fruits are realized after the fall of the body, engagement would not be possible without knowledge of a self distinct from the body; thus, the cognition of such distinction is useful.

[Objection: But surely, because of such qualifiers as "freedom from evil" (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth, the Upaniṣadic vision concerning the non-transmigrating Self cannot be a factor for [worldly] activity. [Reply: No;
for it is the transmigrating Self itself, indicated by its "beloved" and other attributes, that is taught as the object to be seen.
As for the qualifiers such as "freedom from evil," they will serve the purpose of glorification (stuti).

[Objection: Has it not already been established in various places that this Brahman, which is beyond transmigratory existence, is the cause of the world, and that it alone is taught in the Upaniṣads as the ultimate essential nature of the transmigrating self? [Reply: True, it has been established; however, for the sake of firmness, objections and their resolutions are now being presented by way of the result, like the driving in of a pillar. // 2 //
Because we observe such conduct:
"Janaka, the King of Videha, performed a sacrifice with many sacrificial gifts" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1);
"Venerable sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.5).
Thus, there are such observations of a connection with ritual action even in the case of knowers of Brahman within sentences that have other primary purposes.
Likewise, from the observation of Uddālaka and others instructing their sons and so forth, their connection with the householder’s life (gārhasthya) is understood.

If the fulfillment of the human goal were to occur through knowledge alone, why would they perform rituals involving manifold exertions? As the saying goes: "If one should find honey on an arka tree, why should one go to the mountain?"
Because it is logical. // 3 //
Because of that scriptural statement;

and because knowledge is heard of as being subordinate to action in the passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad—that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), knowledge by itself is not the cause of the supreme human goal. 4.
Because of the mention of "simultaneous undertaking" (*samanvārambhaṇāt*);

and because of the observation that knowledge and action act as concurrent causes (*sahakāritva*) in the commencement of the fruit, as stated in the passage, "Knowledge and action both take hold of him" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.2), knowledge does not possess independence. // 5 //
Because it is enjoined for one who possesses that [knowledge].

The scriptural passage of this kind—"Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher, according to the prescribed rule, and having returned home at the conclusion of his service to the guru, let him dwell in his household, studying his own portion of the Veda in a pure place" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1)—shows that the qualification for ritual action belongs to one who possesses the knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda. Therefore, for this reason as well, knowledge does not have the status of being an independent cause of the fruit.
But surely, here [in the injunction], only the mere recitation of the Veda is heard, not the comprehension of its meaning.
This is not a fault;
for it is an established principle that the study of the Veda, because it serves a visible purpose, extends until the comprehension of the meaning is attained. // 6 //
And because of the scriptural injunction:
"One should desire to live here for a hundred years performing actions alone;
thus it is with you, and not otherwise than this; action does not cling to a man" (Īśa Upaniṣad 2).

Likewise, from such injunctions as, "This Agnihotra is indeed a sacrificial session (sattra) that ends with old age; for one is released from it either by old age or by death," it follows that the knowledge of the Self is merely a subordinate part of ritual action.
This being the position reached, the author provides the following rebuttal:
"But because of the teaching of something additional, Bādarāyaṇa holds [the view] thus, for that is seen. (BS 3.4.8)
By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed.
That which was stated— namely, "Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.2)— is not tenable.
Why?
Because of the teaching of something additional.

If the transmigrating self alone—the embodied one who is both agent and enjoyer—were taught in the Vedāntas as being distinct merely from the body, then, in the manner described, the mention of the fruit would be a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

To begin with, the Supreme Self—the non-transmigrating Lord who is superior to the embodied self, devoid of transmigratory attributes such as agency, and characterized by qualities such as being "free from sin"—is taught in the Vedāntas as the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, the knowledge of that Self does not incite one to ritual actions; on the contrary, as will be stated in the sūtra "And [it teaches] the destruction" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.16), it cuts them away.
Therefore, [the attainment of] the human goal results from this [knowledge], as established by scripture (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.1).
Thus, the view of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa stands exactly as it is; it cannot be shaken by fallacious arguments such as [the soul being] a subordinate factor (*śeṣatva*).

For indeed, the Śrutis reveal that Supreme Self, the Lord who is distinct from the embodied soul: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9), and "From fear of Him the wind blows" (Taittirīya 2.8.1).
"A great terror, a raised thunderbolt" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.2); "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9);
"It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and it emitted heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
Such are the passages beginning with these.
As for the subsequent reference to the transmigrating self alone—indicated by terms such as "dear"—as the object of knowledge, as in: "But it is for the sake of the self that everything becomes dear;
indeed, the self, my dear, should be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
"He who breathes with the breath— that is your Self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1);
and beginning with "This person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.4),
it continues, "I shall explain this very one to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3).
And such passages as these also [support this view]: "This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10);
"He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1);
and "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form; he is the Supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Through such supplementary statements as these, there is no contradiction, for they intend absolute non-difference precisely because there exists a desire to teach the higher [Self].
Indeed, the ultimate, real nature of the embodied soul is that of the Supreme Lord alone;
its status as an embodied soul, however, is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
This is known from such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
Furthermore, all of this has been described by us in detail previously in various places. // 8 //
But the observation of [the sages'] conduct is equal.
