Regarding what was said—that knowledge is a remainder of ritual action because of the observation of their conduct—we reply: the observation of conduct is equally applicable even if knowledge is not a remainder of ritual action.

For thus there is a scriptural passage: "Regarding this, indeed, the Ṛṣis, the descendants of Kavaṣa, knowing this, said: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices?

Indeed, knowing this, those of old did not offer the Agnihotra. Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas, rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lead the life of mendicants."

[The texts] of this kind, such as "they move about" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�ṣad 3.5.1), show that even Yājñavalkya and others who were knowers of Brahman remained steadfast in the practice of yoga. Thus it is said: "Having said, 'This much indeed, my dear, is immortality,' Yājñavalkya departed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, the observation of this indicative mark— "O venerable sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.5)— has the Vaiśvānara-vidyā as its subject matter.
Furthermore, it is possible to observe the association of ritual action with the knowledge of Brahman when that knowledge is conditioned by limiting adjuncts;
however, even in this case, there is no status as a subordinate part of the ritual, because of the absence of context and other such indicators. // 9 //
Furthermore, regarding what was stated [in Brahma-sūtra 3.4.4], "On account of that being heard," we reply here:
it is not universal.

The scriptural passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), does not refer to all forms of knowledge, because it is connected specifically with the knowledge under discussion.
And the Udgītha-vidyā under discussion is that found in the passage: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1). // 10 //
The distribution [of the fruits] is like that of a hundred [coins].

As for what was said— that the statement, "Knowledge and action both take hold of him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2), which speaks of their simultaneous taking hold, is a mark (*liṅga*) of the lack of independence of knowledge— that is now answered.
In this case, a distinction is to be understood: knowledge takes hold of one person, while karma takes hold of another.
It is like a hundred [coins].
Just as when it is said, "Let a hundred be given to these two," it is given by dividing it—fifty to one and fifty to the other—in the same way.

Furthermore, this statement regarding "commencing" does not concern one who seeks liberation, because it concludes with a reference to the transmigrating soul in the passage, "Thus, indeed, he who desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), followed by,
"But he who does not desire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
And because there is a separate introduction for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*),
in that context concerning the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), both prescribed and prohibited knowledge is included, as there is no distinction; likewise,
both prescribed and prohibited action is included, since it is merely restated as it occurs in worldly experience.
This statement regarding simultaneous undertaking is thus also intelligible even when there is no distinction between the truths. // 11 //
And regarding this, he recites the following [sūtra] after "Because of the injunction for one who possesses that" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.6):
"[The fruit belongs] to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. (BBs 3.4.12)

Since the text "Having studied the Veda from the family of the teacher" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1) mentions study alone, we conclude that the injunction for ritual action applies only to one who possesses merely that study.
[Objection: But if this were so, the lack of qualification for rituals due to ignorance would follow as a consequence.

This is not a fault. We do not deny that the understanding of ritual action arising from Vedic study is a cause for qualification [for rites]; rather, we establish only this much: that the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads, being perceived as having its own independent purpose, does not function as a cause for qualification for ritual action.
And just as the knowledge of one sacrifice is not required for the eligibility to perform another sacrifice, so too should this be understood. // 12 //
Regarding what was also stated in [Brahma Sūtra] 3.4.7, "And because of the restrictive rule," it is here replied:
"No, because there is no distinction. (BBs 3.4.13)
In such scriptural injunctions as "One should desire to live performing actions here indeed" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2), there is no specific qualification that they apply only to the knower;
for these rules of necessity are prescribed without distinction.
Or [it may be] for the sake of praise, or for permission.

Regarding the passage "Performing actions here indeed" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2), another distinction is stated: although by the force of the context the word "performing" is connected specifically with the knower (*vidvān*), nevertheless, this permission for action should be understood as being for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*).
For it will be stated [later]: "Action does not cling to the man" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2).
This is what is meant: [the Self is not affected by action].
For it will be stated that even for a wise person performing action throughout his entire life, the action does not lead to defilement due to the power of knowledge (*vidyā*).
This is what is meant:
even while a wise person performs action throughout his life, the action does not cling to him because of the efficacy of knowledge; thus, knowledge is being praised. 14.
"And by their own will, some.
Furthermore, some wise men, having directly realized the fruit of knowledge, rely upon that [knowledge] and reflect on the lack of purpose in offspring and other means for attaining further results.

Regarding "by their own will," there is a Śruti passage of the Vājasaneyins: "Indeed, the ancient wise men did not desire offspring, [saying], 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self and this [world] are [attained]...'"

We have stated more than once that the fruit of knowledge is established in experience itself—as in the passage, "The world [is Brahman]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)—and does not belong to a later time like the fruit of ritual action.
For this reason as well, it is impossible to maintain either that knowledge is a subordinate part of ritual action, or that the scriptural declarations of its fruit are not true to reality. // 15 //
And [they teach] its destruction.

Furthermore, through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), they declare the destruction of the essential nature of the entire phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)—consisting of action, agent, fruit, and characteristics—which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and has karma as its cause: "When, indeed, for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what..."
[This is shown] by such passages as, "What should one see, and by what? What should one smell? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

However, if the attainment of eligibility for ritual action were to depend on the knowledge of the Self taught in the Vedāntas, it would follow that the very basis for eligibility for ritual action is destroyed.
Therefore, for this reason also, knowledge is independent. // 16 //

And because knowledge is heard of even among those whose vital energy is drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas*); for in the case of the stages of life (*āśrama*) characterized by the drawing upward of the vital energy, knowledge is indeed taught,
and it is not possible for that knowledge to be a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*).
Because of the absence of karma;
for they do not possess Vedic rituals such as the Agnihotra and so forth.
This might be the case.
As for the claim that "the stages of life characterized by the upward-directed vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) are not heard of in the Veda," that is also not the case;

for they are indeed understood from Vedic words, such as: "There are three branches of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1) and "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
"Those who dwell in the forest, possessing austerity and faith" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11);
"Desiring this world alone, mendicants go forth from home" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22);
"One should go forth into the life of a mendicant directly from the stage of studentship" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).

In such passages as these, the state of being a perpetual celibate (ūrdhvaretas) for those who have entered or not entered the householder's life, and for those who have discharged or not discharged the three debts, is well-established in Śruti and Smṛti.
Therefore, knowledge is independent [of ritual action]. // 17 //
2. The Section on Reference (Parāmarśādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 18–20.

Jaimini [holds that there is] a reference [to the householder's life], because it is not an injunction; for [the scripture] censures it. (BBs 3.4.18) "There are three branches of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).

These and other words cited for the purpose of establishing the existence of the stages of life (*āśrama*) for those whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) are not capable of proving that [existence].
For the teacher Jaimini considers these words to be a mere reference (*parāmarśa*) to the other stages of life, not an injunction (*vidhi*).
Why? Because none of the indicators of an injunction, such as the verbal suffixes of the imperative and so forth, are present here.
Moreover, in each of these cases, a different meaning is observed.

Regarding the passage "There are three aggregates of dharma": first, sacrifice, study, and charity; second, austerity alone; third, a student who dwells in the teacher's house for his entire life, exhausting himself completely in the teacher's house—all these [attain] worlds of merit.

Having proclaimed, preceded by such a reference, that the stages of life (āśramas) yield non-eternal fruits, the state of being established in Brahman (brahmasaṃsthatā) is praised as having eternal fruit: "One who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).
Now, it may be argued that even in the case of the reference, the stages of life are indeed understood.
It is true that they are understood;
however, their establishment is through tradition and custom, not through direct Vedic revelation.
Therefore, in the event of a conflict with direct Vedic revelation, they will be disregarded.
Or [the term "renunciation"] refers to a domain not [yet] authorized.
But is it not the case that even the householder's life is mentioned together with those of perpetual chastity, as in: "Sacrifice, study, and giving—this is the first"?
True, it is so; nevertheless, because the rites such as the *agnihotra* are prescribed specifically for the householder, their existence is indeed well-established by the sacred scriptures (*śruti*).

Therefore, this reference is solely for the purpose of praise and not for the purpose of an injunction. Moreover, direct Vedic revelation indeed excludes the other stages of life: "He who lets the sacred fire go out is a slayer of the heroes of the gods," and "Having brought dear wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.11.1).
"There is no world for one who has no son"—thus all animals know;
likewise: "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1), and "Those who in the forest worship austerity and faith" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11).
And thus, this is an instruction regarding the path of the gods (*devayāna*), not an instruction regarding other stages of life (*āśrama*); moreover,
the mention of other stages of life in passages such as "Austerity itself is the second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1) is ambiguous.
Likewise, [the passage] "Thus, desiring this very world, mendicants go forth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) is a praise of the world, not an injunction for the life of a wandering mendicant.
But is it not the case that among the Jābālas there is this clear and direct injunction for mendicancy: "One should go forth from the stage of studentship itself"?
This is true;
however, it should be understood that this inquiry is conducted without regard for this scriptural passage. // 18 //
Bādarāyaṇa holds that it is to be performed, because of the scriptural statement of equality.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers the other stage of life to be mandatory,
on account of its being heard in the Veda.

Since the Agnihotra and other such rites must necessarily be performed, he refutes the view that another stage of life (āśrama) is to be practiced by those not qualified for them because it would conflict with those rites; rather, he considers that another stage of life must be entered just like the householder's stage, even by one who does not desire it. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching of their equality.

For the scriptural reference to another stage of life (*āśrama*) is seen to be equal to that of the householder's state (*gārhasthya*), as in the passage beginning, "There are three branches of duty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).
Just as here the householder's state, which is enjoined by another scripture, is referred to, it must be understood that the other stages of life are likewise [referred to].

And this is just as there is a reference to the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* modes of wearing the sacred thread—both of which are already established by other scriptures—in a sentence whose purpose is to enjoin the *upavīta*.
Therefore, the status of being something to be practiced is equal for the other stage of life (āśrama) as it is for the householder's state.

Likewise, there is a syntactic coordination between the statement, "Desiring this very world, mendicants go forth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), and the practices such as the recitation of the Vedas.
And regarding the passage, "Those who here in this world worship faith as austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1),
this refers to the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
As for what was stated, "Austerity itself is the second [path]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3.1).
If it is argued that the mention of other stages of life (*āśrama*) in such passages is doubtful,
this is not a fault,
because there exists a means for certain determination.

For it is declared that "there are three divisions of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1); and since numerous duties such as sacrifices exist with distinct origins, they cannot be subsumed under the threefold division of stages of life (āśrama) elsewhere.

In that context, one division of dharma is specified as the householder's stage of life, characterized by sacrifices and so forth; another is clearly indicated as the stage of the student (*brahmacārin*); and there is also "austerity" (*tapas*). What other division of dharma could be accepted [as such] than the stage of life in which austerity is predominant? [As it is said: "And those who dwell in the forest... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).

Thus, from the mark of the forest-dweller and from faith and austerity, there is the undertaking of the [forest] stage of life (āśrama). Therefore, even in the context of the "comprehensive reference" (parāmarśa), another stage of life is to be practiced. // 19 //
Or it is an injunction, like the rule regarding the carrying [of the firewood].
This is not a mere reference to another stage of life (*āśrama*), but is indeed an injunction.

[Objection: But if it is accepted as an injunction, the perception of syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) would be contradicted; yet here syntactical unity is clearly perceived, in that "the three divisions of dharma have the worlds of merit as their fruit, while being established in Brahman has immortality as its fruit."
This is true; however,

even though there is the perception of a single syntactical unity, one must nevertheless accept that it is an injunction (*vidhi*), because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*) and because no other injunction is observed.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to construe a single syntactical unity by assuming it to be a figurative statement (guṇavāda) when there is a clear cognition of a different stage of life (āśrama), just as in the case of "carrying" (dhāraṇa).

For example, in the passage, "He should run along while holding the fuel-stick below; for he holds it above for the gods," even though a single syntactical unity is perceived through the act of carrying which is not contradictory, the "holding above" is indeed enjoined because it is something previously unknown (apūrva).

And so it has been stated in the *Śeṣalakṣaṇa*: "But there is an injunction regarding the wearing [of the sacred thread], because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatvāt*). Likewise here too, the scriptural mention of the stages of life (*āśrama*) is to be understood as an injunction.

Even if this were merely a reference (*parāmarśa*) to other stages of life, nevertheless, being firmly established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) must necessarily be accepted as an injunction, by virtue of its power of praise (*saṃstava*).

And it must be discerned whether that [state of being "established in Brahman"] belongs to anyone among the four stages of life (*āśrama*), or to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) alone. If, when the stages of life beginning with the student (*brahmacārin*) are being referred to, the wandering mendicant is also included therein, then— since there is no distinction in the fact that all four stages of life have been referred to, and since it is impossible for one not belonging to any stage of life to be so established— anyone at all among the four stages of life will be "established in Brahman."

If, however, he is not included [among those previously mentioned], then, as the only one remaining, the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) alone will be established as "one who is grounded in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha).
In that regard, some maintain that the wandering mendicant is also included by the word "austerity" (tapas), which refers to the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa).
That too has already been addressed.
For it is not the case that, when a [distinct] path exists, the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) is included by means of the qualification "forest-dweller" (vānaprastha).

Just as here the student (brahmacārin) and the householder (gṛhamedhin) are each qualified by their own respective qualifications in a general sense, so too is it logical that the mendicant (bhikṣu) and the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) are likewise [distinguished].
Furthermore, austerity (tapas) is the unique duty of forest-dwellers, because their practice primarily consists of physical mortification.
For the word *tapas* (austerity) is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in that context [of the forest-dweller];
however, the duty of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), characterized by the restraint of the senses and so forth, is not at all denoted by the word *tapas*.
Furthermore, it is improper to refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*), which are well-known to be four, as being three.
Moreover, there is a designation of distinction here: "These three partake of the worlds of merit; one partakes of immortality.
And such a designation of distinction is only appropriate when there is actual difference.
For it is not said, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, but another among them is highly intelligent."
However, it is indeed said that Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, whereas Viṣṇumitra is highly intelligent.
Therefore, while the first three stages of life (āśrama) share in the worlds of merit, the remaining one—the wandering mendicant alone—shares in immortality.
But how can the term *brahmasaṃstha* (established in Brahman), which applies through its etymological connection (*yoga*) to everyone, be restricted to the wandering mendicant alone?

And if one were to accept [the word *brahmasaṃstha*] in its conventional sense, it would follow that immortality is attained merely by belonging to an āśrama, which would result in the uselessness of knowledge (*jñāna*).

To this it is replied: the term "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*) indeed denotes being grounded in Brahman—characterized by the completion [of all duties] within Brahman and the absence of any other activity.
And that [state] is not possible for those belonging to the three [lower] āśramas.

Because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the non-performance of duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (*āśrama*), whereas for the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), since he has renounced all actions, no transgression caused by non-performance can possibly arise. Furthermore, his specific duties such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*) serve to strengthen his state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*); they do not contradict it.

For his duty, augmented by tranquility, self-control, and so forth, consists precisely in being devoted to Brahman, as well as the sacrifices and other rites prescribed for his own stage of life (*āśrama*), whereas for others it consists of those [rites]. Furthermore, upon the transgression of that [duty], he incurs sin; and thus it is said: "Renunciation is Brahman; for Brahman is supreme, and the supreme is indeed Brahman. These other austerities are indeed inferior; renunciation alone surpasses them" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 78).

The scriptural texts (śruti) such as, "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.6; Nārāyaṇa 1.2.3; Kaivalya 3), and the traditional codes (smṛti) such as, "With their intellects fixed on That, with That as their Self, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal" (Gītā 5.17).
These and other such passages demonstrate the absence of ritual action for one who is established in Brahman.
Therefore, the objection that knowledge would become useless because the wandering mendicant attains immortality through the mere state of his stage of life (*āśrama*) does not apply here either.

Thus, even by way of this reference (*parāmarśa*), the state of being a wandering mendicant is indeed obtained as characterized by being established in Brahman, while the other stages of life remain [as subordinate].
This inquiry was undertaken by the venerable teacher without even taking into account the Jābāla-śruti, which prescribes other stages of life (*āśrama*).
However, there indeed exists a direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) regarding other stages of life:

"Having completed the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce."
"Or otherwise, one may renounce from the state of studentship itself, or from the house, or from the forest" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).
Nor can it be said that this scriptural statement refers only to those who have not been initiated [for Vedic study],
because the text is heard without such a distinction.

Furthermore, because they are mentioned separately as those who are not qualified [for renunciation]—as in the passage beginning, "Now, whether he be one who observes vows or one who does not, whether he be a Snātaka or one who is not a Snātaka, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4)—and because wandering mendicancy is an ancillary part of the ripening of the gift of Brahman, it does not concern those who are unqualified.

This is shown by the text: "Then the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, without possessions, pure, non-malevolent, subsisting on alms, becomes one with Brahman" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 5).

Therefore, the stages of life for those of perpetual chastity are established; and it is established that among those of perpetual chastity, knowledge possesses independence because of its being directly perceived. // 20 //
The Section Concerning Mere Praise. Sūtras 21–22:
"If it be argued that it is mere praise because of the mention [of other things], we say no, because of its being something new (apūrva).
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.3: "This very udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth."

Regarding such scriptural passages as, "Thus, fire is the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1), "This world indeed is this piled fire-altar; this very [world] is the Uktha, and this earth itself is [the Uktha]," there arises a doubt: do these serve the purpose of praising the Udgītha and so forth, or do they serve the purpose of enjoining meditations? In this doubt, it is appropriate to hold that they serve the purpose of praise.
If it is argued that this is because [the texts] are heard in connection with the constituent parts of ritual action, such as the *udgītha*,
just as the passage "This earth is indeed the *juhū* ladle, the sun is the tortoise, and heaven is the *āhavanīya* fire" is for the purpose of praising the *juhū* and other implements—
[the author] says: No.

It is not appropriate that the purpose of these scriptural passages (*śruti*) is mere praise, because they would then lack *apūrva* (novelty). For when they serve the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), a novel matter is enjoined; however, if they served the purpose of praise, they would be entirely redundant. Indeed, it has been stated in the passage, "But because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, they exist for the sake of praising the injunctions," that praise is useful only when it functions as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of an injunctive word.

However, for the *udgītha* and other elements enjoined in one location, this mention in another location—failing to function as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)—would be entirely purposeless.
But [the passage] beginning with "This indeed is the *juhū*" is recited in close proximity to an injunction; thus there is a difference.
Therefore, scriptural passages of this kind have only the purpose of enjoining. // 21 //
And because of words denoting action:
"One should meditate on the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1); "One should meditate on the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1).

Furthermore, clearly injunctive words such as "One should know: 'I am the hymn'" (*aham uktham asmi iti vidyāt*) are heard [in the texts], and these would be contradicted if their purpose were merely for the sake of praise.

Accordingly, there is a traditional rule (smaraṇa) among those who know the principles of logic: "One should do (*kuryāt*), it should be done (*kriyeta*), it ought to be done (*kartavyam*), it may be (*syāt*), and the fifth is 'it would be' (*bhavet*); this is the fixed definition of an injunction (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*) throughout all the Vedas. Thinking that an injunction consists in the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, they remember it in this way.

And in each section, the fruits [of knowledge] are proclaimed: "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7); "For he alone rules over the singing of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.9); "The worlds, both ascending and returning, become available to him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3), and so forth.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the scriptural passages concerning the *udgītha* and so forth are intended to enjoin meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
4. The Section on the Pāriplava (Sūtras 23–24).
If it be argued that [the stories] are for the purpose of the Pāriplava, we say no, because of their being specified.
BBs 3.4.23: "Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.1).

Regarding the narratives recorded in the Vedānta texts, such as "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, approached the beloved abode of Indra" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1) and "Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a liberal giver, a provider of much food, and a host of many guests" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.1), a doubt arises: are these intended for the performance of the *pāriplava* recitations, or are they intended for the comprehension of the proximate meditations (*vidyā*)?
These scriptural narratives have a wandering meaning,
because they are common to all narratives and because the application of narrative is enjoined for the purpose of diversion.
And if it is argued that, consequently, the Upanishads (Vedāntas) would not have knowledge as their primary purport because they are subsidiary to ritual application like mantras—
that is not so.
Why?
Because they are specified.
For, having introduced the subject with "One should relate the pāriplava," only certain specific narratives such as "King Manu Vaivasvata" and so forth are specified therein.

If it is argued that [the stories] are to be told because they share the common nature of being "narratives" (ākhyāna), then all narratives whatsoever would have to be included; consequently, this qualification would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, these scriptural mentions of narratives are not intended for the Pāriplava recitation.
And likewise, because they are connected as parts of a single sentence (ekavākyatā),
and since it would be improper for the narratives to have a merely incoherent purpose, it is logical that they serve to establish the knowledge presented in their proximity,
because they are connected as parts of a single sentence.
For instance, in those cases, syntactical unity with the proximate passages is observed, due to the utility of generating interest and the utility of facilitating comprehension.
In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, for example, syntactical unity with the knowledge [passage] is observed in such statements as, "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

In the case of Prātardana as well, there is the passage beginning with "I am the vital breath, the conscious self," and here too, in the case of Jānaśruti, there is the passage beginning with "Air, indeed, is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1). Just as the narratives found within the ritual scriptures, such as "He cut out his own omentum," serve the purpose of praising the proximate injunctions, so it is here.
Therefore, it does not have the purpose of mere narrative recitation. // 24 //
5. The Section on Fire, Fuel, and so forth. Sūtra 25:
For this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth.
[Brahmasūtra 3.4.25] "The human goal [is attained] from this, according to the scripture" (Brahmasūtra 3.4.1).

Although this [phrase] is separated [from the previous], it is referred to by the words "ata eva" (for this very reason), because knowledge is the cause of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Thus, since the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*), such as maintaining the sacred fires and gathering fuel, are not required for the accomplishment of the goal of knowledge itself, the author concludes the result of this very section—the *Sarvāpekṣā-adhikaraṇa* (Section on the Requirement of All)—with a desire to state further points. (Sūtras 26–27)

"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (BBs 3.4.26) Now this is considered: is there an absolute non-dependence of knowledge upon the works of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*), or is there some degree of dependence? In that regard, since it has already been established that the works of the stages of life—such as maintaining the sacred fires and kindling the fire—are not required for the accomplishment of knowledge’s own purpose, and thus an absolute non-dependence having been reached, this is stated: "And there is dependence on all."
Furthermore, knowledge requires all the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*); it is not entirely independent of them.
An objection is raised: "Is this statement not contradictory—to say that knowledge both requires the duties of the stages of life and does not require them?
We reply: No.
For once knowledge has arisen, it requires nothing else for the accomplishment of its fruit; however, it does require something else for its own arising.
Why? Because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and so forth.

For thus says the Śruti: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

Thus, he shows that sacrifices and the like are means for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, because they are connected with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), they are determined to be means for its production.
Moreover, when it says, "Now, what they call sacrifice," it praises celibacy by means of sacrifice and so forth; thus, the status of sacrifice and the others as means is also indicated.
And such scriptural passages as, "The goal which all the Vedas propound, which all austerities declare,

desiring which they lead the life of a student— this goal I tell you briefly" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15), indicate that the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) are means for attaining knowledge (vidyā-sādhanatva).
Smṛti also states: "The nature of the impurities is karma, while knowledge is the supreme goal;
when the impurities have been ripened by karmas, then knowledge arises," and so forth.
The phrase "like a horse" is an illustration of suitability (yogyatā).

And just as, by virtue of its specific capacity, a horse is not employed for pulling a plough but is employed for driving a chariot, so too the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) are not required for the accomplishment of the fruit through knowledge, but they are required for its origination. Thus ends [the discussion of] verse 26.

Nevertheless, one should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; for since there is an injunction for that [knowledge], those [qualities] must also necessarily be practiced as its constituent parts.

(BBs 3.4.27) If someone should think that it is not logical for sacrifices and the like to be means for the attainment of knowledge because there is no injunction for them—since scriptural passages such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) are of the nature of restatements intended to praise knowledge, and are not intended as injunctions for sacrifice and the like—[the response is as follows:]...

Thus, this knowledge would be of great value; for a seeker of knowledge, because tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth are enjoined as means to knowledge in the passage, "Therefore, one who knows thus, desiring [this], having become self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, sees the Self by means of the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23), and because that which is enjoined must necessarily be performed.

Now, one might object: even here, the expression "having become endowed with tranquility and so forth, he sees" is found as a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), not as an injunction (*vidhi*).
We say no;
for from the phrase "therefore" (tasmāt), which adopts the praise of the subject under discussion, an injunction is understood.
Indeed, the Mādhyandinas clearly read the injunction itself as "one should see" (paśyet).
Therefore, even when there is no requirement for sacrifices and the like, tranquility (śama) and other qualities must still be required;
however, sacrifices and the like must also be required, precisely because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifices and so forth.
Now, it was argued that in the passage "they desire to know through sacrifices and the like," no injunction is perceived.
True, this has been said; nevertheless, because the connection with "desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) is not previously established, an injunction is postulated.
For this connection of sacrifices and so forth with the desire to know is not something already obtained that could be merely restated.

Therefore, even in sentences where no injunction is explicitly heard—such as "Therefore, Pūṣan has the portion of ground flour, for he is toothless"—an injunction is postulated due to the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of the matter. Consequently, there arises the investigation: "The grinding for Pūṣan is to be understood as applying to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)," and so forth.
This was set forth in the first Tantra [the Brahmasūtras], as it has been stated: "Or rather, it is an injunction, like the wearing [of the sacred thread]" (Brahmasūtra 3.4.20).

Furthermore, in the Smṛtis such as the Bhagavad Gītā, it is elaborated that sacrifices and other rites performed by one seeking liberation without aiming for their fruits become means for attaining knowledge.

Therefore, all the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*), such as sacrifice and so forth, as well as tranquility, self-control, and the rest, according to one's stage of life, must be relied upon for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Even among these, it should be distinguished that because of their connection with knowledge—as indicated by the term "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvid*)—tranquility and the like are proximate means to knowledge; whereas because of their connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), sacrifice and the like are more remote. // 27 //
7. The Section on Permission for All Food (Sūtras 28–31).
*Sūtra 28:* "And there is permission for all food in case of danger to life, because that is seen [in scripture].
In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is heard among the Chandogas: "Verily, for one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1).

Likewise, among the Vājasaneyins [it is said]: "Verily, for him no food becomes eaten, nor does anything become un-eaten when received" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14). The meaning is that everything indeed becomes fit to be eaten by him. Regarding this permission to eat all food, there arises a doubt: is this enjoined as an auxiliary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*) like tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, or is it mentioned merely for the sake of praise? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an injunction.

For instance—an instruction serves to produce a specific modification of conduct; therefore, due to its proximity to the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā), this cessation of restrictive rules is taught as an ancillary part of that [knowledge].
But if this were so, would there not be a contradiction with the scriptural injunctions distinguishing between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit?
This is not a fault.
Because sublation is established through the relationship between the general and the particular;
just as the prohibition against harming living beings is sublated by the injunction for the immolation of sacrificial animals,
and just as [it is said], "He should not avoid anything— that is his vow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.2).

By this statement regarding the Vāmadevya-vidyā, which permits the consumption of all food, the scriptural injunction concerning the distinction between those who may be approached and those who may not—which has a general scope—is set aside.

Likewise, by this statement regarding the Prāṇa-vidyā, which permits the eating of all food, the scriptural injunction concerning the distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten is set aside.
This being the position reached, we reply: this is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all food.

For no injunctive word is perceived here, since the statement "Indeed, for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1) is a mere description of an existing state.
Nor can an injunction be assumed merely out of a desire for it to produce a specific kind of activity, even in the absence of any perception of an injunction.
Moreover, having stated that "the food of the vital breath (prāṇa) extends down to dogs," it is further said: "for one who knows this, there is nothing that is not food.
Now, it is not possible for a human body to consume food as far as dogs;
however, it is indeed possible to contemplate that "all this is the food of the vital breath."

Therefore, this explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of food as vital breath (prāṇa), and it is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all kinds of food.
This he shows by stating: "And the permission for all food [is valid] only when life is at stake.
What is meant is this: only when life is at stake—that is, in the most extreme distress—is every kind of food permitted to be eaten; for such is seen in the scriptural texts.

For instance, scripture shows the sage Cākrāyaṇa engaging in the eating of forbidden food during a state of extreme distress in this Brāhmaṇa passage: "When the Kurus were struck by hail" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.1).
It is said that the sage Cākrāyaṇa, having fallen into calamity, ate some half-eaten kulmāṣa beans from a wealthy man.

However, he declined that [water] as a drink because of the fault of being leavings; and he stated the reason for this, saying: "I would not have lived without eating these," and "Water was my desire. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.4)
Furthermore, on the following day, Piṅga ate those very same stale kulmāṣa grains that were the leavings of himself and others.

From this scriptural passage, which shows the eating of such leavings and stale food, the profound intention of the Śruti is perceived: that in the event of a life-threatening emergency, even what is normally unfit to be eaten may be consumed for the sake of sustaining life;
however, in a state of health, it must not be done even by one possessed of knowledge. This is understood from the rejection of the drinking of water [as a permissible alternative].
Therefore, the passage beginning with "For indeed, for one who knows thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1) is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

And because there is no contradiction: if this were so, then the scriptural injunction regarding the distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten—such as "when food is pure, the being (sattva) becomes pure"—would remain uncontradicted. (29)

Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Furthermore, even the eating of all kinds of food in times of distress is prescribed for both the knower and the ignorant without distinction: 'He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.'"

Likewise, the avoidance of liquor is recorded in the Smṛti texts: "A Brāhmaṇa must always [avoid] liquor," "They should pour hot [liquor] into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa who drinks surā," and "Those who drink surā become worms because of eating what is unfit to be eaten. // 30 //

FN: "Hot" means excessively heated. And the sound [of the word *surā*] occurs here in the sense of not acting according to one's desire (akāmakāra). Furthermore, the sound of the word *surā* is heard in the *Kaṭhaka Saṃhitā* as a prohibition of food, intended for the cessation of acting according to one's desire: "Therefore, one should not drink *surā* from the mouth of a Brahmin. (BBs 3,4.31)
Thus, the statement "Indeed, for one who knows thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1) also becomes more appropriately explained as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Therefore, such passages of this kind are explanatory eulogies and not injunctions (vidhi). // 31 //
8. The Section on the Duties of the Āśramas. Sūtra 32–36:
"And because they are enjoined, the duties of the āśramas also [must be performed]. (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.32). "And there is a need for all [these works]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26).
Thus, in this passage, it has been established that the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) are means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*).

Now, however, it is considered whether these duties must be performed even by one who does not desire liberation (*amumukṣu*), who is devoted solely to his stage of life and does not seek knowledge; or whether they need not be.
In this regard, [the scripture says]: "The Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the recitation of the Vedas" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22).

Since the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) have been prescribed as means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*) by such passages, they must be performed regularly even by one who does not desire knowledge but desires some other fruit.
Now, if they are to be performed even by him, then they cannot be means for attaining knowledge, because of the contradiction between being both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*anitya*).

To this prima facie view, the author of the Sūtras replies: "The obligatory rites must indeed be performed even by one who abides merely in a stage of life and does not seek liberation, because they are enjoined by such texts as, 'As long as one lives, he offers the Agnihotra.'"
For there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a statement. // 32 //
Now, regarding the objection that this being so, these [works] would not be means for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*), the author reads the following reply:
"And by way of being auxiliaries" (BS 3.4.33).

These [works] would be auxiliaries to knowledge precisely because they are enjoined as such in passages such as, "Brahmins seek to know this very [Self] through the recitation of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
As it has been said: "And there is need for all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26).

Nor should this statement regarding the works of the stages of life (āśrama-karman) acting as auxiliaries to knowledge be understood as referring to the fruit of knowledge—like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—because knowledge is not characterized by being an injunction (*avidhilakṣaṇatvāt*).
And because the fruit of knowledge is not something to be accomplished [by means].
For a means characterized by injunction, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, requires another auxiliary means due to the desire to accomplish the fruit of heaven; knowledge is not like that.
And so it has been said: "For this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of the fire and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.25).
Therefore, the expression "being a cooperative cause" applies to these [factors] only insofar as they are means for production.
Nor should one suspect here a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, because even though the action is non-different, the conjunctions are distinct.

For the one eternal connection, fashioned by such scriptural statements as "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*), does not have the fruit of knowledge as its result; however, the other non-eternal connection, fashioned by such scriptural statements as "This very [Self] by the recitation of the Vedas" (*tametam vedānuvacanena*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), has the fruit of knowledge as its result.

Just as even for a single instance of being made of khadira wood, there is service to the sacrifice through its connection with something permanent, and service to the person through its connection with something impermanent, so it is in this case as well. // 33 //
"In every way, those very same [rites] because of the twofold indication" (BBs 3.4.34).

In every way—both in the view that they are duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) and in the view that they are auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*)—those very same duties such as the *agnihotra* and so forth are to be performed.
By emphasizing "those very same," what does the Teacher exclude?
We say that there is no difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*).

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice where it is said, "For a month he offers the *Agnihotra*," a distinct ritual action is taught there from the obligatory (*nitya*) *Agnihotra*, such is not the case here; there is no difference in the ritual action.
Why? Because of the presence of both types of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
This is due to both the indicative mark of Śruti and the indicative mark of Smṛti.

First, regarding the indicative mark of Śruti: the passage, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), enjoins sacrifices and other rites—which already exist as established entities—toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*); it does not, like the injunction "he offers oblations," produce a previously non-existent form of these rites.

The indicative mark of Smṛti as well— namely, "He who performs the obligatory work without depending on the fruit of action" (6.1)— shows that only one who has understood what is to be done performs action for the sake of the arising of knowledge.

Furthermore, the well-known designation of Vedic rites as "purifications" (*saṃskāra*), as in the passage beginning "For whom these forty-eight purifications exist," occurs in Smṛti with the intention that knowledge arises for one who has been purified by them.
Therefore, this determination of non-difference is correct. // 34 //
And it demonstrates non-overpowering.

This observation of a sign serves as a corroboration of the very fact of being a cooperative cause; the Śruti demonstrates that non-overpowering through such passages as, "For this Self does not perish, which one finds through celibacy" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3), regarding one who is endowed with the means such as celibacy and so forth, [and is thus] not overwhelmed by afflictions such as passion.
Therefore, it is certain that sacrifices and other duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) are both [independent] and cooperative factors for knowledge. // 35 //
9. The case of Vidura and others. Sūtras 36–39:

*antarā cāpi tu taddṛṣṭeḥ* (BBs 3.4.36). Regarding those such as Vidura, who were devoid of the perfection of wealth and other requirements, and who occupied an intermediate position by lacking formal entry into any of the stages of life (*āśrama*), there arises a doubt: do they possess qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*) or not? The prima facie view is that they do not.
This much has been established:

that because it is determined that the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) are the cause of knowledge, and because these [householders] lack such duties, they are not entitled [to knowledge].
To this prima facie view, the author says: "But even one who exists in the interval as a non-ascetic (*anāśramin*) is qualified for knowledge."
Why? Because of the observation of that [state];
for we find scriptural testimony regarding the status of Brahman even in the case of such individuals as Raikva, Vācaknavī, and others. (36)
Moreover, it is recorded in tradition:

in the Itihāsas, it is remembered that Saṃvarta and others attained the status of great yogis through practices such as naked wandering, even though they disregarded the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama). // 37 //
Now, it may be asked: "Surely this indicative mark consisting of the observation of Śruti and Smṛti has been set forth; what then is the actual means of attainment? This is now stated:
"And there is the favoring by specific [means].

(BBs 3.4.38) Even for those such as the widowers and others, the favoring of knowledge is possible through specific dharmas—such as recitation, fasting, and the propitiation of deities—which are not prohibited and are connected to human beings in general.
And so the Smṛti says: "A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.

Whether he performs other duties or not, one who possesses the mantra is called a Brāhmaṇa. This shows that even those for whom the duties of the [specific] stages of life (āśrama) are impossible have the qualification for recitation.
Furthermore, the assistance toward knowledge is indeed possible even through the duties of the stages of life performed in previous births.
And thus the Smṛti says: "One who has attained perfection through many births then goes to the supreme goal" (Gītā 6.45).
This shows that knowledge favors even specific latent impressions (saṃskāra-viśeṣa) accumulated in other births.
Furthermore, since knowledge has a perceptible result, it qualifies one for hearing [the scriptures] and other practices by the mere absence of prohibitions.
Therefore, the eligibility of even those such as Vidhura is not contradicted. // 38 //

But the other is superior, both because of the scriptural indication and because of its intermediate position. Therefore, living in the other [stages of life] is a superior means for attaining knowledge,
because it is supported by both Śruti and Smṛti.

And because of the indicative mark of the Śruti: "By that [path] goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of meritorious deeds, and those who possess splendor" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1); and because of the indicative mark of the Smṛti: "A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama even for a single day; having remained without an āśrama for a year, he should perform one Kṛcchra penance. // 39 //
10. The Section Concerning Those Who Have Entered [an Order] (Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 40:

But for one who has entered [an order], there is no non-becoming of that [state], according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of the characteristics of that [other state].
It has been established that there are stages of life (āśrama) for those of perpetual chastity (ūrdhvaretas).
However, regarding one who has attained that state, there arises the doubt as to whether there is a falling away from it or not.

One might argue that even after attaining it, there could be a falling away—either through the desire to perform former ritual acts or by the power of passion and the like—since there is no specific distinction [in the texts].

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: But for one who has become that—that is, for one who has entered the state of an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward)—there can be no becoming other than that; there can be no falling away from that state under any circumstances whatsoever.
Why? Because of restrictive rules, the absence [of such rules], and the nature [of the texts].
To explain: "Wearing himself out completely in the family of his teacher" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1);

"He should go to the forest—this is the word; from there he should not return again—this is the secret doctrine" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.10.1); and "Permitted by his teacher, [he should enter] one of the four stages of life... (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).
And such rules as "he should practice according to his knowledge until the liberation of the body" demonstrate that there is no power [to prevent] falling away; likewise,
there are texts such as "having completed the student life, one should become a householder" (Jābāla 4) and "one may renounce even from the student life itself" (Jābāla 4).
Thus, statements of this kind and others of a similar nature regarding ascent (*āroha*) are found in the scriptures, but there are no such statements regarding descent (*pratyavaroha*).
Nor do the learned (*śiṣṭa*) observe such practices.

As for the claim that one descends out of a desire to perform the duties of a previous stage of life, that is incorrect; for it has been said: "One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed" (Gītā 3.35).
This is because of such a traditional authority (smṛti) and because of logic as well.
For that which is prescribed for someone is his duty (dharma), but not that which can merely be performed by him.
Because dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*),
there is no falling away from it due to the influence of passion and the like,
since the restrictive teaching (*niyama-śāstra*) possesses superior authority.
By the word "also" in the phrase "of Jaimini also," [the author] teaches the agreement between Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa on this point for the sake of strengthening the conviction. // 40 //

11. The Section on Entitlement (Adhikārādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 41–42: "Nor even that which pertains to one holding an office [is applicable], because of the inference of a fall [from his status] and because of the impossibility of that [status].

(BBs 3.4.41) If a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) should, through negligence, break his vow of chastity, would the expiation prescribed by the rule, "One who has broken his vow of chastity shall sacrifice a donkey dedicated to Nirṛti," apply to him, or not?
It is said: "No.

Even that expiation which was determined in the section on eligibility—namely, "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity [is prescribed], because, as in that case, the time for the consecration of the fires has not yet arrived" (Jaimini Sūtra 6.8.21)—that too cannot apply to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).

What is the reason? Because of the traditional teaching that a downfall is irredeemable: "I see no expiation by which one who has fallen from the perpetual vow (*naiṣṭhika-dharma*) after having ascended to it might be purified; he is a self-destroyer. Since a remedy is impossible for him, just as it is for one whose head has been severed, such expiation is not applicable.
However, for the student (*upakurvāṇa*), since there is no such traditional teaching regarding a downfall, that expiation is indeed possible. (41)

However, some [teachers] maintain that even a transgression occurring after [initiation] is a minor offense (*upapātaka*), like eating forbidden food; this has been stated [in the *Brahmasūtra* 3.4.42].
Furthermore, some teachers consider this to be merely a minor offense (*upapātaka*).

This is because if the lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika*) should violate his vow of chastity (*brahmacarya*) with anyone other than the wife of his guru and so forth, that does not constitute a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), since it is not enumerated among the mortal sins such as violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*).

Therefore, because there is no difference in their status as celibates (*brahmacārin*) and no difference in their having broken their vow (*avakīrṇin*), they maintain that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) exists for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) just as it does for the temporary student;
this is like the case of eating food.
Just as for a celibate student, the consumption of honey or meat constitutes a breach of the vow and requires a rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), so it is here.

For those who maintain that there is no expiation, no scriptural basis is found. However, for those who maintain that there is expiation, the basis is the specific scriptural statement: "A student who has broken his vow of chastity [shall sacrifice a donkey].
Therefore, the existence of expiation is more reasonable.

This has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "There would be an equal conflict [of authorities]" (*Jaiminisūtra* 1.3.8), and "Or rather, that which is established in the scripture [is authoritative], because it is based on that" (*Jaiminisūtra* 1.3.9).

Furthermore, the traditional rule regarding the absence of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) in such cases is explained as being intended to generate a sense of great effort [toward following the scriptural injunction].

In the same way, for a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), if there is a breach of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the forest-dweller should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and then increase the great thicket (*mahākakṣa*). A mendicant, like a forest-dweller—with the exception of the *soma* and the *liṅga*—should also undergo the purificatory rites prescribed by his own scriptures;
such traditional injunctions regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*) are to be followed accordingly. // 42 //
12. Exclusion from the Community. Sūtra 43:
"But they are excluded, for both reasons, according to Smṛti and custom.

(BBs 3.4.43) Whether the falling away of those who have mastered their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) from their respective stages of life (*svaśrama*) constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or a minor offense (*upapātaka*), in either case, they must be excluded by the learned (*śiṣṭas*).

This is because of such Smṛti texts expressing extreme condemnation, such as: "I see no expiation for one who, having ascended to the dharma of perpetual celibacy (naiṣṭhika), falls away again; that self-destroyer shall not be purified," and "Having touched a Brahmin who has fallen from the state he had ascended, or one who has been expelled from the [Vedic] circle, or one who has hanged himself, or one bitten by a worm, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
And because of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*);
for the learned do not perform sacrifices, Vedic study, marriage, and so forth together with them. // 43 //
13. The Section on the Master (Svāmy-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 44–46.
"Because the fruit is declared for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya" (BBs 3.4.44). There is a doubt regarding the meditations on the subordinate members [of the sacrifice].

Are these the duties of the sacrificer or the duties of the officiating priests? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are the duties of the sacrificer. Why? Because of the mention of the fruit [accruing to him].

For the fruit is indeed heard [in scripture]: "Rain falls for him and he causes rain to fall, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the rain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.3.2), and so forth. And that fruit rightly belongs to the master [of the sacrifice], because he is the one authorized in the performance of the rite along with its constituent parts.
Furthermore, because such matters fall within the scope of authorized duties, the fruit of these meditations is heard to accrue to the agent: "It rains for him who meditates on it," and so forth.
But is it not observed that even the officiating priest receives a fruit, as in: "Whatever desire he desires for himself, he procures by singing"? No; [that is not the case here].
Because that [agency] is expressly stated in scripture,
the teacher Ātreya maintains that the master alone possesses the status of agent in those meditations that yield fruit.
"Regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*), Auḍulomi [says]: for that [office] is hired for by him.
This is not so; the meditations are the duties of the master.
These must be the duties of the officiating priest—this is what the teacher Auḍulomi thinks.
What is the reason?
For the sacrificer hires the officiating priests for that ritual action together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga-karman*);
and since the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth fall within the performance of that ritual, they are governed by the same qualification as the primary rite.
Therefore, this must be accomplished by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), just like the restrictive rule regarding the *godohana* vessel and so forth.
And thus, the text "Baka Dālbhya knew it; he became the Udgātṛ priest for the residents of Naimiṣa" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.13) shows that the knowledge has the Udgātṛ as its agent.

As for what was stated—that the fruit is heard to reside in the agent—this is not a fault; because the officiating priests exist for the sake of another, and since there is no other scriptural statement, a connection with the fruit is logically untenable for them. // 45 //
And because of scripture:

"Whatever blessing the officiating priests invoke during the sacrifice, they invoke it for the patron alone," so he said. Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say: "What desire of yours shall I sing forth?
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.8–9).
This shows that the fruit of the consciousness produced by the agent who has tasted that [juice] accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Therefore, it is established that the meditations on the constituent parts (*aṅga-upāsanā*) are the work of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). // 46 //

14. The Section on the Injunction of Another Auxiliary Means (Sahakāryantaravidhyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 47–49: "There is an injunction of another auxiliary means; it is the third [stage] for one who possesses that [the previous two], as in the case of the injunctions and so forth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1):

"Therefore, having attained proficiency in sacred knowledge from Brahman, one should remain in a state of childlike simplicity; having attained both childlike simplicity and proficiency in sacred knowledge, one becomes a sage; and having attained both the state of non-sagehood and the state of sagehood, one then becomes a true Brāhmaṇa. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1)

Thus it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is the state of being a muni (mauna) enjoined or not? For now, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is not enjoined.

Because the injunction is concluded right there with the words "one should remain in childhood," and because no injunctive case-ending is perceived in the phrase "then he is a sage" (*atha muniḥ*), it is therefore appropriate that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If it is asked, "From what source is its attainment? [the answer follows].
Since the words *muni* and *paṇḍita* both signify knowledge, it follows that "having become disillusioned with scholarship" (*pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*) implies "becoming silent" (*mauna*).

Furthermore, in the passage "having become disillusioned with both non-silence and silence, one is then a Brāhmaṇa," the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is not enjoined as something new, because it has already been attained previously;
therefore, the phrase "then a Brāhmaṇa" is merely a statement of praise. By analogy, the same must apply to the phrase "then a sage" (*atha muniḥ*), as the two descriptions are parallel.
This being the case, we reply: "It is an injunction for another auxiliary.

Just as in the case of childhood (*bālya*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), an injunction must indeed be accepted for silence (*mauna*) as an auxiliary to knowledge, because it is something not previously established.
But was it not already understood by the very word "scholarship" that silence is included?
This is not a fault,
because the word *muni* signifies an excellence of knowledge (*jñānātiśaya*),
and because the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "a sage (*muni*) is so called because of reflection (*manana*)" is possible.
And because we see such usage as, "Among sages (*muni*) too, I am Vyāsa" (Gītā 10.37).

Now, it may be objected that the word *muni* is also heard in the sense of the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*), as in the passage: "The householder's state, the teacher's family, the state of silence (*mauna*), and forest-dwelling. This is not so.

Because deviation [from this rule] is observed in such cases as "Vālmīki, the bull among sages," and because the mention of the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*) there occurs by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) due to the proximity of the other stages of life— and since that highest stage has knowledge as its primary characteristic— therefore, this third stage called "munitude" (*mauna*), which consists of an excellence of knowledge, is prescribed in relation to childhood and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*).

As for the claim that the injunction terminates with childhood alone, nevertheless, because of its unprecedented nature (*apūrvatva*), the state of being a sage (*munitva*) is accepted as something to be enjoined in the words "one should be a sage" (*muniḥ syāt*).

Furthermore, because it is designated as something to be realized through personal experience (*nirvedanīyatva*), the state of being a sage is likewise accepted as an injunction, just like childhood and wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*).
This refers to one who possesses that [state], namely, a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) endowed with knowledge.

And how is it understood that renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) possess knowledge? Because of the context [of the passage]: "Having known the Self, rising above the desires for sons and so forth, they then lead the life of a mendicant. Now, one might object: "If they already possess knowledge, excellence [in practice] follows as a matter of course; what then is the purpose of the injunction for silence? To this he replies: "By way of an alternative" (*pakṣeṇa*).
This is what is meant:
in that case where [the fruit] is not attained due to the predominance of the perception of difference, this rule applies;
it is like the beginning of an injunction (*vidhyādivat*).

Just as in injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the collection of subsidiary elements such as the kindling of the fires is prescribed as auxiliary factors;
so too, in this statement concerning knowledge, which is not itself a primary ritual act, there is an injunction for silence. This is the meaning. // 47 //

Since the stage of life characterized by solitude (kaivalyāśrama), which is distinguished by [the stages of] childhood and so forth and is supported by scripture, exists, why is there a conclusion in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad with the householder, in the passage: "Having returned home, [he should live] in his family" (Chānd. 8.15.1)?
For by concluding [the discussion] in that way, it shows a preference for that [householder's state].
To this, he recites the following answer:
"But the summary [of the stages] is made with reference to the householder because of his complete state.
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of qualification;
it qualifies his "complete state" (kṛtsnabhāva).

For many duties of the stages of life (āśrama), such as sacrifices and the like, which involve great effort, are enjoined upon him as things to be performed; and other duties of the stages of life, such as non-violence and restraint of the senses, exist for him as far as possible.
Therefore, the concluding summary with reference to the householder is not contradictory. 48.
Because there is instruction regarding the others as well, just as for the vow of silence.

Just as the stages of life of the silent sage (*mauna*) and the householder (*gārhasthya*) are supported by Vedic scripture (*śrutimantau*), so too are the other two: the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the student residing in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*).

For the scriptural authority has been shown previously: "Austerity itself is the second; he who dwells in the teacher’s house practicing celibacy is the third" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1), and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no difference in the instruction regarding all four stages of life (āśrama), their practice is to be understood as being equal, whether by way of option or combination.

As for the phrase "of the others," it should be understood that the plural number refers to two stages of life, either with respect to the diversity of their modes of livelihood (vṛtti) or with respect to the diversity of those who perform them. // 49 //
15. The Section on Non-Manifestation. Sūtra 50:
"By not manifesting [himself], because of the connection" (BBs 3.4.50).
"Therefore, having discarded scholarship from that Brahman, one should remain in the state of a child" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).

Thus, *bālya* (childlikeness) is heard in scripture as something to be practiced. In this context, since the term *bālya*—derived from the sense of "the state or action of a child"—refers to the state of childhood, which is a specific stage of life, it is impossible to achieve that state or its desires; therefore, it refers either to the purity of disposition found within the conduct of a child, such as urinating and defecating wherever one happens to be, or to the non-development of the sensory organs (*aprarūḍhendriyatva*).

There arises a doubt as to whether "childlikeness" (*bālya*) might consist in being free from deceit, pride, and so forth. What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that it is more well-known in the world for "childlikeness" to mean acting, speaking, and eating according to one's whims, as well as voiding urine and excrement wherever one happens to be; therefore, it is appropriate to adopt that meaning. But surely, because it would entail faults such as falling from one's status, it is not right to resort to such arbitrary conduct. No.
"Because of the traditional authority of the words of a learned renunciant (saṃnyāsin), there is an absence of fault [in his actions], as in the case of animal sacrifice and the like.
This being the position reached, it is replied: No;
for there is no other possible interpretation of the statement.
For when another state denotable by the term "childhood" is available that is not contradictory [to the context], it is not reasonable to assume a sublation of other injunctions;
moreover, a subsidiary (aṅga) is prescribed for the sake of assisting the primary (pradhāna),
and here, for ascetics, the primary duty to be performed is the practice of knowledge.
Furthermore, if the entire conduct of a child were accepted [as the model], the practice of knowledge would not be possible.
Therefore, that which is intended here as "childhood" is an internal state characterized by the non-development of the senses and so forth.
Thus he says: "without manifesting."
One should be free from hypocrisy, pride, and the like, not proclaiming oneself on account of one's knowledge, learning, piety, or other such qualities.
Just as a child, because its senses have not yet fully developed, does not strive to reveal itself to others, so too should one act.
For in this way, the conformity with the primary purpose of this statement is logically established.
And so it has been said by the authors of the Smṛtis: "He whom no one knows—whether as existent or non-existent, as unlearned or learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved—that man is a Brāhmaṇa."

A wise person, relying on the hidden Dharma, should conduct himself with actions unknown to others; he should traverse the earth like one who is blind, like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is mute.
"Having unmanifest signs and unmanifest conduct," and so forth. // 50 //
16. The Section Concerning the Present Life (Aihikādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 51:
"Even that which pertains to the present life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what is not yet commenced, because that is seen.
(BBs 3.4.51) "And there is dependence on all [works], on account of the scriptural statement regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26)
From this point onward, the various means for the attainment of knowledge have been determined;
now it is considered whether that fruit, namely knowledge, when being accomplished, is accomplished in this very life or sometimes even in the next world.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
"In this very life" means:
for what reason?
Because knowledge is preceded by hearing [the teachings] and so forth.
Furthermore, no one engages in hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices with the intention, "May knowledge arise for me in the next world.
Rather, it is observed that people engage in these very practices with the intention that knowledge should arise in this very life.
Even sacrifices and the like produce knowledge only by way of hearing and so forth, because knowledge is produced by means of valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the birth of knowledge occurs only in this life.
This being the position reached, we reply: the birth of knowledge occurs in this life provided there is no obstruction to what has been undertaken.

This is what is meant: when no obstruction is placed upon the means for attaining knowledge already set in motion by some other karma whose fruition is imminent, then knowledge arises in this very life.
But when that obstruction is indeed created, then [the result occurs] "there.
Furthermore, the ripening of karma becomes manifest due to the convergence of place, time, and causal conditions.
It cannot be determined that the very same places, times, and causal conditions that bring about the ripening of one karma will necessarily do so for another as well.
For actions can have even contradictory results;
moreover, the scripture concludes merely by stating that "this is the fruit of this action," and does not specify the particularities of place, time, or causal conditions.
However, due to the specific power of the means employed, a certain person's supersensuous capacity manifests, while that of another remains bound by it.
Nor does the intention for knowledge arise without distinction [regarding its timing], because the intention—"May my knowledge arise either here or in the hereafter"—is unrestricted.
Even when knowledge arises through the means of hearing and so forth, it arises only in dependence upon the destruction of obstacles.
Thus, scripture demonstrates the difficulty of realizing the Self: "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many; though many hear him, they do not know him."
"The speaker of this is wonderful; the one who has obtained it is skillful; the knower of this is wonderful, being well-instructed by the skillful" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.7).

Furthermore, by stating that Vāmadeva attained the state of Brahman while still in the womb, [the scripture] demonstrates the arising of knowledge in one birth from means accumulated in another birth;
for no such means belonging to this life can possibly be conceived for one who is in the womb.

Furthermore, in the *Samṛti* [the Bhagavad Gītā], when Arjuna asked, "O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does one go to who has not attained perfection in yoga? (Gītā 6.36), the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva replied, "No doer of good, my dear, ever comes to a miserable end" (Gītā 6.40).

Having stated this, and further described his attainment of the worlds of merit and rebirth in a virtuous family, he immediately thereafter said: "There, he regains the mental disposition belonging to his former body" (Gītā 6.43).
By the passage beginning with this [Gītā 6.43] and ending with "Having attained perfection through many births, he thereafter reaches the supreme goal" (Gītā 6.45), the same point is demonstrated.
Therefore, it is established that the arising of knowledge—whether in this life or the next—depends upon the destruction of obstacles. // 51 //
17. The Section on the Non-Regularity of the Fruit of Liberation (Muktiphalādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 52:
"Thus, there is no such restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state [of Brahman] is determined; because that state is determined.

Just as for one seeking liberation who relies upon the means of knowledge, a specific determination regarding the fruit characterized by knowledge—namely, the distinction between its being realized in this life or the next—is observed based on the particular efficacy of those means.

Anticipating the objection that even regarding the characteristic of liberation there might be some specific determination based on excellence or deficiency, he says: "Thus, there is no fixed rule for the fruit of liberation.
Indeed, one should not suspect any such specific determination regarding the fruit of liberation.
Why? Because that state is determined to be uniform. For in all the Vedāntas, the state of liberation is determined to be of one and the same form;
indeed, the state of liberation is Brahman itself, and there can be no connection with multiple forms for Brahman.
Because it is determined to have a single nature, as seen in the passages: "It is neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8),
"This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), and "Where one sees nothing else" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
"Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11);
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6);
"Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

Furthermore, while the means of knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*), due to its own specific potency, may produce some excellence within the knowledge itself, it cannot produce any excellence in liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge.
For we have stated more than once that this [Self] is indeed unattainable through effort, being of an eternally accomplished nature, and is realized only through knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, no excellence consisting of increase or decrease is possible even in that knowledge, because what is deficient cannot be considered knowledge; for knowledge is necessarily excellent.
Therefore, any excellence in that [knowledge] could only consist in its arising after a long time or after a short time.
But in liberation, there is no possibility of any excellence whatsoever;
furthermore, because there is no difference in knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no restriction of difference in its fruit, unlike the case of the fruits of ritual actions (*karman*).
For there is no difference in the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation, as there is in the case of ritual actions.

But in the case of meditations with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*), such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2), since a distinction between them is established through the addition or subtraction of qualities, a fixed rule regarding the difference in their respective fruits is logical, just like the fruits of ritual actions (*karma*).
And there is a scriptural indication (*liṅga*) to this effect: "In whatever way they meditate upon him, that very thing they become."
It is not so in the case of the qualityless (nirguṇa) knowledge, because of the absence of qualities there.

And thus says the Smṛti: "For there is no further progress for anyone; it is only when a quality exists that they speak of inequality. The repetition of the words "tadavasthāvadhṛteḥ" (because of the determination of that state) indicates the completion of the chapter. // 52 //
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
